speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note that we are now down to 10-minute speeches. I believe that back-to-work legislation for Canada Post, which is being imposed on the House today with closure, goes beyond the Government's inability to honour its commitment. It goes beyond its total disregard for fairness and honesty. At stake here, what is actually being decided, is really a question of freedom. It is the breaking of a social contract.
What kind of a free country gives people the right to free collective bargaining and then takes it away if it does not like the consequences? Dictatorships do not allow the right to strike. Dictatorships throw union leaders and striking workers in jail, which is one of the provisions of this Bill. Are we now a dictatorship? Labour legislation is part of our social contract. The rules of the game are enshrined in our law. The workers at Canada Post followed all the rules and have ended up in a legal strike. They have the right to strike, as my colleague who spoke before me indicated.
But now the Government wants to step in arbitrarily and change the rules. I think we have seen from the speeches of the Minister and others that they want to impose management's demands on the workers. This is a blatant interference in the free collective bargaining process. We must ask ourselves why the Government is setting such a bad example in this Bill, an example that is imposed on a Crown corporation but certainly has very significant ramifications for other employers across the country.
Is this the kind of leadership the Government wants to provide for other large employers? Are contracts now to be settled by the use of scabs? I think it is just deplorable that this Government has condoned the practice of using scab labour by the Crown corporation that is under its jurisdiction.
October 15, 1987

Are contracts to be settled by back-to-work legislation, as has happened in this case and in others under the jurisdiction of this Government? If this Government is set in changing the rules of the game, then it is dangerously undermining the social contract. We know from history that social unrest may very well be the consequence right across the country. If this happens, social disintegration will be directly attributable to this Government.
The Government should be re-examining Canada Post policies and Canada Post management. It should be looking once again at the basic causes of this present dispute, basic causes which have been substantiated in speeches in this House, which are really based on the Government's policy of privatization.
The root of the problem lies with this Government's insistence on franchising postal services. This Government wants to run a public service like a private enterprise. We know full well, and I am sure that the unions who are concerned about their jobs and their workers as well as being concerned about the postal service know full well, that there are going to be very many negative impacts of franchising out. There will be impacts on jobs. Many jobs will be reduced from full-time jobs, with a living union wage, to part-time jobs at half the amount. Many of those jobs, I am sorry to say, will also be taken by women, many of whom are the sole support of their families.
Job loss will fall most heavily on women, children and families. There will be a particular impact on rural communities. Franchising out is not only bad for workers and has not only been the main cause of the dispute and the legislation that we are debating today, it is also very bad for consumers. I hope that the public out there who may be listening to our debate will consider it from their point of view as well. I would like to give a couple of examples.
Recently I had a letter from a constituent of mine who was expecting a parcel, a very important parcel, that he was to pick up. It was under a customs bond. He received the card, which we now receive, stating that he could not pick this up at the post office, he had to go to another place, in this case a small drugstore in the neighbourhood. So he started out to try to locate his parcel. He found, when he went to the small business, that a very valuable parcel, which had been clearly marked with a customs bond, could not be located. The clerk in the corner store was busy with other things and did not know what procedure was to be followed. Eventually, he himself looked around and found his very valuable parcel located on the floor in a very public area. This is a result of franchising out.
He told me that later on he tried to pick up another parcel. To add to his frustration he found that it was still en route. Between the Post Office and the notice coming to his house and going back to the Post Office and going from there to this small business that was now dealing with parcels, the procedure took several days. Apparently, the package had been
Postal Services Continuation
delivered to his home by the Post Office, then taken back when no one was at home. A notice card was sent out and then the parcel was delivered several blocks away to the pharmacy while the Post Office shelves remained empty and postal workers who are public employees were not given the right to handle such merchandise.
What kind of a foolish, impractical, inefficient and costly system is this? I would like to say to my friend from Calgary that if this is the kind of real improvement in postal services that she is advocating by supporting privatization, I do not know how she can talk about economic feasibility.
Postal services must be improved, we all agree with that. We are all completely frustrated with the time it takes the mail to be delivered. This is a problem of everyone. We do not want to victimize any particular part of the whole service. But I fail to see how franchising out will improve the service.
I would just like to quote an article by June Callwood in The Globe and Mail of a couple of days ago. She states:
Canada Post and the Canadian Government are co-operating to confound a strike over the issue of the Post Office's decision to reduce costs, by getting rid of unionized post offices and replacing them with outlets staffed by non-union people who will work for debased wages-
A village is a small place ... Some villages are home to fewer than 200 people, but home they are ... A child growing up in a village is known and tended to some degree by everyone who lives there-
All over the country-people describe the post office as the heart of the village-
It is doubtful, however, that the villages can survive the latest catastrophe, Canada Post's decision to abolish rural route deliveries.
Last November Canada Post announced it would cut back on both as part of its strategy to end the huge post office deficit by 1988. Of the 5,221 rural post offices across Canada, some 1,700 are slated for extinction and 3,500 others will be "transferred to the private sector''.
Mr. Speaker, 82 per cent of rural postmasters and their assistants are women. I talked not too long ago to members of Dignite Rurale, women from the Gaspe, who have started a movement to oppose this. They told me that closure of rural post offices means a drastic loss of jobs for women. Some 37 were lost last year alone in Saskatchewan by sub-contracting out at not even a wage but at 22 per cent of the sales intake. This means they figure that women and other workers will be earning only about $2,000 a year. In many cases this means that they are working in the store for six days a week. This is in a rural situation. Those particular workers have been under CPPA not under CUPW, but the same principle applies.
It is basic to the current strike that the government policy of privatization is what is the most prevalent cause of unrest. Of course CUPW workers do not wish to lose their jobs. Of course they want and should have the right to decently paid jobs. They have come to my office, and I expect to others, with suggestions for improvements to the postal service. They have presented a number of very positive recommendations, but they have not been given a chance. They oppose franchising

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
out, and so do we. It is bad for workers and consumers. It destroys one of our most important community institutions, particularly in rural communities.
In closing, I must say that I regret the action taken by the Government in imposing back-to-work legislation. I very much regret the policies of the Government which have been imposed upon Canada Post, which in turn has imposed them on its workers and which have contributed to such unrest in Canada.

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my obligation and duty as a Member of Parliament who believes in the right of working people to organize and bargain collectively, to speak out against Bill C-86. It is important for the Canadian people to understand what the Government has done first to the Post Office, then to postal workers, and finally to the entire bargaining process.
We have seen what the Government has done to the Post Office ever since it came to power, and we had the Nielsen Commission report. For 120 years the Post Office has been serving Canadians and providing a vital service. The Government has this fixation that instead of providing a service, the Post Office should be a money-making corporation. This has been driving the Government in its ideological fixation to attempt to make the Post Office a money-making corporation, never mind the impact upon Canadians who look to the Post Office for service, never mind the impact upon those Canadians who work at the Post Office.
We have seen the Government refuse to initiate new postal walks, so in effect we have two classes of service in Canada today. People who live in established communities continue to get door-to-door delivery. People who live in new suburbs or in smaller communities that have grown to a sufficient size for door-to-door delivery, do not receive door-to-door delivery. Instead there is the fiasco of the Government's supermailboxes. There is a threat to close down rural post offices that my colleague from Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) mentioned.
Now there is an attempt at franchising which means that the Government is going to be doing away with good union jobs and replacing them with a franchising-out situation that will depend upon low paid labour with no job security and no benefits.
The Government moved very quickly in the direction of provocation of the union when it advertised for strike-breakers. This is unheard of. I come from a community where there is a long tradition of honouring people who have fought and struggled for the rights of working men and women to have a decent wage and decent working conditions. I use the word "strike-breakers" instead of the word "scab", because to me the word "scab" has some pretty heavy connotations. In the community where I live people remember members of a family three and four generations down the line because that member scabbed. It is a very serious allegation.
I would like to share with Members part of the definition of a scab written by Jack London. It summarizes the manner in which many working people feel about someone who undercuts their attempts to better their working conditions. Jack London stated that a scab is a two-legged animal with a corkscrew soul, a water-logged brain, a combination backbone of jelly and glue. Where others have hearts he carries a tumour of rotten principles. When a scab walks down the street, men turn their backs and angels weep in heaven, and the devil shuts the gates of hell to keep him out. Esau sold his birthright for a meal of pottage. Judas Iscariot sold his Saviour for 30 pieces of silver, Benedict Arnold sold his country for a promise of a commission in the British army. The modern strike-breaker sells his birthright, his country, his wife, his children and his fellow man for an unfulfilled promise from his employer. Esau was a traitor to himself. Judas Iscariot was a traitor to his God. Benedict Arnold was a traitor to his country. A strikebreaker is a traitor to his God, his country, his wife, his family and himself.
That indicates the depth of feeling that union people have toward someone who undercuts their struggle. Yet, on the other hand, we know that in some situations people are desperate. They are desperate for a job and to put something on the table. They might not feel very good about strikebreaking, but they feel that they are driven to it.
The question that I wish to place before the House, and the question that the Canadian people should be asking, is, what type of employer pushes people to strike-break? What type of employer sets one group of workers against another? What type of employer uses one group of workers to undercut deliberately the standards of another group that has been bargaining collectively to better their situation? I must ask, what type of government will act as that type of employer? The answer for the Canadian people is that only a Tory Government would be prepared to do that. This is a scab Government.
Unfortunately, the men and women who are driven by desperation to act as strike-breakers get the name "scab" attached to them, a name they will carry to their graves, and a name that their children and grandchildren will sometimes have hurled at them. They receive the name of scab, while the members of the Government continue to call themselves honourable. There is something not quite fair about this.
When we look at the current strike, we must realize that it was deliberately provoked by the Government as part of its over-all strategy to destroy the Post Office as a service to the people of Canada. It did not care who paid the price. The major price is being loaded upon the workers. We saw the manner the Government did that with the letter carriers. Now the Government is doing it to the inside workers who are members of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers.
CUPW took a very moderate approach as it began this strike. Instead of having an all-out strike, it had rotating strikes in order that it would not have too serious an impact
October 15, 1987

1001 1
upon the Canadian public. The Government chose to escalate that. Here is a situation where the Government has deliberately provoked an all-out strike by introducing Bill C-86.
Some of the members of my Party have referred to this legislation as Draconian. Yesterday some members of the Conservative Party felt that perhaps we should not use the word "Draconian". I checked, and the word "Draconian" comes from Draco who was a 7th century B.C. Athenian lawmaker. The types of laws that he made were written in blood rather than ink. For even the most trivial offence^ people received the death penalty.	^
Draco is also the name of a lizard. I would like to suggest to Hon. Members that this legislation is Draconian in both meanings of the word; it is lizard-like, it crawls on its belly, it is cold-blooded, and is a relic from another age that should not be around in the 1980s. Certainly, it does not extract the death penalty for any of the workers, but it sounds the death-knell for collective bargaining. It sounds the death-knell for the rights of working people to elect their own leaders freely.
Clause 11 of Bill C-86 means that the Government can prevent any leader who advises his workers, his members, not to follow this legislation, from holding any office in the union or having any job with Canada Post. That is what we mean when we say that the legislation is Draconian. It puts an end to free collective bargaining on the part of the Post Office. It strikes at the very root of our right as Canadians to association. Freedom of association is guaranteed under Section 2 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, yet Bill C-86 strikes at that right.

Last Friday, just after the legislation had been tabled in the House, I had an opportunity to visit the picket line at the main sorting station near Victoria. I talked with some of the workers. They are very concerned. Their struggle is a just one. They are not asking for increased wages, but they are concerned about job security and about protecting the quality of their jobs. Many of them have worked for years at night shift jobs and have finally got the opportunity to work a day shift job at the wicket. This business of franchising will take that away from them. While the Government says that they will continue to have job security, they will be relegated to some kind of job on the night shift.
I do not know how many Hon. Members opposite have worked night shift. Well, I have, and it is not something which most workers in Canada appreciate, particularly if they have put in their years on night shift and have obtained a day job, only to see it taken away and hived off to some franchise outfit which will pay substandard wages.
They are also concerned that in the long run it will destroy union jobs. Apart from their own job security, as union men and women they are concerned about the impact it will have upon society in total, because it will destroy decent paying jobs and replace them with jobs at substandard wages without any
Postal Services Continuation
benefits. I emphasize that if we pay substandard wages, we will be building a substandard economy and we will have a substandard society.
Why is the Government insisting upon destroying the Post Office? Why is it insisting upon destroying the living standards of Canadian men and women? Why is it insisting upon building a substandard society? I urge the Government to withdraw Bill C-86 and let collective bargaining take its proper route.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not scheduled to speak in the debate, but I want to put a few comments on record. I will be supporting Bill C-86, but with some reluctance.
I find the same difficulty today as I had a number of weeks ago when we looked at legislation to end the rail strike. What we are seeing is an impasse, both in the case of railway workers and in the case of Canada Post employees, which has developed as a result of a long period of time when management and workers were not talking, were not discussing the problems, and were not taking into consideration the job that had to be done and the best way to do it.
As a result, today we as parliamentarians are being used as pawns in that we now have to step in and settle a dispute which really should have been resolved at the negotiating table.
I find a little fault with the system whereby we indicated that if they did not reach a settlement we would bring in back-to-work legislation. That certainly puts the gun to the heads of the negotiators on behalf of Canada Post and on behalf of the unions. Unfortunately, the management of Canada Post looks at that as being a situation where it can sit back and perhaps not negotiate any further in good faith because it knows that Parliament will run to its assistance and provide legislation that will cause the dispute to end. I find that a very difficult situation to be put in.
I also find a couple of issues in the dispute somewhat discomforting. I am personally not in favour of replacement workers. Canada Post has used them twice and it has caused a great deal of disruption on the picket lines. Canada Post has the right to lock out its employees and, conversely, those employees have the right to withdraw their services. That is part of the process, yet every time they use replacement workers to do the jobs of those who have removed their services in order to cause discomfort to the corporation, so that they can hopefully get a collective bargaining settlement.
I find a difficulty in that regard. If it is so essential that the 23,000 CUPW people work at Canada Post, or the workers involved in the last dispute, perhaps we should not be considering Bill C-86 to end the dispute. Perhaps we should be considering legislation to take away or remove that right to strike. If every time there is a dispute we call in Parliament to settle it, perhaps we should look at some sort of legislation to remove that right to strike and provide a dispute settling mechanism through arbitration.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
The other problem with which I have difficulty is franchising. 1 have no problem with franchising new services as Canada Post tries to extend its network into new population areas. However, I have difficulty with the thought that some existing postal operations may be franchised. I know that Canada Post is guaranteeing employment, but there is a certain quality of employment to which these people are entitled.
For example, 1 have a community of 17,000 people in my constituency with virtually no postal service. It has a few over-the-counter wickets in stores and so on. I can support franchising in the future for new facilities in order to provide service to the people, but I do not support the concept of taking existing post offices and putting them in the Kentucky Fried Chicken store next door. Nonetheless, I agree that in order to provide expanded services we may have to look at franchising.
However, those issues are not being settled by Bill C-86, the legislation which is before us today. Bill C-86 is merely calling an end to the dispute and is providing for 90 days of negotiation, with the benefit of a mediator, and eventually, if that is not successful, an arbitrator will be appointed who will have the binding powers to settle the dispute.
That is the only reason that I am supporting Bill C-86. I do not believe that Parliament should settle the issues, and we are not settling the issues. The issues are better solved between the parties sitting down in a responsible manner and negotiating. Given the nature of the management of Canada Post and the nature of the leadership of the union, I do not know whether we could really expect to have serious bargaining at the table without a lot of posturing and confrontation. I think that is why we are here today.
I also support the legislation because I know that Canadians are telling me "get them back to work". Canadians are paying good money in taxes for the subsidies and in stamps for the services, and they expect service. Earlier we talked about $24.89 being the average hourly cost of an employee including salary and benefits. It is a lot of money. I do not dispute that most Canadians are not making that amount but would like to make it. Nonetheless, it is a fact. It has been achieved through years of negotiating, and I do not think we can turn around and take it away in one step. However, the Canadian public has every right to expect service for that amount of pay.
When Canadians walk into a post office and see six wickets, one open, a 50-foot line-up, and four people standing back talking because it might be their coffee break, they do not react very well. That is a problem which both management and union have. They must solve the problems facing Canada Post.
I can tell the House that the staff in my office do not take a break if there is a constituent who wants service. They may get their break at some other time, but their priority is to provide service. That is what the Canadian public expects for $24.89. They do not expect us to take that away from the workers today. They may be a little jealous of that amount of money,
but they expect productivity, courtesy, and service. They certainly expect their letter, when it is posted, to get to its destination in a reasonable length of time.
I am supporting Bill C-86 because we must get on with that objective. We obviously have a problem between management and union. I would say that as a Government we have a problem with the management.
I am not happy with the response I get from Canada Post. If my constituents get the same kind of nonchalant attitude when they call Canada Post, they have every right to be upset.
I understand why the relationship between the union and management has deteriorated. My relationship with Canada Post has certainly deteriorated over the years because it does not return my phone calls. They gave me the same gob-bledegook as they gave my constituents when they called.
When a new house is built beside an old house, and one gets postal service and the other does not, and Canada Post says that it will take six months to review the route, in the meantime people are made to go downtown to a post office box. They are not even given a green box or a supermailbox. I do not blame the public for being frustrated with Canada Post, and they are taking that frustration out in this dispute.
Let us get it settled. Let us get a handle on the problem. It is not only a problem of management. It is a problem of the Government, the opposition Parties, the Canadian public, and the unions. We must make that organization work because Canadian taxpayers expect us to make it work. If we cannot do the job of making it work, they are prepared to accept other alternatives which will make it work.
The job must be done. They want us to do it. They want efficiency. They want service. They want fairness. They are not prepared to put up with what they are getting now and paying the kinds of bills they are paying. I will vote to put them back to work because the dispute will, hopefully, be resolved in the 90 days with the benefit of a mediator.
I find this kind of legislation very difficult. We are being brought into this to settle a problem which did not start six weeks or six months ago, it probably started six years ago with the unions and management getting further and further apart.
I will be supporting Bill C-86 with some reluctance because I have reservations about the dispute. Nonetheless this is not ending or settling particular issues, it is putting them back into the process. I can certainly tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in 90 days if the matter is not settled then an arbitrator will be needed. We will have a job to do to rebuild and provide the service which Canada Post is expected to provide Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in what the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane) had to say. I thought I heard between the lines that he was more uncomfortable with this legislation than he feels
October 15, 1987

he is able to admit on the record in the House. I was interested in his comment about line-ups at wickets. 1 wonder whether he has had the opportunity to be in a bank lately or in a number of other private enterprise institutions where line-ups are not infrequent. I sometimes find it irritating that we hear so very often about this kind of thing when it happens in the public sector but we never hear about identical things happening in the private sector.
I want to begin what I have to say this afternoon by taking issue with a statement made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) when he introduced this legislation. He said that the Government was determined-I am paraphrasing-that no private dispute would be allowed to tie up the country the way the postal strike was allegedly tying up the country. Actually it was not tying up the country until the Minister intervened, but that is beside the point.
I want to take issue with the notion that this is a private dispute, that this somehow belongs totally in the realm of the private sector, namely, that it is not related in some way or another to public policy, because this dispute is related to public policy. It is not a private dispute. It is related to the policy of the Government set down by the Government for Canada Post. It is in reaction to those policies that the Canadian Union of Postal Workers has found itself in the situation in which it now is, being unwilling, quite rightly, not to accept the policies which Canada Post is trying to force upon it, policies which have their origin in the policies of the Government. It is quite false, inaccurate, hypocritical and misleading for the Minister of Labour to refer to this as a private dispute which he and his Government really have not had anything to do with but which the Minister now out of a great sense of responsibility to the nation, is intervening to settle.
This is a dispute which has been precipitated by the policy of the Progressive Conservative Government. It is quite deceptive for the Minister of Labour to refer to this as a private dispute. It is government policy that Canada Post has with its plan for the franchising of postal offices. It is government policy that Canada Post not hire any more letter carriers and set up these rinky-dink supermailboxes all over the country. It is government policy that there be this constriction placed upon postal service.
I have had many constituents complain to me, not about inside postal workers or line-ups at wickets, but about things related to Canada Post policy. They are service-related, but in a way that is related to policy and not to the quality of the work being provided by postal workers. It is not postal workers who are to blame for supermailboxes. It is not postal workers who are to blame for the policies which the Post Office has adopted with respect to a great many issues which makes service more difficult for Canadians. Very close to where I live, I am aware of a supermailbox now having been set up. It has been there for a week or two. People are still having to go to the main post office in Transcona to get their mail. If they have to live with a supermailbox, they wonder why they cannot
Postal Services Continuation
get their mail delivered to it now. We contacted Canada Post for them and we were told that that mailbox is not scheduled to be used until the beginning of November.
Not only does Canada Post irritate the devil out of people by forcing them to have these supermailboxes, but having set them up, will not even use them, making people go elsewhere for their mail. These things make absolutely no sense, Mr. Speaker. That is why there has not been the public outcry against the postal workers that some people might have expected or might have wanted, particularly on the government side.
Canadians have come to realize that the Post Office is run by a bunch of dummies. The public has a lot of sympathy for the postal workers who have to work under these dummies and under the people who devise these policies. 1 say to every Canadian who might be listening and tempted to accept the Government's invitation to perceive the Canadian postal workers as scapegoats in this dispute that it is their post offices which are on the Government's hit list. It is their post offices that will someday be franchised out, and it is their post offices which will disappear, particularly those in rural Canada. It is their relatives, friends and perhaps themselves, if they move into a newer area, who will never again receive door-to-door mail delivery.
This situation affects everyone. I think everyone has had just enough of a taste-some have had more than just a taste-at the way the Post Office is run not to be willing to accept the Government's view that it is the postal workers who are to blame.
The Government has clearly taken sides in this dispute. The Government has not acted neutrally. It has taken sides by referring in the way it has to the Foisy report, contradicting the position the Government took at the time of the back-to-work rail legislation when the Government refused to make reference to the conciliator's report. It has become absolutely clear that this is not a neutral act by the Government. This is a partisan act in which the Government has taken the side of management, not surprisingly, because management is implementing the Government's policies.
Going back to what I said originally, this is not a private dispute between Canada Post and its employees; it is a dispute centered around the appropriate resistance of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers on behalf of all Canadians to the policies which the Government has asked Canada Post to put in place. All Canadians owe CUPW a certain debt of gratitude, if you ask me, for not being willing to roll over and play dead with respect to these issues, for fighting back and for calling the attention of Canadians to just what is involved in the Government's policies with respect to Canada Post.
I had an opportunity to comment on the larger issue the other day. So far, I have been talking mostly about the policies of Canada Post with respect to franchising and things like

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
that. 1 would like to turn now to the economic well-being of the workers.
What is happening here is part of a larger attack on the standard of living of working Canadians. The right-wing solution to the crisis in the western economy is that if there is to be a reallocation of power, capital and income, the people who will have to make the sacrifices are not those who have loads of money to begin with like the owners and the wealthy, but the well-paid working people. They will have to make that sacrifice in order, to use the euphemism of the right, that Canada and other countries which in the post-war era had enjoyed a good standard of living can become competitive.
With whom will these countries become competitive? "Competitive" is one of the words that is bandied about here, in the free trade agreement and in multilateral trade arrangements as if everyone knew what it meant. The fact is that "competitive" means that instead of having a Government that wants to work for a new, just and sustainable international economic order, as many have suggested it ought to do, we have a Government which wants to accommodate itself, rather than resist, through the sacrifices of working Canadians, to trends in the global economy which will pit working Canadians against working Koreans, Brazilians and Americans.
In order to have this kind of competition, we will all become the poor. When I say "we", I mean people who come from working class communities in which people have been able to have a decent standard of living for the last 30 or 40 years. The Government has said: "In order for us to be competitive, you people out there in Transcona and elsewhere have to give up that standard of living. It was nice for a while, four decades, not bad, particularly if it was from when you were 20 to 60 years old, but for the rest of you young people out there who thought you would have the kind of economic security your parents had, forget it. We are in the brand new world of a global-free enterprise, a brand new world of competitiveness, a brand new world of free trade with the United States".
Workers in Canada will be able to compete with workers in the sun belt of the southern United States where there is an anti-labour environment, very few environmental laws, very little regulation and a political context that is antithetical to social justice. These are the people with whom we are supposed to compete, and we are supposed to be excited about it. We are supposed to be excited about the fact that we can be given the opportunity by the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada to give up everything for which the people have worked over the last 50 years in building a more socially just Canada in order to be competitive.
That is not something with which working people will put up. Wherever working people take a stand against that kind of economic and political agenda, whether it be with CUPW, the rail unions or the workers at Super Value in Winnipeg, the NDP will be standing with those people.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Act, 1982, should be amended in order to include property rights and, that the Governor General issue a Proclamation under the Great Seal of Canada to amend Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms so that it reads as follows:
"7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice."
and this House urges that the Legislative Assemblies of all provinces and the Senate pass similar resolutions.
Property Rights
The intent and rationale of this motion is very straightforward. I am asking the House of Commons to pass this motion, allow this question to go to the Senate and then to the provincial Governments through the amending process for our Constitution, seeking its consent to add the words "enjoyment of property" to Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights.
This action would thereby provide the necessary and natural corollary to the words "life, liberty and security of person", rights already secured in Section 7 of the Charter.
It is true that the right to enjoy property is now included in the Canadian Bill of Rights. However, the Canadian Bill of Rights is but a statement of general principle and does not of itself confer or create real rights. When property rights were proposed for inclusion in our Charter in 1981, the matter was discussed, then explicitly rejected, a regrettable omission about which I will say more later.
Suffice it to say that once a decision was made in 1981 to list all the rights of Canadians in the Charter, then surely all such rights should have been included. However, the omission of property rights from the present text of the Charter is an obvious and very serious omission. It remains a constitutional imperative to ensure it is included.
In my earlier speech I spoke in some detail on the philosophical rationale for this motion and do not feel the need to repeat myself at length here today. Simply put, however, I would argue that to omit and deny the right to private property is to diminish, indeed to render meaningless, the existing rights to life, liberty and security of person. Surely, our existing freedom to purchase a car, home, farm or business is severely restricted if our basic right to make, buy, keep or sell is not also protected. Likewise, surely the principle of freedom "to pursue the gaining of a livelihood", in Section 6, Part 2(b) of the Charter, as a labourer, housewife, farmer or businessman, is severely diminished if one's freedom to simply keep, sell or buy is not secure. All this is simple common sense.
Permit me to give two concrete examples. Under the ill-conceived and ruinous National Energy Program, the previous Liberal administration confiscated from the oil companies 25 per cent of all land assets north of the 60th parallel, called the "frontier lands", and gave them to PetroCan without any compensation whatsoever, not a single penny.
Another obvious area of concern are the nationalization policies of the New Democratic Party which would allow the seizure of assets without necessarily providing full compensation. So the socialist New Democratic Party could nationalize a bank or a business and refuse to pay fair market value. By adding the words "enjoyment of property" to the Charter, such actions would be severely restricted.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the second opportunity I have had to introduce and defend before this House a motion calling for the constitutional protection of property rights. The first time was on May 28, 1985, during the last session of Parliament.
Therefore, lest there be any doubt, let me reiterate the fundamental rationale of this motion. Logical consistency demands that those fundamental rights now guaranteed by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, words such as, "life, liberty and security of the person", be given their

October 15, 1987
Property Rights
natural, undeniable and essential correlate, namely, "enjoyment of property". I would suggest it is incumbent upon those who would disagree with the motion to state their position with respect to this rationale.
In addition to the self-evident inherent logic of this motion, there are several other compelling factors in its favour. First, the historical precedent is overwhelming. The basic human right to own what we make was included in such documents as the Magna Carta in 1215 and the English Bill of Rights in 1627. In 1948, Canada signed the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Article 17 of that declaration reads:
(1)	Everyone has the right to own property as well as in association with others.
(2)	No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his property.
Additionally, property rights is also recognized in the 1960 Canadian Bill of Rights. Clearly, then, it is now time to bring our Constitution in line with these historic documents.
Second, the entrenchment of property rights is currently recognized by a wide range of modern democratic counties including Australia, the United States, West Germany, Italy, Finland and, for my socialist colleagues, even socialist Sweden. Third, various Canadian national organizations, such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Real Estate Association, have been constant in their efforts to have Parliament act on this issue.
Fourth, this is a matter which applies to all Canadians and it is a right which each of them wants and deserves. This fact has received undeniable support in a recent Gallup poll which shows that 81 per cent of Canadians say that it is either "very" or "fairly" important to them that the Constitution be amended to include property rights.
The ordinary person's vested interest in the protection of property rights is recognized by all responsible public leaders. Britain's Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher has said: "We need a property owning democracy". Why? Because, to quote Barbara Amiel, a well-known Canadian journalist, Mrs. Thatcher understands:
That for ordinary working people, who might not be blessed with the intellectual property of the intelligentsia or the abstract property of the bureaucracy, the most important thing is the house they own or the few shares they can get. That bit of real property means that they can arrange their lives independently of the state.
Permit me now, Mr. Speaker, briefly to anticipate and respond to some of the concerns which have often been voiced with respect to this issue. These concerns are invariably related to two basic questions; first, what exactly is meant by "property", and, second, what would be the impact of the inclusion and subsequent interpretation of "enjoyment of property" upon various bodies such as the provinces, natives, environmentalists, womens' groups, business and labour, and so on. While these are important questions and, as such, cannot be exhausted here, it is crucial that they be held in proper perspective.
First, it is true that the concept of property has evolved from a rather basic interest in land and personal property to a more complex concern with intellectual property, that is, patents, trade marks and copyrights. There is also passive property such as stocks and shares, and now there is even the so-called "new property", such as social security systems and public employment. Admittedly, therefore, defining "property" is now a necessary and sometimes complicated exercise.
Second, the legitimate reservations of certain groups must be taken very seriously whether it be Prince Edward Island which is concerned about foreign land ownership, womens' groups wanting to safeguard gains in family law legislation, or environmentalists justifiably interested in protection from pollution. But these concerns should not be overstated. For example, some have argued that large corporations stand to benefit most from property rights and, therefore, protection of property rights is in itself not a good thing. Such an argument is logically absurd.
Are we, therefore, to deny and revoke our constitutional right to free speech simply because certain people or parties, for example, the Toronto Star, are large enough to exercise that right with the potential for greater influence than smaller newspapers or individual citizens? Of course not. Yet some persist in arguing that the constitutional protection of property rights will only benefit big business. Does that mean freedom of speech or freedom of the press is only of value to the Toronto Starl That is absurd.
Furthermore, it must be recognized that all aspects of the Charter are subject to Section 1 of the Charter which reads as follows:
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees the rights and
freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law
as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
I maintain that this qualifier safeguards against the kinds of extreme scenarios envisioned by oppenents of property rights.
Consequently, while the "enjoyment of property" may require both careful definition and legal interpretation, this is in no way sufficient to negate the rationale and the value of this motion. Just because it may be difficult to define and interpret what is meant by words such as "life", "liberty" or "security of person", that does not mean that we therefore refrain from enshrining these fundamental rights. Likewise, just because it may be difficult to define and interpret the words "enjoyment of property", it does not necessarily follow that it must be excluded from the Charter. To so argue is, at best, to allow necessary caution to negate a valid and fundamental principle; or, at worst, it is absurd logic used to distort completely the issue at hand.
If this rationale is sound, and I believe it is, and if there are compelling reasons in its favour, and I believe that there are, and if the major objections can be met, and I believe that they can be, then the way is clear for this Government and this
October 15, 1987

House to take the necessary and decisive action. Not to do so would be intellectually and morally dishonest. It would be an abdication of our responsibility as Members of Parliament.
So I must emphasize the need for decisive action. We cannot perpetuate the negligence of the previous administration whose performance during the 1981 constitutional debates on this topic was nothing short of scandalous.
On Tuesday, January 20, 1981, the Conservative Party in opposition introduced an amendment seeking the inclusion of property rights in the Charter. On Friday, January 23, the then Solicitor General, in his capacity as acting Minister of Justice for the Government, accepted this amendment on behalf of the Liberal Government. However, that Sunday evening, the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), having conferred with his provincial socialist counterparts in Saskatchewan, informed Canadians on national television that the NDP would be withdrawing its support for the Constitution if property rights were to be included.
The following Tuesday, Prime Minister Trudeau told Parliament that the property rights amendment had to be dropped. True to form, the Liberal Government had sacrificed a fundamental principle on the altar of political expediency. Its philosophy should have told it that it should have been in favour of it, but it gave up for political expediency.
Since this motion will be coming to a vote, it will be interesting to see whether the Liberal Party will again try to sit on both sides of this issue. It will also be interesting to see whether the NDP will continue to tell the constituents in my riding, and people right across Canada, that they cannot have the constitutionally protected right to make, sell, keep, buy, or own. They have that right; they must.
To cite the compelling logic of the 1972 decision, as just one example, of the Supreme Court of the United States:
Property does not have rights. People have rights.. . [However] A fundamental inter-dependence exists between the personal right to liberty and the personal right to property. Neither could have meaning without the other. That rights in property are basic civil rights has long been recognized.
The Conservative Party is in favour of the constitutional recognition of property rights. Consistent with this, the present Government has taken very specific initiatives toward this end.
When I introduced and defended this motion during the last session of Parliament, a number of impediments stood in its way. First, there was the fact that the Province of Quebec was not yet a signatory to the Constitution. However, the recent historic Meech Lake Accord has gone a long way to resolving this deficiency. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) speaking on Law Day, April 15, 1987, noted:
The successful resolution of the Quebec issue will unlock the constitutional reform process and allow us to turn our attention to other issues-such as... property rights-in a second round of constitutional discussions.
This next round is already under way. A second impediment to my former motion was the need to address various concerns
Property Rights
at the provincial level. Since then, following federal Government impetus, the provincial Attorneys General have established a working group to examine the property rights question.
As an example of recent action at the provincial level, at the initiative of my provincial colleague from Waterloo, Mr. Herb Epp, the Ontario Government on November 27, 1986, passed a resolution that Section 7 of the Charter be amended to include the "enjoyment of property".
A third impediment is related to the format of Private Members' Business. It was felt that one hour on a non-votable debate in the House was not an adequate format in which to debate such a significant subject as this. However, following the recent parliamentary reforms introduced by the Prime Minister, this new motion has been selected for extended debate with a mandatory vote to follow. This provides ample opportunity for all Members of the House to express their positions and to vote accordingly.
Permit me to summarize, Mr. Speaker. The premise of this motion is philosophically sound. The right of ownership flows naturally and logically from the uniqueness of every free individual to make, to invent, to keep, to buy, or to sell. The reasons in favour of the constitutional protection of property rights are compelling, both historically and constitutionally. The reservations with respect to definition and legal interpretation can all be met. The impediments to legislative action are now being removed.
We all know that the overwhelming majority of Canadians want the federal Government to act on this issue. Therefore, in conclusion, I call upon the House to accept and approve this motion.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on this Private Member's motion put forward this evening. It is a question which will evidently come up quite often in the House. I think it is one that really needs a great deal of debate. I feel it is unfortunate that this evening we are limited to one hour, even though, of course, the Hon. Member proposing the motion has stated that there are other ways of having extended debate.
However, I think that this question goes much deeper than a great many Members are prepared to admit. This issue goes back to the time when we were repatriating the Constitution in the early 1980s. It was not only a question, as the Hon. Member stated, of political expediency; it was a question of provincial disagreement on the question of including the clause on property rights in the Constitution. He is correct in stating that Prince Edward Island was opposed, largely because of its restriction on foreign ownership of land in the province. But other provinces such as Saskatchewan were opposed as well.

October 15, 1987
Property Rights
I think that they had reasons. Whether it can be said that the reasons were reasons with which one would agree or not, 1 think one would have to say that their reasons were sound reasons as far as they were concerned. Although we may not agree with them, it will not be simple to bring this dialogue to a point where we can talk about putting this clause in the Constitution. If the Government is serious about doing this, then the dialogue with the provinces will have to be brought along much further than it has been to the present time.
The Hon. Member stated that we do not have a definition of property. That is true. That is a concern to me. The Hon. Member mentioned that this may not be necessary. He mentioned that there is support for this from the Canadian Bar Association. If we do not have a definition of property, I can understand why the Canadian Bar Association would be in favour of it, because it will make millionaires out of many of them.
The Hon. Member is correct in stating that the term "property" has evolved. One can look at history, back in the 1780s, the time of the drafters of the Declaration of Independence in the United States, and read about the disagreement between two such prominent men as Thomas Edison and James Madison and their definition of property and whether it should be included in the Constitution. At that particular time, they could not agree. It was a very dicey point even at that time, although subsequently through amendment it has been included in the Bill of Rights in the United States. We have had this evolvement of what is property. Initially it was narrowly termed as real property, the ownership of land. Now it means other things such as personal property and intellectual property. There are also rights in personal property and intellectual property.
For instance, people who are entitled to an Old Age Security pension, Canada Pension, or unemployment insurance have the receipt of those cheques and that is their personal property. That is not only personal property but it is a right that they have to receive that personal property. So there are rights not only in real property but in personal property.
The Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer) also correctly stated that we are now talking about property in relation to intellectual property such as patents and copyrights. That is very true. Of course, if a person has a patent or a copyright, they have every reason and every right to be able to depend on the fact that that will stand up and that the law will enforce that right. So there has been an evolvement, and the definition continues to evolve. It is very important that we define property, and know from the outset exactly what property we wish to include.
There also are other aspects of property. As government becomes more involved in the lives of people, with incorporations, licences, and the list goes on, the definition of property continues to expand.
As the Hon. Member states, there is a very strong segment of people in Canada who believe that property should be included. There is also a strong segment of people who believe that property should not be included. A lot of people go by the old axiom, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it". We do have property rights in this country, and those property rights to be rights do not have to be included in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The courts have passed judgment on this. I wish to refer to a case in 1975, Harrison v. Carswell, where it states:
Anglo-Canadian jurisprudence has traditionally recognized, as a
fundamental freedom, the right of the individual to the enjoyment of property
and the right not to be deprived thereof, of any interest therein, save by due
process of law.
That is a Supreme Court decision. The Supreme Court has come out firmly on the side of property rights. While property rights are not enshrined in the Constitution, they are definitely rights in this country.
We must also look to Section 26 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states, "The guarantee in this Charter of certain rights and freedoms shall not be construed as denying the existence of any other rights and freedoms that exist in Canada".
In the Charter of Rights and Freedoms specifically set out is the statement that because the rights of property are not included in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, that does not mean that they do not exist. Nor is there anything in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that would say that these rights do not exist. That is very important.
We must also look at the history in Canada. The Hon. Member may talk about other countries, but in Canada we have had a unique situation in that we patriated our Constitution when we were fairly well advanced in our history, after we had been a country for over 100 years. We had this Charter of Rights and Freedoms well after we had been a country for over 100 years. So there is a good body of civil law and common law which looks after the rights of Canadians with respect to their property. This has evolved, and is evolving.
Canadians should not be concerned in any way about the fact that property rights are not enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Their rights to property remain sound and inviolate. We must keep that in mind. I can appreciate the concern of the Hon. Member. I do not agree with him that this is a necessity, and I think that there are many who do not. However, if he feels it is something he wishes to pursue, 1 would encourage him to take it to his colleagues in caucus, the Government, and the provinces. If there is to be any meaningful change, it has to be aired with the provinces, and the provinces have to come along as equal partners in trying to make this change.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer). The motion is for the
October 15, 1987

enjoyment of property. It states that it is to amend the Constitution of Canada in order that Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms read:
Everyone has the right to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment
of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with
the principles of fundamental justice.
I very strongly oppose this. I wish to confirm what the Hon. Member for Kitchener said that it was the NDP that scuttled this in 1981. I was proud at that time to be the NDP constitutional spokesman when this happened. If the Member for Kitchener wishes a reference on exactly when it happened, it was at the committee stage of the hearings back in 1981, and I believe it was on November 1, which was a Friday. I remember that day very well when the Acting Minister of Justice accepted an amendment from the Conservative Party. The Hon. Member from Burnaby and myself talked out the clock. We consulted over the weekend and persuaded the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to drop this. 1 wish to explain some reasons why we did that.
I went over my remarks to the committee at that time, and one of the things I said was that one of the most persuasive arguments against property rights in the Constitution was put forward by a Conservative Justice Minister named Horst Carver, the Minister of Justice for Prince Edward Island. He came to our committee and was extremely persuasive when he said that, if property rights were enshrined in the Constitution of Canada, he was afraid that the provincial rights in this country would be jeopardized and tampered with. Foreign ownership regulations and laws in Prince Edward Island over the restriction of farmland and the restriction of the purchasing of tourism land by foreigners would be put in jeopardy. He was afraid that if property rights were in the Constitution, as stated in the motion where it talks about the enjoyment of property and persons enjoying their property, this would be a wide open invitation to Americans to buy farmland in Prince Edward Island, buy recreation land, corporations could do so, and it would be a great invasion of provincial rights.
I also recall some Albertans in the Conservative Government of Peter Lougheed making a similar argument without as much passion about why wle should not be doing this. Of course the NDP Government of Allan Blakeney did the same thing. I am very proud to have been the NDP spokesman in those days when we scuttled that extremely reactionary and retrograde move by the Conservative Party, a move which would have been a great invasion of provincial rights.
I am happy that it is a constitutional amendment and that it must be approved not only by the House of Commons and the Senate of Canada but by seven of the ten provinces representing 50 per cent of the people.
I make it very clear that Albertans under Lougheed, P.E.I. Conservatives, and many other Conservatives in Canada at the provincial level do not support it. I am very pleased that this kind of amendment will not go through.
Property Rights
I want to explain why it should not go through. As I said, it was proposed back in 1981. Mr. Bennett, the Premier of British Columbia, reproposed it in 1983. It failed to get through the Premiers despite the fact that there were many Conservative Premiers in the country. I am very proud that it went down to defeat.
I come from the Province of Saskatchewan. There has been tremendous intervention in its economy by Governments of Saskatchewan, such as the take-over of potash mines and things of that nature over the years. This kind of constitutional amendment may have prohibited that kind of intervention in the economy, in that that kind of prohibition would have been opposed by an overwhelming number of Saskatchewan people.
I am not only talking about New Democrats. Saskatchewan has a Conservative Government now which maintains the Saskatchewan Potash Corporation. The very right-wing Government of Liberal Ross Thatcher, who was more conservative than most Conservatives, maintained Crown corporations in Saskatchewan. They are a very important part of our heritage. I do not want to see that heritage jeopardized by a Supreme Court decision which says that a person may enjoy property rights when that person might be an American company which would prohibit us from expanding the Saskatchewan Potash Corporation or indeed Saskoil.
Another example is the Province of Quebec. Quebec intervened in the asbestos market. The federal Government has intervened in the oil market with Petro-Canada. In 1984, the Government expanded the role of Petro-Canada through the takeover and purchase of other oil companies. That might be put in jeopardy by property rights being enshrined in the Constitution of Canada.
I have already mentioned Prince Edward Island and the very passionate stand taken by Horst Carver, the Conservative Minister of Justice of that province. I assume Joe Ghiz, the present Premier, would take the same stand on behalf of Prince Edward Islanders.
I think this kind of amendment is very dangerous for ordinary people or ordinary citizens, small businesses, and farmers. I say that as a person who said back in 1981 that I wanted to see economic rights put in the Constitution. At that time I said that we should have economic rights in the Constitution-the right to a job, the right to an income, the right to medicare, the right to decent wages, the right to own a farm, the right to own a small business, and the right to own a home. I am very much in favour of those rights for ordinary people, but I am not in favour of the amendment before the House today.
I have already mentioned some of the reasons I am not in favour of the amendment. However, let me point out that there would be no guarantee if we had the amendment in the Constitution. "Everyone has the right to life, liberty, security of the person" is already there, and the Hon. Member would like to add the following:

October 15, 1987
Property Rights
-and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except
in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.
I know how the Supreme Court of Canada can interpret that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was totally inadvertent on my part. I know Section 7 of the Charter. I was a member of the committee this past summer, and I am very familiar with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Section 7 reads:
Everyone has the right to life, liberty, security of the person, and the right
not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of
fundamental justice.
What the Hon. Member would add is "enjoyment of property". However, I am concerned about interpretation by the courts.
You are a very distinguished lawyer and member of the Bar of Quebec, Mr. Speaker. In that you are sitting in the chair, of course you cannot comment, but I am sure you could probably give us some very interesting opinions on this point. There is no guarantee at all that the Supreme Court of Canada and other courts would not interpret the protection of property in such a way as to rule out a wide variety of government initiatives aimed at, for instance, improving the workplace, regulating technological change, regulating labour relations, restricting the right to pollute, safeguarding the environment, protecting tenants and all kinds of other rights which workers, tenants, and other ordinary Canadians might have.
It seems clear that these and other government actions could be construed as affecting the right to the enjoyment of property. Not only is there the fact that one has property, but one has the right to enjoy that property. What does that mean in the courts of Canada? "Enjoyment of property" are very elastic words, and this is what Horst Carver, the Conservative Justice Minister of Prince Edward Island, was concerned about.
I should also like to note the so-called due process clauses in the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments in the United States Constitution. Between 1905 and 1937 in respect of these clauses "to strike down laws providing for minimum wages, maximum hours of work and maximum prices, and prohibiting anti-union activity", the court reasoned that such laws were unjust denials of the employer's liberty to bargain with his employees and control the use of his property. 1 think these are points which we should note.
What does the word "everyone" mean? I ask that question of the Hon. Member for Kitchener. I know he has very good intentions in his motion. I do not question his motives whatsoever. However, what does the word "everyone" mean? What does the word "property" mean? These words can have broad
definitions by Supreme Court justices over whom neither he nor I have control once it is out of the domain of Parliament. It is not so much that we are taking control out of the hands of Parliament. We are taking control out of the hands of the provincial legislatures of Canada and giving it to the Supreme Court of Canada. That is what I do not like about the particular amendment. The word "everyone" could be a Japanese investor, an American investor, a Canadian company, CPR, the Hon. Member for Kitchener, or anybody. Again I say that it is one of the things I do not like about the amendment before the House today. It almost certainly includes corporations.
What about the word "property"? Property includes the rights to control and dispose of a very broad range of assets and so on. That also concerns me. As I said before, it falls under provincial jurisdiction. I do not think that we in the Parliament of Canada should initiate a constitutional change which affects the provinces almost exclusively. Of course we have that right. The Hon. Member has that right. However, I do not think that we should be the ones to initiate it. It is in their domain. If they want changes, they should be initiating the particular move.
Once again I appeal to my friend who comes from a Party which has always stressed that provincial rights are important in rethinking this position. I could go on and on, but I see you signalling, Mr. Speaker, that my time is up. As I said, I think the resolution would do more harm to the rights of ordinary Canadians and do more to protect the rights of big companies and big investors, including many foreign investors. It would also take away many of the rights of provincial legislatures to do what they want with their resources and their farmland. I have already mentioned the case of Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan, but I see that my time is up.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, indeed it is a pleasure to rise to participate in debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer). I commend him for his initiative in bringing an extremely important matter to the attention of the House.
I know that with the Hon. Member's heritage the matter is important to him. He appreciates even more how precious property rights are to many, if not all, Canadians. Many of his constituents have come from persecuted countries, and I know how important the motion is to them.
Since being elected in 1984, I have made no fewer than five interventions in the House of Commons on the inclusion of property rights in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Many individuals have chosen Canada as their new home because of the freedoms which we enjoy to work hard and to acquire wealth and property. It is difficult for me to understand why in 1981-82 the NDP would not allow the inclusion of property rights in the Charter.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join in the debate. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Reimer) who has, not only on this occasion but on a number of occasions, brought forward a number of important subjects for debate in the House. I congratulate him for that. I think it is a good reflection on the people of Kitchener that they had the foresight and wisdom to send this individual back to Parliament a second time.
Constitutional change as proposed by the Hon. Member for Kitchener is very timely inasmuch as we have also been discussing the Meech Lake Accord. I will say in passing that I believe the Meech Lake Accord sets a new tone for cooperative and constructive federal-provincial relations. The Accord has shown that constitutional change is possible in Canada when it is done collectively and in co-operation with the provinces, and I am sure that this is what the Hon. Member for Kitchener has in mind.
At the outset I would like to emphasize that in my view property rights have played a central role in the evolution of our society. Indeed, property rights are an essential part of British parliamentary democracy. These rights can be traced back to the year 1215 with the signing of the Magna Charta. Today the right to own, use and enjoy property is fundamental to the economic life of our country and of other western democracies. For that reason I believe it should be enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The role of property in the economy of our country, the right to own, use and enjoy property, is fundamental to the basic feature of democracy, which is individual freedom. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party has had a long and honourable association with this idea. It was the Conservative Government under the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker who in 1960 introduced the Canadian Bill of Rights which included protection for the enjoyment of property. In the recent process leading to the patriation of the Constitution, it was the Progressive Party again that wanted the inclusion of property rights. Unfortunately that process was not included at the end, and I am very pleased that the Hon. Member for Kitchener has come forward in an attempt to correct the situation.
There have already been a number of discussions and debates about this question. I am the first to admit that questions concerning the Constitution are never simple. They are usually difficult, but I do not think that as a result of that we should shrink from the task.
Property Rights
The Member from the New Democratic Party says that the definitions of property are very complicated. I agree with that. We have real property which concerns land. We have personal property which deals with everything from cars to negotiable instruments. Just because the definition of property is very broad and it will, of necessity, have to be interpreted by the courts there is no reason not to embark on the course, a very important one, to have it included within the Charter of Rights.
I say the motion before us would add the enjoyment of property to Section 7 of the Charter thereby guaranteeing the right not to be deprived of the enjoyment of property, except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. In conjuction with that, it is reasonable, I believe, to say that what we are talking about is the unreasonable deprivation of an individual when it comes to property rights. I would suggest that some of the fears I have heard enumerated here that people's rights will be trampled on by the rights of the Government to conduct the business of either the province or the federal Government are misplaced. I do not think that is what we are talking about at all. It is not the intention of the Member from Kitchener. He wants to strike a reasonable balance between the property rights of the individual and the legitimate concerns of the state. I would not feel so strongly about this if I had not seen examples in Canadian history where property rights of the individual had been trampled upon.
You would be aware, Mr. Speaker, coming as you do from the Province of Quebec, of all the problems that surrounded the expropriation of land for Mirabel Airport. The facts are this: much more land than necessary was expropriated for the airport. Everybody knew it and acknowledged it. The people whose farms and homes were expropriated fought the issue for years, indeed decades, to do something about it. I became a believer in this resolution just on that issue alone because I always thought that if property rights had been enshrined in the Constitution, people would have had a legal access and would have been able to take a legal route to show and demonstrate to a court of law that their rights had been unnecessarily deprived. It was a very moving moment for all of us when the then Minister of Public Works-I was not there to see it, I saw it on television-spoke to all the farmers who had been deprived of their property and acknowledged-something that should have been acknowledged years ago-that a terrible mistake had been made. All the suffering all those years by those individuals was unnecessary.
Whether this motion goes through or not, I hope other Crown corporations take a long hard look at their property management system. We can start with the St. Lawrence Seaway which owns land in my area. I would suggest the St. Lawrence Seaway should perhaps take a look at how much land it has expropriated over the years. That company should look at the question in the light of what is reasonable for its requirements. I do not limit the issue to the St. Lawrence Seaway. Other companies should do the same thing.

October 15, 1987
Property Rights
If this motion had been passed and had been part of the Constitution, individuals would have had a remedy in law, and 1 think that is what we all want. I feel very strongly about this motion which has been supported by a number of organizations. On December 18, 1986 I was very pleased to present a petition spearheaded by the St. Catharines and District Real Estate Board. I know 1 was joined by the Members from Welland, St. Catharines, Erie and Lincoln, all the Members of Parliament from the Niagara Peninsula, in support of this very worth-while endeavour. This motion has the complete support of the Niagara Falls Fort Erie Real Estate Association. They have made representations to me as one of their two Members of Parliament who represent the area and have asked that we act.
1 ask Hon. Members to begin the process of enshrining property rights in the Constitution. It is a long and difficult process but I know it will need the support of the provinces. It is long overdue and we should begin the process now.
