subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak against this very unjust and destructive back-to-work legislation of the Conservative Government. The

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
amendment which we are now debating is part of the package which we are seeking. It talks of an agreement for certain action to be taken at a date to be fixed by the arbitrator. More generally, we are getting at the difference between mediation and arbitration.
In the half century during which labour law has grown up as a body of practice and law in North America, most contracts have been settled without a strike and without any compulsory back-to-work legislation. Many contracts are settled without the aid of a mediator and the large majority are settled without any such intervention at all.
The country has been moving toward a policy of resolving conflicts by negotiation. Sometimes negotiations break down and the owner may lock out or the workers may go on strike. However, that is not the normal way of proceeding.
As my colleague, the Member for Churchill, said, we urged the Government to appoint a mediator before this strike happened and the Government refused to do it. Now it seems that the Government wants to destroy the very concept of mediation, the very concept of negotiation, in order to bring about a willing compromise with each side giving a little bit and neither side getting all it asked for, a willing compromise for the sake of peace and good order. The Government does not want a willing compromise. It is clear that the Government has decided that it will either destroy unions or enslave them.
There have been continual attacks on the postal unions by the Government. They are continually being blamed for the inefficiency of the Post Office. Even the public, which is relatively impartial, understands that it is very often a rude and inconsiderate management that is to blame. The public strongly supported the letter carriers and is now beginning to support the inside postal workers notwithstanding the heavy propaganda which has been spread against the inside postal workers who are now on strike.
I have read letters to the editor and have received telephone calls and letters in my constituency office from people saying that they disagree with the franchising out of the wicket work of the Post Office to drug stores or small variety stores in my riding of Spadina. They have complained bitterly about having to travel some distance to a little store to pick up a registered letter or parcel. The postage has been paid but the management of the Post Office will not do the work. Instead, in many cases the recipient of the mail is required to do the work which until a few weeks ago was being done by the Post Office. A management decision has now been made that that paid-for service will no longer be fully provided.
People who in principle do not sympathize with the Canadian Union of Postal Workers do sympathize on the issue of franchising. That is a central issue in this strike. If the Government had been willing to negotiate on the matter of franchising, there would be no strike. That has been made plain in many ways, including by the union's offer to negotiate franchising in certain defined situations such as new residential areas.
If the Post Office had been willing to negotiate it, could have arrived at an agreement with the postal workers and not only would there be no strike, there would be better service than is now being received by my constituents who have complained to my office. People are being required to go a mile or two to pick up mail for which postage was paid. They often have to go to a location which is not served by good public transportation or has no proper parking.
The Post Office is forcing the customers to do the work which management has declined to do. This will result in people making less use of the Post Office. Perhaps that is another purpose of the Minister in forcing this strike and imposing this settlement. Perhaps there is a campaign to drive away the ordinary users of the Post Office so that friends of the Government who operate private postal services will inherit the business when the public service has been destroyed.
I have said that there has been great progress in the last half century in Canada and the United States in developing labour law to the point where contracts and disputes are normally settled without a strike. Nevertheless, we have not arrived at anywhere near full democracy for the people who earn their living through wages as compared to those who earn their living from the property they own.
Trade unionists in particular are second-class citizens in Canada. The Constitution and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms do not say that. Those words are not found in any law passed by Parliament or any other jurisdiction in Canada, but the fact is that only trade union members get fined or sent to jail for not working.
Doctors can go on strike and no one talks about putting them in jail, although their patients may suffer when they are refused service. Bankers go on strike. They refuse to give loans at 9 per cent. They will not give loans unless they are paid 12 per cent, or whatever the rate of interest is. There is no negotiation, mediation, arbitration or back-to-work law telling the bankers that since they made $200 million profit last year they must lend money at 9 per cent. No such thing is even considered.
Bankers, professional people, owners of any business or any property can go on strike with impunity. They can refuse to make their service or property available to tenants or customers on the terms that have been customary or which the customers might consider reasonable. They can ask any unreasonable price or impose any unreasonable condition they like. If they do not get their way they can shut the place down and hope to force, by deprivation, their customers to meet their price. Only members of trade unions can be prohibited by law from doing what every other person in this country is free to do.
I have been a trade unionist for many years. I worked in a factory for 18 years and am proud to have been a member of the Canadian Paperworkers Union. I respect the work of rank and file trade union men and women and their local, regional, and national officers and representatives who have built up the
October 15, 1987

self-respect of people who work for wages and are otherwise deprived of their right to give or withhold their labour freely.
In our factory, the only way we could bargain to get a decent wage, to have normal courteous treatment from a supervisor rather than contemptuous insults or orders; the only way we could bargain to avoid racial discrimination and the sowing of racial conflict by certain foremen and to have safety in order to protect ourselves from the risk of life and limb due to unsafe working conditions, was by agreeing as a union that if we could not get a reasonable settlement we would not do the work of the factory. In 30 years there was only one strike in our factory for some two or three weeks. Normally, disputes were settled by negotiation.
My point is that the union has been the means of raising the self respect of Canada's working people such as the ones who make it possible for this Parliament to run. Many of them are still deprived by this Parliament of the right to have a union. They include the people who clean the buildings, who build and repair them, who provide the services in the cafeteria, who drive the buses, the constables and others. There is only the beginnings of recognition of union organization.
This Parliament is one of the worst employers in Canada and one of the most out of date, anti-union and anti-human employers in Canada. Now, Parliament wants to extend that anti-union, anti-worker attitude into the Post Office.
The principle we are trying to put forward in this amendment and the following amendments is that there should be at least a move by this Parliament toward restoring the principle that we mediate in an attempt to get an agreement before we go to arbitration, especially considering the bias terms in which the Government is giving direction to the arbitrator, that he shall give due cognizance to the Foisy report, which means enforcing enfranchising. Not only is franchising being forced on the postal workers, it is being forced on millions of Canadian customers who are objecting to it. However, they have no voice.
The Minister spoke very scornfully of the 23,000 members of the union and how they can hold Canada to ransom, as he put it. However, he has turned the situation upside down. It is not 23,000 union members who are holding Canada to ransom, it is the Minister and his appointed manager of the Post Office who are holding Canada to ransom by destroying a good delivery service and forcing my constituents, most of them non union, to go to much extra trouble to get their mail.
To their surprise, my constituents are beginning to see the Canadian Union of Postal Workers as their only defender. Since Parliament, dominated by a Tory Government that has grown contemptuous because of its three-quarters majority, will not protect the interests of the users of the Post Office, they find that the only defender they have left is this despised Canadian Union of Postal Workers. The union is attacked by
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
the Minister and misrepresented by the postal management and the Minister.
We are saying that all of Canada suffers because postal workers in the union, like other trade unionists in Canada are still not given the full right of citizens in Canada. They are not allowed, like other people, to give or withhold their labour by their decision. Because postal workers are treated as less than free citizens of Canada, the users of the postal service are suffering through loss of proper delivery of their mail. They will continue to suffer as long as this insane and greedy costcutting service-cutting system is imposed by the Government.
I urge Parliament to adopt this amendment concerning the date being fixed by the arbitrator, to adopt the other amendments that my caucus will be moving, and to restore at least a little of the health that has been developed over the past half century in labour negotiations on this continent.
I urge the Government to reconsider its suicide course and not try to use the Post Office as a means of destroying a union and damaging the whole principle of labour relations and labour negotiations in Canada.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
would inevitably lead to a strike if it did not negotiate the matter?

Anyone who has read the Foisy report has to come to the conclusion that long before the Government decided to bring forward Bill C-86, the two parties had gone a long way toward reaching an agreement on a number of items. In fact, if I am
allowed to quote page 3 of the Foisy report, we find that the parties have been successful in agreeing to a number of items. I will quote the French version of the Foisy report:
[ Translation]
On page 3 of his report, Mr. Foisy says: "After many meetings, the parties finally agreed to strike a compromise, which was mainly limited to withdrawing their respective demands and the signing of other provisions". The status quo. However, Mr. Foisy goes on to say, and this is important: "When I met the parties for the last time-". That was sometime ago, as he says: "-on August 12, 1987, about 75 percent of the clauses in the collective agreement had been renewed." In fact, that is one of the reasons why Bill C-86 got such a poor reception on this side of the House. The Government claimed there was a national emergency and that negotiations were not working out, while if we go back to the middle of August, by then already three-quarters of the clauses of the collective agreement had received the approval of Canada Post and the Union of Postal Workers. This means negotiations were going at a brisk pace. That happens to be one of the positive aspects of the Foisy Report but unfortunately, there is more. The report contains a number of pages I find alarming, and that is why I intend to move an amendment. In some areas the Foisy Report clearly supports the employer, the Canada Post Corporation, especially on job security, franchising and technological change. I intend to concentrate more particularly on franchising, since that is one of the controversial issues separating the Union and Canada Post.
If we look at page 25 of the Foisy Report, Mr. Speaker, we see that Mr. Foisy says the following: "In a context where the employer can legally ask the private sector to offer its services, we consider Canada Post's option to deal with the private sector a legitimate one. I would of course expect the mediator-arbitrator to take the time to read the Foisy Report. But I would not want him to feel he has an obligation to implement the report. We believe that the wording that the Government originally had was much stronger than, "Look at the conciliation officer's report", but was instead giving a direction to the mediator-arbitrator, a direction as to what he or she should be doing in the next few months.

Any sense of fairness would say that the Government using its legislative hat cannot pick and choose when arbitrators are going to look at reports of conciliation commissioners. It destroys the whole sense of fairness in collective bargaining. It destroys the whole sense of having conciliation commissioners, conciliation officers, and conciliation boards if one knows that the Government is going to use its legislative power to pick those conciliation reports it likes and include those in legislation in one form

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
or another, and when it does not like a conciliation commissioner's report, to reject it and make sure that it is not looked at by whoever is appointed to be a mediator or an arbitrator.
We suggested at second reading, as well as in numerous meetings with the Minister over the last few days, that he take out that whole subsection referring to the conciliation commissioner's report. We suggested that the Government has for its own reasons expressed an unwillingness to do so. I regret that because I think that in a bitter dispute, and with the history of friction that has existed between the Post Office and its employees, the last thing that is needed is for the House to be perceived as passing legislation which not only orders people back to work but which, because the Government likes a conciliation commissioner's report, includes that as part of the legislation.
The sense of fairness is being violated. People look upon the House of Commons as a final court. They assume that when the Government is using its legislative hat it is not also taking advantage of that hat to cover up the management hat that is underneath. That is what is happening with the legislation and with this particular clause, if it goes unamended.
While we do not believe that the amendment solves all the problems, we do believe that it reduces the degree of reference involved. I hope that when the Minister gets up, as he promised to do earlier, to explain what he believes the interpretation of this clause to be, that he will indicate especially after the amendment will be accepted by the House, that this is an indication to the mediator-arbitrator to look at the conciliation report in the same way he or she can look at the Act setting up Canada Post, or the Canada Labour Code, or all sorts of other precedents, but that the conciliation commissioner's report will not have any primacy. If that is the intent of this amendment, and that is what we understand its intent to be, then we will support it. It does help to remove a very strong sense of bias that is in this legislation. It is very important that this amendment be accepted.
I want to say that the fact that a conciliation commissioner's report is referred to in the legislation when the Government likes it and is not referred to in Government legislation when the Government does not like it does not speak well of the fairness of the Government in general terms. How can one feel safe if one is bargaining in a Crown corporation, whether it be Air Canada, Canadian National, or whether it is any of the other Crown corporations, or even government departments for that matter, if the Government is going to use its legislative power in this way?
In the past the Government has indicated that this reference of the conciliation commissioner's report is not binding on the mediator-arbitrator. report because it has been done. It has been paid for and is an available document, just as many other pieces of information are available to you". Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987
The conciliation commissioner's report looks favourably on privatization, and we find it surprising that the Government included in the Bill a clause asking the mediator-arbitrator to give due cognizance to this report. Mr. Chairman, I rise, as did my colleague, in support of the amendment to Clause 7 which would delete the word "due" from the following sentence: "give due cognizance to the report of the conciliation commissioner".
In an attempt to understand the import of these words, I turned to a dictionary. For once the dictionary-and in this case it was Oxford-was not of much help, except when it came to defining the word "due". It indicated that the word could mean a debt or an obligation. It is clear that those of us on this side of the House have taken the word "due" in this case to mean an obligation on behalf of the mediator to take cognizance of the Foisy report.
Earlier in the debate we heard that there was an imbalance in the words as between the English version and the French version. This is important because by having the word "due" in this piece of legislation, the Government is seeking to put more weight on the Foisy report or on a particular set of policy recommendations. The French version simply says the following.

-prendre serieusement connaissance du rapport du commissaire-conciliateur-

I am not an expert in French or an expert translator, so I cannot weigh the differences between the two languages. However, lawyers have looked at the word and have concluded that the English version gives a lot more weight to the instructions to the mediator-arbitrator to look at the conciliation report.
We really question the value of doing that. We also question the fairness of placing a great deal of weight upon the Foisy report. I suppose the real question would concern why we do that.
It is because the Foisy report, at least as it has been read by most commentators, starts from the assumption of accepting the Government's plan for the Post Office, the Government's plan for franchising local neighbourhood post offices. Since that is one of the key issues on the table, the Foisy report starts with a bias on one side of the table, on the management side of the table. This bias really says that if there is to be a negotiated settlement, it must start by accepting the Government's plans for the Post Office.
What would be wrong with that? The difficulty is that even the conciliator recognized that the Government's plans for franchising put at risk job security, the employment security of the people who work at the Post Office. Therefore, job security is a key issue in the dispute. If the Government's plan for franchising really raises serious questions about job security, then to be giving instructions to the mediator-arbitrator to accept the Government's plans for the Post Office is to be giving an unfair balance to the situation. It ties the hands of the mediator-arbitrator so that the person cannot consider all possibilities with an open mind.
The legislation should not give undue weight to the Government's plan for privatization. These plans have been one of the major obstacles to getting a negotiated settlement at the Post Office. Also, the plans did not come about as a result of negotiations with the union or the people who work at the Post Office. They were not consulted in terms of the drafting of the plans. In the final analysis, the public was not consulted in the drafting of those plans.
In the adoption of the objective of franchising neighbourhood post offices, turning over neighbourhood post offices to local Shoppers Drug Marts, those plans were devised behind closed doors. There was no opportunity for the public to become involved in any debate about the Post Office-why we have a Post Office, what kind of service objectives we have for the Post Office, how we want to pay for the service we receive from the Post Office, how the Post Office shall be structured, whether the Post Office is a public service or some sort of neoConservative, private, profit-making enterprise, or whether it is a way to have one more business in the community.
The opposition Parties feel that the actions of the Government in terms of the postal dispute have been biased. They have not been even-handed in terms of standing between management and labour. The Government has really taken sides. The Government is sending messages to the management at the Post Office that it does not have to negotiate with the workers, it just has to sit tight. Legislation will be passed putting in place the kind of contract wanted, so there is no need to bother about negotiating with the workers.
Clause 7 bears this out by giving undue weight to the Foisy report. This is not the only way the Government has found out how to give a message to the management at the Post Office that it really does not have to negotiate with the employees.
October 15, 1987

Ever since the postal disruption started, the Government has threatened back-to-work legislation. The problem with making that threat once the strike started, and making it on a constant basis, was that management at the Post Office knew that as long as the Government was prepared to bring in back-to-work legislation, it would put in place the kind of contract which management at the Post Office wanted. There has always been this one-sided approach to the dispute.
While we would have preferred that the Government had gone the route of mediation rather than that of back-to-work legislation, we think that it would be an improvement to the legislation if the Government would withdraw the word "due" from "give due cognizance to the report of the conciliation commissioner". This would free up the hands of the mediator arbitrator to be a little more objective in approaching the issues on the table between management and the union. It will perhaps put less weight on the conciliator's report.
While this report seems to start out from the premise of accepting the Government's plans for the Post Office, accepting in principle the fact that the Government and the management at the Post Office should proceed with privatizing post offices-one of the matters of dispute-it also pointed out that Foisy, the conciliator, had to do a lot of speculating on his own. When he met with the union and the management at the Post Office they were at loggerheads over principle questions, such as whether there should be franchising out or not. Because it is the Government's policy to bring in franchising and because the union quite legitimately feels that this is a threat to job security, the conciliator was not able to get beyond broad questions of principle into the details of what a collective agreement would look like. He did not have the opportunity to sit down with both sides and ask what this kind of a clause would mean to them if it were in a collective agreement or if wording was this way or that. He did not have a chance to look at the wording or to study things closely because the impasse was at the question of principle.
We feel it is a mistake for this legislation to give too much weight to the conciliator's report because it really gives direction to the arbitrator to put in place a kind of collective agreement which the management at the Post Office wants and which the Government appears to want. What is in the legislation is in line with the Government's plans for the Post Office and it is the Government's plans for the Post Office which are a matter of dispute.
Another thing about the Foisy report was the statement that the conflict at the Post Office would be a conflict between the Titans, that the battle would go on for a long period of time and that it would be a win-lose situation in which one of the Titans would win and the other would lose. That was the only way the conflict at the Post Office could be resolved. But ironically that is not what happened. The postal workers then went on a rotating strike. People continued to receive their mail so the public was not greatly inconvenienced. It was only when the Government moved to introduce this back-to-work legislation that they went to a full scale national postal strike.
Postal Services Continuation
This legislation caused the violent scenes that we see on television every night. This legislation caused the out and out conflict on the streets between the Titans predicted in the Foisy Report.
To sum up, I want to say that this is a good amendment. It reduces the amount of weight placed on the conciliator's report. It should give the mediator-arbitrator more of a free hand in evaluating what kind of a solution can be arrived at in place of a negotiated settlement. It will give him more room in mediating the situation.
By removing the word "due" from this clause, we hope that less weight will be placed on the conciliator's report, that there will not be a clear message for the mediator-arbitrator to follow government policy and be flexible. We hope the person who takes on this job will be given more elbow room and that he or she can take into consideration the concerns of job security which the workers will bring to the table even when those concerns come in conflict with the Government's policy of franchising. That is why we support this recommendation to remove the word "due". We consider it to be a positive step.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take too much of the House's time trying to answer all the points that have been made. Before I do that, although I hate to quote myself, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I would like to quote a short part of the speech I made at second reading:
Following release of the conciliation commissioner's report, the parties had before them a reasoned and reasonable document which should have served as a basis for negotiations towards settlement.

Consequently, on September 29, 1 asked my Associate Deputy Minister, Bill Kelly, to meet with the parties to assess what progress had been made since the release of Commissioner Foisy's report, how far the parties were apart, their willingness to compromise, and whether in his view this dispute could be resolved through the collective bargaining process short of a protracted strike with all its inherent dangers.

October 15, 1987

Mr. Kelly advised me that the parties had made no progress on the major issues in this dispute since the release of the conciliation commissioner's report on September 22, 1987. Whether or not they agree with this, of course, is their privilege, but 1 would like to remind my hon. colleagues that if we had passed this legislation through all stages last week perhaps what they call the strike would not have occurred. This being said, I would now like to address the specific amendment.
Clause 7(2)(b) reads as follows:
(b) If the mediator-arbitrator is unable to bring about agreement in respect of any such matter, hear the employer and the union on the matter, give due cognizance to the report of the conciliation commissioner that was released to them on September 22, 1987, arbitrate the matter and render a decision in respect thereof;
The French version reads:-

"if the mediator-arbitrator is unable to bring about agreement in respect of any such matter, hear the employer and the union on the matter, give due cognizance to the report of the conciliation commissioner that was released to them on September 22, 1987, arbitrate the matter and render a decision in respect thereof."
There are two points I should like to address, Mr. Speaker. First is the reference to the conciliation commissioner's report. One could argue for a long time over that, but I should like to emphasize that when the report was made public, it was commented upon by both parties and Mr. Parrot was reported to have said:

-"Commissioner Foisy made some recommendations that reflect our demands, some recommendations that reflect the employer's, others that go half-way for both and others which are not addressed. This report therefore sets the stage for serious negotiations but does not necessarily provide the basis for an agreement". It sets the basis for serious negotiations, pronounces on certain demands that are pro-management and pro-union, others that go half-way and others upon which he did not pronounce. We thought it important in the particular circumstances of this dispute to make the reference.
The reference being made, they are to give due cognizance, as the clause reads in English. In French-

"-prendre serieusement connaissance-
In French.

I know that some of my colleagues here in the House have been and may still be lawyers, and I am sure they would agree with me that one can draw different interpretations from a given text of law. I must admit that I have often pleaded on various interpretations in the past. I indicated to the Hon. Member for Churchill that I would tell him my interpretation of what I believe the text will mean once the amendment is voted upon, such amendment with which I am in agreement, just to take away a little bit of the stress.
There are various ways of determining what something means. My colleague from Winnipeg Centre referred to a dictionary. I do not know to which dictionary he referred. Usually when I want to interpret legal words, and this is just a suggestion for the future, I go to Black's Legal Dictionary. I believe that that is a well-known reference book.
Notwithstanding what can be found in various dictionaries, my interpretation of "give due cognizance" or-

-prendre serieusement en consideration-

-in the context of Clause 7(2)(b), is that it says exactly what it means. That is that he will take it into consideration since the report cannot make representations as the parties themselves can.
My hon. friends have suggested that the words may be ambiguous. I am prepared to accept that argument, notwithstanding the fact that my interpretation does not necessarily change. The mediator-arbitrator is not bound by the report. He takes cognizance or, in French-

entendre Pemployeur, le syndicat et prendre serieusement en consideration-

He takes cognizance of the report and draws his own conclusions. As the clause indicates, he can arbitrate the matter after he has looked into the report and heard the parties. Surely the mediator-arbitrator knows enough to do that.
Postal Services Continuation
Why does the Minister not stand up and admit that he is basically telling the mediator-arbitrator to do things which would favour management? In effect, through this particular clause the Government is trying to influence the decision of someone who is supposed to be objective, who is not supposed to be influenced in any way, who is supposed to look at all the facts and come to a conclusion based on those facts.
It seems to me that the Government has a hidden agenda. Why does it not stand up and own up to the fact that this clause and others are meant to dictate to the mediator-arbitrator what the Government wants in the collective bargaining agreement?

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I move:
That Bill C-86 be amended in Clause 7 by striking out lines 24 to 46 at page
3 and lines 1 to 28 at page 4 and substituting the following therefor:

7.(1) The Minister shall, after the coming into force of this Act, appoint a mediator and refer to the mediator all matters relating to the amendment or revision of the collective agreement that, at the time of the appointment, remain in dispute between the union and the employer, including the issue of franchising.
(2)	The mediator shall, within sixty days after the mediator's appointment or such longer period as the Minister may allow,
(a)	endeavour to mediate all the matters referred to in subsection (1) and to bring about agreement between the union and the employer on those matters; and
(b)	report to the Minister on the resolution of all such matters.
(3)	The mediator has, with such modifications as the circumstances require, for the purposes of the mediation referred to in paragraph 2(a), all the powers of a conciliation commissioner under Section 175 of the Canada Labour Code."
Mr. Chairman, as a preface I would like to say that I was a little taken aback by the Minister's threat to withdraw his support for the amendment that we have just passed. I did not dare get up on my feet at that moment to react. If I had said anything at that moment, if I had pointed out that the Minister was being a little touchy, a little thin-skinned, we might have lost that amendment.

You showed restraint.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation

1 restrained myself. I resisted the temptation to get up and speak the truth to the Minister to his face because I was afraid that he might carry out his threat and withdraw his support for the amendment.
I point that out because that has characterized these negotiations. The Government is thin-skinned. If you rock its boat it will get even with you. That has been bothering people with regard to the Government and the way it has been handling the negotiations at the Post Office. That is why we moved this amendment which is a comprehensive amendment dealing with the issue of the mediator.
Through this amendment we are seeking to amend Clause 7 entitled: "Mediator-Arbitrator". We want to make the distinction between a mediator and an arbitrator. Once you move to the concept of a mediator-arbitrator, a two-headed monster with two purposes, mediation and arbitration, you have in effect done away with the role of mediator.
A mediator is supposed to be impartial. Ele is supposed to be able to sit down with both sides at the table to hear the concerns, assist with the communication, and help the parties come to a negotiated agreement. The mediator has no big club. He does not have a guillotine to hang over the heads of the parties at the table. He does not have the power of law to force an agreement. The mediator's role is to bring about an agreed upon resolution between the parties, not to bang heads together and force a settlement or tell the parties what they must do.
We want to preserve the integrity of the concept of a mediator rather than reducing it to the concept of mediator-arbitrator because the arbitrator's role is different. The arbitrator's role is to be like a judge, to hear both sides of the story and then make a decision or a judgment. The arbitrator has decision-making powers.
it is important to make a distinction between the role of the mediator and the arbitrator, i hesitate to rise and speak on this matter tonight because we have in our presence one of the most distinguished mediators in our country, Mr. Bill Kelly. He made a distinguished contribution to the last dispute at the Post Office and helped to bring the parties to a negotiated settlement. He demonstrated the value of the function of a mediator.
I hesitate to even rise and speak on a matter involving labour management relations with such a distinguished gentleman with us tonight.
In any event, it is essential that we make the point that the integrity of the concept of a mediator be respected, particularly in this case. The Government failed to make use of its option of having a mediator in this dispute. While we see the word mediator in this legislation, it is linked to the arbitrator role. Therefore, the person who is supposed to be an objective
conciliator is tied to the person who makes the decision and thereby destroys the role of the mediator.
The Government created a very difficult situation by setting up a pattern of confrontation with the union at the Post Office. First, it dismissed the previous Minister responsible for the Post Office who was a rather gentlemanly person and at least gave an appearance of reasonableness. It replaced that reasonable Minister with the pit bull terrier of the front benches of the Conservative Party, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. If that is not a signal of confrontation, I do not know what is.
The Government is sending these signals with everything it does. Its first message was: "We want to fight. We want confrontation. We want to pound you into the ground". That was its message: "We will not listen to what you have to say."
We must remind the Government of the integrity of the concept of the mediator. It must explain why it bypassed its opportunity to use a mediator. We hope the Minister takes the opportunity to explain in a comprehensive way why in this legislation he is abusing the notion of a mediator and why the Government failed to use its option of appointing a mediator.
Did the Minister of Labour decide himself that he did not want to use a mediator, or were his hands tied by his Cabinet colleagues, or was it the right-wing Conservative backbenchers who handcuffed him so that he could not use all the options available to him?
It is important to respect the concept of mediation. That is why we have moved our amendment with regard to substituting the present wording of mediator-arbitrator with the concept of the mediator.
You are against anything that is a change.
I hear a faint echo.
You are not used to a sounding vessel.

Now I hear a tinkling cymbal.
The Government is following a policy of confrontation because it wants to garner some public support and show that it is strong. The Government followed that policy of confrontation and provoked a strike at the Post Office. However, now that it can see that there is not much prospect for a settlement, rather than taking the opportunity to send in a mediator as was called for by the opposition Parties, the Government took other steps which gave a bad taste to the whole situation. It prolonged the policy of confrontation and added to the public impression that the Government was interested in confrontation rather than a settlement.
First, the Government sent in the gentleman who is here with us this evening as a fact-finder and evaluator of the situation, to determine whether a settlement was possible, rather than giving him the authority to act as a mediator. Furthermore, they sent him in on the eve of the strike, which
October 15, 1987

immediately raised many suspicions. In light of a situation in which the parties were already polarized, it was not surprising that he would say a settlement was not likely under the circumstances. The Government was then free to use that as an excuse to introduce back-to-work legislation, rather than use all the options available to it.
The Government has been pursuing a policy of confrontation. That is why a mediator was never used. That is why we are dealing with this legislation.
The Government has a firm policy for the Post Office. It wants to franchise all the neighbourhood post offices and turn them over to the local Shoppers Drug Marts. Naturally, post office workers are saying that if it turns these jobs over to the private sector they will not only lose them, the pay will be cut in half. People will have to work at the minimum wage.
This policy was obviously designed for confrontation and has been a key factor in having a strike. That is why our amendment attempts to reinstate the concept of the mediator. That is why we include the phrase:	"including the issue of
franchising". We want the mediator to look at all the matters relating to the revision of the collective agreement that remain in dispute between the union and the employer, including the issue of franchising, at the time of the appointment. We do not want the mediator's hands to be tied as they are under the Government's legislation.
This legislation refers to the Foisy report which, of course, accepts the Government's policy of franchising. Therefore, it instructs the mediator-arbitrator to begin with the assumption of accepting the Government's policy of franchising. We want some flexibility so that an agreement can be drafted that will protect job security in spite of the Government having its policy of franchising.

Mr. Chairman, I want to deal with the two items contained within the amendment moved by my colleague. I want to thank the Minister of Labour for referring me to Black's Law Dictionary, with pronunciations, Fifth Edition, because there are interesting descriptions under "franchise". I would like to read some of these descriptions into the record because I think they will help all of us to understand what Canada Post intends with regard to its operations and perhaps what it may mean to the workers, as well as to the public.
Franchise.
A special privilege conferred by government on individual or corporation, and which does not belong to citizens of country generally of common right. In England it is defined to be a royal privilege in the hands of a subject.
A privilege granted or sold, such as to use a name or to sell products or services. The right given by a manufacturer or supplier to a retailer to use his products and name on terms and conditions mutually agreed upon.
In its simplest terms, a franchise is a license from owner of a trademark or trade name permitting another to sell a product or service under that name or mark.
Postal Services Continuation
More broadly stated, a "franchise" has evolved into an elaborate agreement under which the franchisee undertakes to conduct a business or sell a product or service in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor, and the franchisor undertakes to assist the franchisee through advertising, promotion and other advisory services.
Under the subheading of "General and Special":
The charter of a corporation is its "general" franchise, while a "special" franchise consists in any rights granted by the public to use property for a public use but with private profit.
I think there we have the nub. Any rights granted by the public, therefore by the Parliament of Canada through a Crown corporation, to use property for a public use but with private profit property. This Government's solution to Canada Post is to turn over as much of its operation as it feels it can get away with to the private sector, so that its private sector friends can make some money, some profit, so they can pay wages one would find paid in a fast-food outlet or in a corner store. These wages would only provide for part-time employment, not for full-time jobs which are necessary to sustain one's family. These would be jobs held by students, part-time jobs held by women, instead of full-time jobs which are now held by women in Canada Post. That is why we want to provide some additional direction to the mediator to ensure that Canada Post will finally negotiate with the Canadian Union of Postal Workers the issue of franchising.
The Foisy report makes specific reference to it. Canada Post rejected union attempts to negotiate. In fact, I was quite amazed by the offer CUPW made during the course of the negotiations going from a position I perceived as one where it was saying no franchise operations at all, to where it was saying perhaps, yes, there are areas of the country where a franchise operation would make sense in order to provide a service where one does not exist today. Canada Post said no, and the reason is because that is not how it wants to work it. Canada Post is not looking to provide additional service. It is looking at replacing existing services which are provided through full-time permanent employees of the Canada Post Corporation. Canada Post wants to shut down postal outlets and post offices in favour of a little nook or cranny in the back of a drug store somewhere.
As I indicated earlier in the House, Canada Post wants to store parcels and registered mail in the livingrooms behind the confectionery stores. That is the kind of system Canada Post is looking for. Because the corporate plan, the business plan, had to be approved by Cabinet, it is therefore the decision of the Government of the day to take this approach. It has taken this approach instead of finding methods that would ensure an increase in the volume of mail being handled by the Post Office, methods to increase the levels of service to ensure that one did not have to wait for 10, 15 or 30 minutes in a line-up at a post office, so that one could get in and out, get the stamps, get the services, get one's parcels at the post office, get the service the Post Office is required to provide.
The Post Office could have looked at increasing the areas of revenue. It is well behind in terms of electronic mail service. It

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
can do as other countries and move into banking services. We have been opening up the financial institutions to non-banking groups. Why not open them up to Canada Post? Why cave in to the demands of the business community. Canada Post started a mail-order catalogue business with Consumers Distributing to provide yet another source of income and another service, but the Government has its own blind idea as to what the Post Office should be like. It has a blind idea of a world without unions, a world where people are paid pennies. But we will continue to fight against that, whether it is in legislation like this, in our ridings or elsewhere.
It will not take much convincing to convince the people of Canada that the Government is going in the wrong direction when it comes to Canada Post. I would ask that the Government accept this amendment because it does two things. It separates the mediator from the arbitrator, and my colleague has very aptly explained the rationale behind that. Second, it forces the issue of franchising into the mediation process very clearly up front as an item that the mediator must address with the two parties.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a short comment about this amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) from the New Democratic Party. To put it briefly, this amendment would have the effect to replace the mediator-arbitrator by a mediator, who would act in this capacity only. So, I have no difficulty with this proposal as I asked the Minister to appoint a mediator, before the beginning of the strike, about 12 days ago. However, for reasons of his own that he has been trying to explain a few times, the Minister chose not to appoint a mediator. The Minister decided to propose this Draconian bill instead.

So in a way this amendment, which says let us do away with the two-hat personality that my friend, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston was referring to earlier, would take us back to a mediator only, which is what I called for days ago. I am still of the opinion that, if a mediator had been appointed, we might have avoided a strike. Or, at least, we might have avoided the tabling of this repressive legislation.
I realize that if this amendment were passed one would either have to agree to scratch the whole Bill or one would have to agree to make a number of very important consequential amendments to other clauses. Symbolically, I have to say that I cannot disagree with the proposition that says, "Let us throw the billy club out of the window, let us do it through bargaining with a mediator". It may be too late to do that at this stage but, symbolically, I think it would be difficult for me to support the idea that I could disapprove of this amendment.
Therefore I would like to commend my colleague for having brought it forward to the floor of the House of Commons
which has allowed us to speak to this particular point, which I believe is very important.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my honourable colleague for his comments. I only want to clarify a few points. Our amendment to Section 7 is very important because its purpose is to make the point that the government forgot to use a mediator in that dispute. A mediator succeeded in solving the last postal dispute with letter carriers. Then, why not use one in this strike? We want to point out that the government forgot this important step, that he had other options and alternatives to that back-to-work legislation. We also wish to point out that the appointment of a mediator-arbitrator is not a valid proposal as it combines two different roles which should be filled by two different people. The role of the mediator is to facilitate communication between the parties in dispute while the task of the arbitrator is to listen to the parties and make a decision afterwards. Our intent is to underline that the combination of those two roles is objectionable because the role of the mediator is undermined. We prefer to put the emphasis on the mediator because his role is to solve the dispute on a voluntary basis. We want the government to realize that it is better to help the parties to come to a settlement on a voluntary basis rather than forcing them to reach a new agreement.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak to the amendment to Clause 7. I think it is very important that the role of mediator in this dispute be separated from that of arbitrator. We know that during the early part of the rotating strike, which only became full-fledged after the Government brought in this legislation, there was a call for a mediator by CUPW. The Government refused to appoint a mediator. Now, it has finally agreed to the request to appoint a mediator. But it will not appoint a mediator to play the role of mediation in this dispute but, rather, forces the mediator to try to reach an agreement, always with the hammer in the other hand to say, "If you do not reach an agreement, then it will be me who will enforce a decision on the parties".
For people who are involved in mediation, the role of mediator is to go to each side, to know things about each side that he does not disclose to the other, to attempt to reach some kind of compromise. He knows where the weaknesses are in the position and goes from one side to the other, finds out if there is a basis for compromise, looks back and forth. There has to be a trust there that this mediator will play that role and not use what is told to him in a way that is contrary to the mediation process. It is a well-defined and well-recognized labour relations technique. It is a very special technique.
The role of the arbitrator, on the other hand, is quite different. The arbitrator has to be a judge. He has to make a decision based on the facts before him without trying to second-guess one party or second-guess the other. To combine
October 15, 1987

those roles into one is avoiding the proper method of dealing with labour relations disputes.
If the Government had appointed a mediator in this dispute before, even if the Government saw fit to go to legislation, we may have had a very different type of legislation. That kind of legislation would be very much like the amendments that are proposed, particularly to this clause. It would have been made clear to a mediator that what was holding up the dispute was the fact that the management of the Post Office was refusing to negotiate on the issue of franchising. That is the very issue which is causing concern about job security. The approach that the management of the Post Office has taken is very much like technological change. Technological change is an aspect of management. In an operation such as the Post Office, it is something that affects the working conditions, the career paths, the working lives of the individuals. It is therefore a very valid subject of negotiation.
When the management of the Post Office refused to deal with the issue of franchising, what it did was to refuse to bargain on the very issue which was at the nub of the dispute. To put a mediator-arbitrator into this situation without any directions as to what issues ought to be the subject of bargaining is to turn a blind eye to the real issue of the dispute. If the Government is not prepared to accept an amendment to this clause it seems that it is very clear that the Government is doing what we have been suggesting, that is, playing the role of an aid to management to force an agreement down the throats of the workers by bringing forward this legislation.
This motion to amend Clause 7 includes the issue of franchising. It appears that there must be direction given to the management of the Post Office to sit down to discuss this issue, not just have the mediator-arbitrator look at the Foisy report, which report gives a certain type of direction but which ignores the fact that the franchising arrangement can be the subject of negotiations. In fact, it has been offered by CUPW. The negotiators have suggested that they are prepared to discuss franchising, and prepared to reach compromises on it. That is the very essence of labour relations and collective bargaining, even in a strike situation, that there is give and take which is required, and that give and take must be on all issues in dispute.
In this situation, there must be a direction to the parties, and particularly to the management of the Post Office to discuss the issue of franchising. Once that step has been taken, a mediator and a direction for Canada Post management to discuss franchising, then we will see if the parties can actually reach an agreement once the Government has stated as a matter of policy that Canada Post's management must discuss franchising with the union as an appropriate collective bargaining item.
If that does not happen, I think that the role of the mediator-arbitrator as proposed by the Government is one which is
Postal Services Continuation
faulty and will not lead to harmony in the Post Office. In fact, it will lead to a further exacerbation of the unhappy relations between management and the union.

Mr Speaker, again I do not intend to indulge in rhetoric as some of my friends seem to be doing tonight. However, Mr. Speaker-

I would like to refer to one particular remark which was made by my friend, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre when he referred to my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who is also responsible for the Post Office, as being the "pit bull" Minister.
I would like to point out, Mr. Chairman, in the case of that particular appointment where the Prime Minister gave my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the responsibility for the Post Office, obviously the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had the benefit of knowing who the critic for the NDP was.
To be a little more serious, with respect to the amendment and the various comments that have been made around it, I would like to point out that my hon. colleague from Saint-Jacques has referred to his request in the House to appoint a mediator which was refused at the time by myself.
I would like to draw the attention of all Hon. Members to the fact that part of the reasoning and the advice that I received when I was making the decision to appoint or not to appoint a mediator, came from my Associate Deputy Minister. As everybody knows, he is one of the most experienced, if not the most experienced, as was suggested by my hon. colleague from Winnipeg North Centre.
At the time when the possibility existed, we decided and concluded that appointing a mediator would perhaps not be a good decision. But to make sure, I sent my Associate Deputy Minister to meet with the parties and to assess the situation, as I indicated in the quote in my speech on an earlier amendment. The decision and conclusion at the time was that it would not be a good solution to appoint a mediator. Obviously those are judgment calls. I believe that my friend, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques, will agree with that. He may not agree with my decision, but he will agree that it was a judgment call. In my mind, it was very well-founded at the time.
I do agree with my friend, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques, that it would not be appropriate at this point to accept the amendments suggested by my hon. colleagues from the NDP, because we have passed that stage. A solution in this particular dispute at this particular time is the mediation-arbitration concept. Perhaps this is not used as often as the appointment of a mediator on the one hand, or an arbitrator on the other hand, but it is a concept that has been used successfully in the past, particularly in the 1978 legislation with respect to the Post Office, if my memory serves me correctly.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
It has also been used in other circumstances where the parties came to an agreement.
I believe in the circumstances, the decision of the Government to refer the matter to a mediator-arbitrator is the correct one, and consequently we will not support that amendment.

As 1 indicated earlier in the evening, in preparing this amendment we wished to point out the fact that the Government did have other options. At the time that it introduced this legislation, it could have appointed a mediator. This was asked for by the union involved, by myself, and also by others.
I point out again that at the time the legislation was introduced, and at the time people were calling for a mediator, there was no national strike. There were rotational strikes. The Government and the Minister responsible for the Post Office did claim that the mail was getting through. We believed that appointing a mediator could have worked. We believed that a mediator should have been appointed. We still believe that that is the case.
Also, in this amendment there is an instruction to include the issue of franchising at the table. We have to remind the Members of the House sitting in Committee of the Whole, and others, that the Government, through the Minister responsible for Canada Post, time after time has stated that the issue of franchising out is a management right, it is not something to be negotiated. It is a government decision. That is the decision that has caused this strike. We believe that is the problem facing the country at the present time with regard to this dispute.
If the Government believes that it can refer to a conciliation commissioner's report that it considers favourable to the Government, one that is liked by the Minister responsible for Canada Post, certainly in the same legislation we in the Opposition should be able to make the point that the House should also be giving an instruction. The instruction is to discuss with the employees affected the whole issue of franchising out. That should be discussed at the negotiating table. It certainly affects the job security of those people. It is something that affects where they will work in the future; if they will be working for Canada Post, the type of work that they will be doing, and it is something that normally would be discussed at the table.
That does not mean that the employees through their union will get everything that they want, because that probably will not happen. But it does mean that the matter of where franchising will take place, how it will take place, and when it will take place will be discussed. Those are logical things to negotiate at the table.
The people who work at the wickets in Thompson, The Pas, Flin Flon, Winnipeg, Montreal, and right cross the country know that the job they are doing at the present time, which many have done for years, will disappear under the Government's plan. They know that, even if they have worked at that
wicket for eight, ten, or a dozen years, although people are still coming to those wickets of their own free choice, because of the government plan that job will disappear. The people know that will happen. Because of that they expect their union, as their representative, to go to management and discuss that item, see how it will be implemented, and where it will be implemented.
It has been management, on the direct orders of the Government, that is refusing to discuss that item. It is important to say in tonight's debate that this is not a strike based upon the union asking for more. Obviously there are other clauses involved in the negotiations, but this is a dispute about where those people will be working in the future. It is ironic that the Government is willing to order these people back to work and, if they do not return to work, they will face heavy fines. However, some two months to four months down the road they could lose their jobs. The Government can order them back to work, but it refuses to order Canada Post to keep those people working. What a contradiction! It thinks it is important for those people to go back to work, but at the same time it is taking that work and giving it to someone else. That is what is happening with this piece of legislation.
As I said at second reading, we are not dealing with technological change for the most part. We are dealing with the Government taking away jobs, quite often from women, jobs which pay decent salaries, the better jobs within the postal system. The Government is saying that they cannot have those jobs any more, that they will be given to sub post offices. The person who takes the new job will probably receive minimum wage, have no pension plan, have no benefits, have no job security.
What kind of affirmative action program is that for a Government? It is not something new. It is something the Government has already done. For example, at one time the people who cleaned major post offices across the country were government employees. Their jobs disappeared. They were laid off. They lost their positions. Then the jobs were contracted out to individuals or companies in the private sector that sometimes hired the same cleaners at minimum wage. It is shameful. It is disgusting.
The Government is saying that it is a management decision, that it is the business plan, and that it must happen. However, it refuses to let Canada Post discuss that with its employees through their representatives in CUPW.
It is not only a matter of having a mediator. It is time for the Government to recognize, through its Crown corporation, that the major issues in dispute must be negotiated and discussed with the people they affect.

Mr. Chairman, I have a brief question for the Minister of Labour. The Minister made some comments about the clause dealing with a mediator-arbitrator, but he did not
October 15, 1987

comment upon the distinction between the role of a mediator and the role of an arbitrator.
I want to ask him about this distinction. The mediator is there as a third party who can gain the trust of the parties to the dispute in order to facilitate communications and to bring about a voluntary settlement. An arbitrator is someone who has decision-making powers. When these roles are put into one, the integrity of the role of the mediator is undermined. I would like the Minister to comment on that. From what he has said so far, I did not get any understanding that he appreciates the difference between the two roles and the points we have been making in that area.

Mr. Chairman, I agree in part with what the Hon. Member for York South-Weston said a little while ago on another amendment, particularly when he mentioned that the people we appoint are very skilled and responsible.
The person who will be appointed as mediator-arbitrator will obviously understand the two hats that he or she will be wearing. I am convinced that the person will do his or her utmost to get the parties back at the table to try to mediate and arrive at a settlement.
If there is one thing upon which we all agree, regardless of politics, it is that the best settlement is a negotiated one. Consequently, the person appointed will do his or her utmost to arrive at that particular settlement without the population of Canada being subjected to a protracted strike or work stoppage during that period of time.
If mediation fails, as, unfortunately, perhaps signs tend to indicate, the person, whoever he or she may be, according to the legislation and the particular articles to which we have been referring, will arbitrate the dispute that exists between the parties at that time.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with the issue of franchising. My comrade from Winnipeg-North Centre who spoke on this matter concerned himself with franchising and said that the management of the Post Office was taking the position that it was a management right.
Would the Minister tell us whether he sees a difference between franchising out, contracting out, and other management rights? Does he see franchising out or franchising as a management right that is not a proper subject for collective bargaining? If so, he would be agreeing with the management of the Post Office in that regard and he would be taking a very archaic view of management rights.
In many collective agreements across the country there are clauses defining the work of the bargaining unit and clauses on management rights. At one time management had the right to do everything, until these rights had been negotiated through collective bargaining. Now they must promote on the basis of merit, not on the basis of favouritism or of promoting one's relatives, and they must give people the opportunity to apply
Postal Services Continuation
for jobs. Perhaps all these things at one time were management rights, but now they are not.
There is no magic in the word "franchising". Contracting out is the subject of many collective agreements. It must be negotiated or agreed upon, as is the case with technological change and many other factors in collective bargaining.
Would the Minister tell us whether he sees the franchising issue as a sole right of management, the union having no right to discuss it, or is it a proper item for collective bargaining?

Mr. Speaker, I believe I have already quoted a clause that was criticized earlier, namely: That the mediator-arbitrator was to hear the employer and the union and give cognizance to the Foisy report.
I think that the mediator-arbitrator will indeed hear both parties. I suppose that the parties, particularly the one that is represented by my hon. colleague, will give their views to the mediator-arbitrator who will take them into consideration, together with the position of the employer and the recommendations of commissioner Foisy who renders a decision in part on the issue referred to by my hon. colleague. And I believe that the mediator-arbitrator, the employer and the union will properly settle the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I am still having some difficulty with the concept known as mediator-arbitrator. I am certain Canadians who are watching tonight are wondering what in fact we are talking about. The labour experts will understand the difference between a conciliator, an arbitrator and a mediator. They all have certain functions, powers and responsibilities. I suppose at some point in time we learned in school about the differences. Now a new monster has been created. The Minister indicated in a different dispute that a mediator-arbitrator entity had been created.
Under a Liberal Government was it?

When you get to the point where you have to resort to back-to-work legislation, you are beyond the point of mediating, you are at the point where the two parties, management and labour, are so far apart that you need an arbitrator, a judge, to say, "This is the decision. This is the collective bargaining agreement". Obviously if during the arbitration process the parties decide to agree on their own without risking what an arbitrator might decide, that is all in the best interests of everyone involved because the parties, in effect, have negotiated a settlement.
I have some difficulty in entrenching this mediation-arbitration concept in this legislation. Let us not try to kid anyone. This Bill is called an Act to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services. That is all fine and dandy. We know what this legislation is all about. It is back-to-work

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
legislation. It is forcing people to go back to work. It is forcing the postal workers to work, and if they do not, they are subject, as Clause 10 says, to some pretty heavy financial penalties. Then there are some additional penalties with regard to suspension from union activity if they contravene a certain section of the Act. We will have more to say when we get to Clause 11.
We do not understand why this concept of mediator arbitrator is necessary. The Minister himself admitted that at one point it was not possible, feasible-he called it a judgment call-or appropriate to appoint a mediator. That was after the strike. The Minister is shaking his head. Sometime, somewhere a decision was made by him and his officials that a mediator was not appropriate, even though we in the Liberal Party suggested that a mediator ought to have been appointed because a mediator might have been able to succeed in bringing the parties together at some point prior to the escalation of the violence in the conflict. Now we are at a point where there is basically a gun to the collective heads of the union. The Minister is a party to this threat of pointing a gun at the heads of the union saying "You are going back to work. If you don't go back to work, you have double trouble. Not only will we fine you $10,000 or $50,000 a day but we will make sure that you do not participate in union activity for up to five years."
The mediator-arbitrator, this experienced, skilled person who will be appointed under this legislation, will be aware of exactly what has transpired to date. He will be fully aware of what is in the legislation. Does the Minister really believe that simply by calling this person a mediator-arbitrator somehow he or she will be able to do something other than what an arbitrator might do on his or her own? I fail to understand why at one point it was his judgment call that mediation was not possible and that somehow now that the parties are so far apart back-to-work legislation is needed and all of a sudden mediation is needed by someone who would pat both sides on their backs and say, "Come on guys. Let's get together and call it a day, get back to work and start delivering the mail". I do not understand why a mediator-arbitrator is needed.
1 think the Minister should admit that this piece of legislation has a sledgehammer approach in it. It says to the union, "Go back to work. We have an arbitrator. We are telling the arbitrator to look at the conciliator's report. We are giving direction to the arbitrator to find in favour, or lean toward, the position of management". That seems to me to be patently unfair and inappropriate in the circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, there are various things 1 could say, but some have already been said and some will not serve any purpose anyway.
With respect to this legislation, that it is back-to-work legislation, I think that is self-evident. One of the clauses in the Bill says specifically that, that the employees must go back to work. It is very clear that that is one of the purposes of the legislation.
At the time I made a judgment call that the appointment of a mediator would not have been appropriate because the parties were so far apart. I still believe that the parties are far apart. 1 believed that the day we introduced the legislation, particularly after having the assessment of my Associate Deputy Minister to that effect. Therefore, I concluded that back-to-work legislation was required. Notwithstanding the decision that back-to-work legislation was required, I also decided that, because of certain requests, including one from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint Jacques, and one from the union with respect to mediation, perhaps it was worth-while, as some would say, to give it a shot. That is provided for in this legislation. I hope, I sincerely hope, that the parties will prove that I was wrong, that there is a possibility of coming to a settlement. I will be the first one to praise the parties the day they come to an agreement. Our Government will not tolerate, as was done before the introduction of the legislation, the playing of musical chairs nor Canadians being submitted to protracted disruptions because of work stoppages, violence, and accrued violence.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the opening remarks of the Minister when he said that he did not believe in any event that anything he said would be listened to. I want to assure him that if he says the right thing we will listen to it very carefully.
That is not what I said.

The Minister said that this is not what he said. I will accept that. Reflecting the dilemma that we have found in negotiations between Crown corporations and unions is an assumption on the part of Governments that somehow or other all the problems that are facing collective bargaining lie at the feet of unions. There are two parties to negotiations. In my experience and observation of the manner in which Crown corporations conduct negotiations, they clearly go into those negotiations knowing full well that if an agreement is not concluded the Government will step in and legislate workers back to work. It has happened continuously. I think it is high time, quite frankly, that Members on all sides of the House should perhaps strike some kind of a committee to investigate the process of collective bargaining with Crown corporations and their employees through their organizations. Certainly the mechanism in place now does not work. It does not work to anyone's advantage, whether it be the public's, the Crown corporations', the unions or its members. It is something worth-while taking a look at.
One of the key problems in these negotiations has been the post offices and, I assume from everything I have heard, the Government's insistence that the Post Office should be reorganized. A very sore point centers on the franchising of operations. It is not only the union that is concerned about reorganization in the Post Office, it is also the customers, the clientele which the Post Office is attempting to serve. I want to read one letter which is typical of the number of letters I have
October 15, 1987

received from constituents on this whole question of reorganization in the Post Office and the effect it is having on the mail service. My constituent, Sandra Hanmer, writes:
Here is an example of how it is serving me-1 received a card saying 1 had a registered mail letter awaiting pick-up. The address on the card wasn't the usual one of Station 'H' on the Danforth, a few dozen yards from where 1 work. It was that of a Shopper's Drug Mart. So I took the half hour's walk down to Shopper's World at Danforth and Victoria Park where there is a large Shopper's Drug Mart. There's also a huge Shopper's Drug Mart much nearer at Main and Danforth but this doesn't have a post office counter. Too convenient for all the thousands of tenants in the Main Square complex, 1 guess.
The postmistress at Shopper's Drug Mart at Shopper's World couldn't find my envelope. She finally took a look at my card and said, "No wonder I couldn't find your letter, you have to go down to Queen St. Shopper's Drug Mart, not this one." Fortunately, I'm a strong person and a good walker and own a bicycle also, so 1 was able to make the trek down to Queen Street. Fortunately, 1 don't work Wednesday mornings so I can reserve it for these little jaunts.
I live, work and shop in different places and none of them is down on Queen St., a place I rarely visit unless I'm going for an early morning cycle on the boardwalk. If you'd really done "a thorough analysis of where we need Post Offices" you would realize that we need one at Main & Danforth or continue to keep parcels and registered letters, etc. at Station 'H'.
I live at Gerrard & Woodbine, where there's a little post office and drycleaners but I can't get my letters there. 1 work very near Station 'H' on the Danforth, I can no longer get letters or parcels there. I shop at Main & Danforth where there's no post office at all. I have to take time to go miles out of my way-I don't call this an improvement in service. Not to mention the abolition of all the mailboxes which used to be around.
Representatives of the Post Office went through my constituency and unilaterally, without any kind of reason or rationale, picked mailboxes up from corners and chucked them into the back of trucks. One fellow who runs a corner store next to one of these mailboxes asked them why they were removing it, and they said it was because it was not used any longer. He said to the two fellows who were picking up this mailbox: "Well, open it up" and the guys opened it up. The thing was stacked with mail. It was well used.
Removing these boxes presents real difficulties for many elderly people, particularly during the winter months when they have to walk several additional blocks on sometimes icy or snow-bound sidewalks. I could go on and on.
It seems to me that the point the Hon. Member for St. John's East made earlier in his argument as to why franchising or contracting out should be a part of the collective bargaining process is something which I would think would be in the Government's interest to encourage. We all want to see that kind of maturity in collective bargaining. We should tell Canada Post that it has an obligation to the public, to its employees and to Parliament and it should put that item on the table for collective bargaining. I would like to hear what the Minister would say on that.
Amendment (Mr. Keeper) negatived.

On Clause 10-Offence by individuals.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a few moments to address Clause 7. I must say that I was disappointed that the Minister did not take the opportunity to respond to the comment my colleague made on the earlier clause. He pointed out the difficulties that exist for senior citizens when mailboxes are picked up off the street and senior citizens have to walk long distances under severe winter conditions. The Minister chose not to respond to that. One of the problems is that the Government does not hear when we bring to its attention what is happening to seniors and ordinary Canadians. It fails to respond or answer to these concerns.
I would like to deal specifically with Clause 10, the enforcement clause. It reads:
An individual who contravenes any provision of this Act is guilty of an
offence punishable on summary conviction and is liable, for each day or part of
a day during which the offence continues, to a fine
(a) of not less than $10,000 or more than $50,000, where the individual was acting in the capacity-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) on a point of order.

I want some clarification, Mr. Chairman. I thought, and I may be wrong, that clause 10 had been agreed to and that we were considering clause 11. But if I am wrong . . . Are we still on clause 10? Very well! I apologize.
