I can understand the impatience of the Minister. I am sure he wants this clause to be adopted. However, we want to deal with it.
The implications of this clause should be brought to the attention of the Canadian public. The clause provides that there will be fines of from $10,000 to $50,000 imposed on any individual who is acting in the capacity of an officer or representative of the employer or the union and of not less than $500 or more than $1,000 in any other case. The clause also provides for fines of $20,000 to $100,000 to be imposed upon the employer or the union.
These are very heavy fines. Why does the Government find it necessary to threaten individuals with fines of upwards of $50,000 and to threaten the union with fines of up to $100,000 a day? Why does the Government feel it is necessary to put this gun to the heads of those who are leading the workers at the Post Office?
Why is the Government using such Draconian legislation to force these workers back to work? The key issue on the table in the dispute is the question of franchising. Why is the Government willing to use such heavy penalties to put in place

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
its policy of franchising? Is this franchising policy such a good policy that it merits the use of such heavy fines?
I would like to raise one question about the whole matter of franchising. Today, I might have a neighbourhood post office, but tomorrow morning it might be in a Shoppers Drug Mart.
A fundamental policy of the federal Government for the last few years has been to provide service in the official language of your choice. If your mother tongue is French, you can get service in French. If your mother tongue is English, you can get service in English. The Post Office has been slow to live up to the policy of bilingualism, which is so crucial to keeping the country together. Franchising will make that even more difficult.
If the Government cannot assure service in the language of your choice when the employees of the Post Office are direct employees of the Government, how can it do so when the service is provided in a drug store? I wonder whether the Government has thought about what will happen to the language rights of Canadians. If the language rights of Canadians are further undermined, what will happen to the unity of the country?
The Government is so set on the policy of franchising that it is willing to impose fines of $10,000, $50,000 and $100,000 per day. I would like to know whether the Minister, the Cabinet and the Government have considered the implications of franchising on the policy of bilingualism. How will they ensure that people can get service in the language of their choice?
Would the Minister do us the courtesy of responding to that? I have yet to hear an explanation from the Government on this. It is obviously something that the Government is pushing for very strongly since it is prepared to impose such large fines in support of it. Would the Minister comment on how the Government will assure the provision of service in the official language of your choice under the franchise system when it has had such a dismal record of providing it until now when it has been more within its control?
I see that the Minister refuses to stand up. I gave him an opportunity to do so. Is the Minister willing to stand up?
Sure.
Would he then comment on that question? This is fundamental to Canadian unity.

Mr. Chairman, I am prepared, of course, to give explanations on this Bill without hesitation. I would prefer to listen to the other Members who have comments on this clause and will answer all questions at the end.

Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed that the Minister has not answered my question. He will perhaps do it later on, but I am nevertheless disappointed that he did not
take right away the opportunity to answer it, because the Government has clearly indicated its willingness to go to any lengths to ram through this back-to-work legislation related to postal workers. As we know, franchising out is one of the key issues regarding the problems of post offices. How does the Government think it will be able to maintain its policy of bilingualism in this country once post offices are privatized, when the level of service the public is entitled to has not even been reached?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to comment on Clause 10 of the Bill. It is hard to say which clause of this Bill is the worst. However, I find it astounding that a minimum fine of $10,000 will be imposed for each day or part of a day that someone violates this legislation. We have many laws in this country. We have the Criminal Code with hundreds of sections which provides for minimum fines and minimum sentences. Lives are endangered and lost every day because of impaired driving and there is a minimum fine for that offence, but is is not $10,000. Until recently it was $50.
Under this legislation a shop steward or minor official in the postal union, perhaps a picket captain or officer of a local, who contravenes this legislation is liable to a minimum fine of $10,000. For example, Clause 4 provides that "each officer and representative of the union shall . . . take all reasonable steps to ensure that employees comply with paragraph 3(b)" which provides that "every employee shall, when so required, forthwith continue or resume, as the case may be, the duties of that employee's employment".
If a judge decides that a shop steward did not take all reasonable steps to ensure that other employees go back to work he will be fined $10,000 for that horrid crime for each day or part thereof.
We must have some very serious situations to deal with if an officer must take all reasonable steps to ensure that employees comply with that paragraph. Maybe a judge would decide that it would be reasonable for the union to expel its members if they did not comply exactly with every section of this Bill. Then the union would be fined a minimum of $20,000 a day even if it complied with this legislation and told its members to go back to work as we have every reason to believe it will. Under this Bill a minimum fine of $10,000 may be imposed for what may be a very minor violation of this legislation. If we were talking about concerted defiance of the legislation in its entirety by the entire union, perhaps there would be a need for such stringent measures.
One wonders where the Government is coming from in proposing such legislation. Perhaps the Minister of Labour could tell us what other legislation provides for such fines for such potentially minor offences.
Minimum fines have always been criticized by defence council in cases where a technical violation of the law may
October 15, 1987

have occurred, which calls for the sympathy of the court. Any members who are lawyers will have often heard judges say that while there has been a technical violation of the law, the case he has heard is a sympathetic one in which there are extenuating circumstances and therefore the punishment of being before the court is enough.
However, while the judge may want to give an absolute discharge or conditional discharge, in this case he would indicate that he cannot do so because he is bound by the law. While there may be a minor technical violation, a judge in this case might say that while he has listened to the circumstances surrounding the case, the breach of the legislation was not very serious, the fine he must impose is $10,000. If the breach of the legislation takes places over two days, the fine will be $20,000.
1 submit that a minimum fine of $10,000 is outrageous. This legislation only involves a summary conviction, and even serious crimes under the Criminal Code which are indictable offences do not have fines of $10,000.
Until two years ago the minimum fine for the indictable offence of impaired driving was $50. It is now $350, yet the minimum fine for a breach of this legislation at any time during the continuance of the collective agreement which is referred to is $10,000. We all know how the courts define a strike. It can range from one or two individuals having a strike to a general strike.
While there are illegal strikes from time to time in this country, they occur more often when legislation is passed making collective bargaining inoperative. The usual remedy for anyone engaging in a wildcat strike is to get an injunction through the court. In this case, however, any time during the course of this collective agreement anyone who is a representative of the union, whether or not it is authorized by the union, will be subject to a minimum fine of $10,000. The minimum of $10,000 provided for in Clause 10 is absolutely outrageous. It does not provide for the judicial discretion, which is very important in the administration of justice in this country.
I understand that this is not a justice Bill. Perhaps the Minister of Labour did not consult with the officials of the Department of Justice when he was establishing minimum fines of such astounding proportions in this legislation.
Perhaps the Minister could indicate whether he believes there are cases where judicial discretion is required and a minimum fine of $10,000 is not appropriate. While our judicial system exists to enforce the laws, there must be some tolerance of the fact that there may be extenuating circumstances in individual cases that call for discretion on the part of the judge. Judges are given very wide discretion to deal with all sorts of crimes.
The Government is telling judges that they cannot use their discretion in this case and take special circumstances into account. The Government is not prepared to allow a judge to exercise discretion and give less than a $10,000 fine to an
Postal Services Continuation
ordinary working person. He does not have the power to say that such a fine is inappropriate and can be reserved for a more serious case.
Did the Minister's officials review the Criminal Code to determine the seriousness of this crime compared to other crimes which had minimum fines? Why did he set a minimum fine of $10,000 and not provide for discretion by a federally appointed judge so he might hear a case like this and deal with the facts before him without the Government telling him that he must fine someone $10,000 a day?

Mr. Chairman, before I comment on Clause 10, I want to ask the Minister when the enforcement provision, Clause 10, ends. In other words, we know that the penalties will begin if there is a breach as soon as the law is passed, presumably sometime tomorrow. Does the enforcement provision lapse upon the expiry of the 90 days or upon the entering into of the collective agreement as provided for by Clause 8?
While he is on his feet, will he indicate how many people in the last 20 years have been prosecuted under enforcement provisions of federal back-to-work legislation and, of those prosecuted, how many were employees and how many were representatives of employers, and what were the penalties imposed by the courts?
Once the Minister has answered those questions, I would like to make some very brief comments on Clause 10.

Mr. Chairman, I do not have the information with respect to the number of convictions during the last 20 years. I do recall one instance of back-to-work legislation which was breached. It is the one concerning CUPW, following the 1978 back-to-work legislation when there was at least one prosecution in which I believe the person ended up in jail for some time. Presumably there may be some others, but I am willing to look into that and report back to my hon. colleague at the earliest opportunity.
With respect to the severity of the fines, I will not try to convince the House that they are not severe. They are. They are severe in this particular legislation for the same reasons that they were severe in Bill C-24, which we adopted in November, 1986, and for the same reasons they were severe in Bill C-85, adopted a month ago with respect to the railway industry. They are the same fines, exactly the same sections, and we will stand by them again.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the Minister could answer my question with regard to when the enforcement provisions expire, then I will make my comments. The Bill provides for very heavy fines here and I would like to know when they expire.

They are in force as long as the collective agreement is in force.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation

Mr. Chairman, we are dealing here with Clause 10, but Clause 10 cannot be considered in isolation. One has to, it seems to me, look at Clause 11 as well. The sidenote beside Clause 11(1) reads "Additional Punishment-Union", and the sidenote on Clause 11(2) is "Additional Punishment-Employer". First, with regard to Clause 10, 1 think the Minister will agree that this particular enforcement provision, although it applies to both employee and employer, in this case postal workers and Canada Post, is directed at employees. I am sure that if the Minister were to review the last 20 or 50 years he would be hard pressed to find a situation where a representative of management has been prosecuted under back-to-work legislation. So let us not kid anyone. Even though it says a representative of the employer is subject to these rather heavy fines, we are really talking about employees and CUPW. Let me read Clause 10(1), Mr. Chairman. It reads:
An individual who contravenes any provision of this Act is guilty of an
offence punishable on summary conviction and is liable, for each day or part of
a day during which the offence continues, to a fine
(a) of not less than SI0,000 or more than $50,000, where the individual was acting in the capacity of an officer or representative of the employer or the union when the offence was committed;-
So that first part deals with union officers and representatives of the employer, but in effect we are talking about union officers. The Minister laughs, but he knows that he is not going to prosecute anyone in Canada Post management under this clause. It is directed at CUPW members.
A court would have no discretion whatsoever. If there is a contravention, regardless of how minor the contravention, the fine is SI0,000 a day or any part of a day. So if a technical breach lasts for 10 minutes or 15 minutes and there is a prosecution, the court would have no discretion whatsoever but to fine that union official a minimum of $10,000 and, depending on who is sitting on the bench and the circumstances, the fine could go as high as $50,000.
That in and of itself is patently unfair and inequitable. It raises considerable concern. This section says: "An individual who contravenes any provision of this Act". What is a "provision of this Act"? This Act, if one reads from Clause 1 through to Clause 13, requires management and union to do a number of things. It is not specific. It is not clear and unambiguous. There are clauses in here that might lead one to question exactly what was meant by the legislation. We all know the workers have to go back to work, that is clear. As the law says, they have to resume their duties. Clause 4 states:
The union and each officer and representative of the union (a) shall, forthwith on the coming into force of this Act,-
And that is within 12 or 24 hours.
-give notice to the employees-
What does that mean? If the employees have to be back at work within 12 hours or 24 hours, how does one give notice to the employees? How many employees are involved at Canada Post?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Of those under the collective agreement, there are 23,000.

Twenty three thousand employees. We know the Post Office is shut down so we cannot mail them a letter and say: "Here is your notice. Go back to work". We could send them a telegram, I suppose, but who will pay for 23,000 telegrams? This legislation requires them to be back at work within a 12 or 24 hour period. Is the Minister assuming that these 23,000 postal workers involved in this particular situation are each watching these proceedings with bated breath and this is their notice? The court could say that when the Minister was standing in the House, that was sufficient notice. The Minister can see the ridiculousness of the offence here. It is meant, I suppose, to deter the union but it is a sledge-hammer approach.
The Minister talks about a mediator-arbitrator. There is still some hope. The Minister is a reasonable guy. He still hopes that somehow there will be a negotiated settlement. But how does he really expect, in all sincerity, the union to come to the table with the arbitrator sitting at the head and management sitting across and be in a very good mood when we have Clause
10	saying, "If you dare breach one section of this particular legislation, we are going to fine you $10,000, and if that is not enough, we are going to leave it up to the court under Clause
11	to prohibit that particular union officer from participating in union activities for five years"?
If the Minister really wants some co-operation from the union officers in CUPW, he would not bring into effect Clause 10 and Clause 11. It is a threat. If this is not provocation to breach this particular Act, I do not know what is. It certainly does not serve to create an atmosphere of co-operation.
If I may continue, Mr. Chairman, there is a minimum penalty of $10,000 if one does not give notice to the employees that, and I quote from Clause 4(l)(a):
-by reason of the coming into force of this Act, postal operations are forthwith to be continued or resumed, as the case may be, and the employees, when so required, are forthwith to continue or resume, as the case may be, the duties of their employment;
What does all this mean? The employees are asking what it all means. It is not that specific. Mr. Kelly is an expert in labour law and the Minister, by virtue of the office he holds, has presumably acquired considerable degree of knowledge on this particular subject, but we are talking about 23,000 ordinary Canadians who do not have the expertise of Mr. Kelly or the Minister of Labour and they are being told that if they breach any provision of this Act they are subjecting themselves to a minimum $10,000 fine per day, if they or an officer of the corporation, and if they are just a run of the mill regular worker, they will be fined $500 per day. These guys are not earning $500 a day, yet they are going to be fined a minimum of $500 a day if they breach any provision of this Act.
It is obvious that there are problems because the Act is not specific enough. Therefore, we will have the technical breaches of the legislation. The Minister might stand up and say: "Let
October 15, 1987

us be reasonable, we are not going to prosecute every minor breach", but that is not the case. When we pass laws here one has to assume that any breach is a breach and it ought to be prosecuted.
I hope the Minister is not going to suggest that we will leave it up to the police to decide whether they are going to prosecute under this back-to-work Bill C-86. 1 hope he is not suggesting that, because that is not the role of the police. We are passing a piece of legislation and it must stand on its own.
This particular Clause 10(1) provides for Draconian measures. As the Hon. Member for St. John's East pointed out, there are not that many pieces of federal legislation that have penalties as severe as these. That leads me to ask the following question. Why are they as severe as they are? What is the purpose of having this particular clause in this Bill? Why a $10,000 minimum fine per day as opposed to $50, $100, or no minimum fine at all?
I note that there is no provision in this Bill for incarceration, in other words, jail. Why is the Minister not providing for a minimum jail term in this legislation? He referred to a situation not so long ago in which a prominent member of CUPW spent time in prison. Did that legislation at the time provide for imprisonment, or was it a similar type of legislation to what we have here today? He has not provided for any period of incarceration. Perhaps that would have been a different approach. I would like to hear from the Minister as to why he decided to impose such heavy fines for breaches under this Bill and why he did not consider other possible penalties.
Not only is the Minister creating an atmosphere of provocation with Clause 10, the union is down on the ground and he decides to feed the union the boots by imposing Clause 11. What the Minister is saying is, "$10,000 a day is not enough. We want to leave it up to the court to prohibit a union member from participating in union activity for up to five years". I ask the Minister-
Not up to the court.

Let me read the clause so that we are clear. Clause 11(1) states:
No individual who is convicted of an offence under this Act that was committed while the individual was acting in the capacity as an officer or representative of the union shall be employed in any capacity by, or act as an officer or representative of, the union at any time in the five years immediately after the date of the conviction.
It is worse.
As the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell, who is not learned in law-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would like to remind the Hon. Member that when we get to Clause 11 there will probably be amendments made concerning the point that he is now talking about.
Postal Services Continuation

Obviously, you are privy to information that I am not privy to, Mr. Chairman. However, we are dealing with Clause 10.
As the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell pointed out, if one is convicted-and this is why it is important-of an offence under Clause 10, not only is one fined but one is suspended from union activity. There is no discretion. Right, Mr. Harris?
None in there.

And it is automatic that one is prohibited from participating in union activities for five years. Well, it goes on to state in Clause 11(2) that if an employer or a representative of the employer breaches any part of this Bill, or is found guilty of a breach of a provision of it, then he cannot be employed by Canada Post for five years. That is nonsense. In effect it is a sentence. One is not going to prosecute any employer. One is not going to prosecute Mr. Lander or any of his cohorts. That is not what this legislation is all about. That is not what this clause is all about.
It is obvious that this particular enforcement provision is in breach of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I do not think one has to go too far to conclude that-
Take it to court.

The Hon. Member opposite says, "Take it to court". That is the typical Tory way. If a member of that Party does not like legislation, then they say that we should take it to court. That is shirking one's responsibilities as a parliamentarian here. Our responsibility is to pass laws that will withstand court challenges, not to pass laws hoping for a court challenge.
But one does not have to go too far, Mr. Minister, to realize that it is in fact a breach of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is cruel and unusual punishment when there is a punishment of a minimum fine of $10,000, and on top of that mandatory or automatic suspension from union activity for five years.
I hope the Minister in the next few hours will reconsider this Draconian clause and delete completely Clause 11 and modify Clause 10 in order to create an atmosphere in which the two parties will try to the greatest extent and to the greatest degree possible to co-operate to create a work environment over the next several years that will be in the best interests of management, labour and the public.

Mr. Chairman, I want to comment on this particular clause because in my discussions with postal workers in Essex-Windsor it has been suggested to me very strongly that it is these kinds of provisions within the proposed Bill which present the red flag in front of the bull, the goad which will make for labour relations in the Post Office, which are already extremely difficult, difficult to put right and more difficult to turn around.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
I think that everybody in this House, everybody in this country, recognizes that there is a very difficult situation in respect of labour-management relations in the Post Office. If the marble worker himself, Mr. Kelly, cannot succeed in bringing about some kind of meeting of minds, as he was able to do with letter carriers, then I think that is one demonstration. It is very important that whatever piece of legislation is brought to bear on the backs of these workers is seen to be in some sense balanced, in some sense fair. There are two aspects of this particular clause which in that respect worry me considerably. They certainly very considerably worry the workers to whom I have talked.
The first is that, as a number of people have suggested, the extreme severity of the fines which are levied, not just as potential maximums but as necessary minimums on condition of conviction. I remind you, Mr. Chairman, the House and the country that this provision is being presented in a piece of legislation which was brought in at a time when there was no full strike. There was just a rotating strike across the country. Service had not been completely interrupted. It was brought in at a time when I think, again, everybody in the country would agree that the service which has been provided by the Post Office in this past period has deteriorated significantly. It was brought in at a time when the union itself had requested a mediator. The Minister refused to accept that request, Canada Post refused to accept that request which would have permitted that possibility to at least be explored. As I noted this morning, it was brought in at a time when provisions had been in place whereby casual workers had found it very difficult, despite their peripheral relationship with the strike, to receive the wages which were rightfully due to them for the work that they had done in the past.
Despite all those circumstances, despite that context, there was still this tremendously heavy burden put on workers of fines of $10,000 up to $50,000 with respect to officers of the union, and fines of $20,000 up to $100,000 with respect to the union. That is not an absolute fine, that is a fine per day. That seems to me, as one of my colleagues described it the other day, to represent the War Measures Act of labour relations. It is not something that the people of this country will see as fair, just, balanced, and equitable.
I ask the Minister if he can provide some type of justification for these extremely strong fines, given the circumstances which existed at the time that this legislation was brought in, that is, no strike, deteriorating service in the Post Office for the past few years, no response to the request for a mediator, and circumstances which made it difficult for casual workers to be paid what was due to them.
The second point I wish to raise is that the country itself has been told that this is back-to-work legislation; it is legislation to get the Post Office going again. In fact, as it is written this clause states that any provision of this Act which includes the imposition of the collective agreement over a significant period
of years ahead, any provision of this Act if it is broken can lead to conviction and these very heavy fines.
I also ask the Minister why, if he felt it was necessary to put heavy fines into effect to get the workers back to work, he also felt that he had to back up every single clause of this potential Act, every single clause of what we do not even know may yet come from the arbitrator who looks at this dispute, why every single bit of that activity shall be backed up by this extremely heavy enforcement mechanism? Even if it is justified to consider heavy fines to send workers back to work, which I do not agree it is, I think most people in this country will look at this as far too heavy for what it sets out to accomplish. But even if that is the case, why apply it to every aspect of labour relations in the Post Office for the next three years so that every provision of this Act, including what the arbitrator might ultimately put into place, is subject to those types of heavy fines?
That is certainly how it reads to me, and I welcome the Minister stating that this will not be the case, if indeed it is not. As the clause is set out, it clearly states that any provision of this Act which, for instance, is broken by a wildcat strike two years from now, or by a union protest against a go-slow activity in protest of some part of the provisions of the arbitration which is settled, that any part of that, any activity of that type, can lead to these massive fines.
I remember sitting in the Press Gallery years ago when the War Measures Act was brought into Parliament. I listened to the Leader of the New Democratic Party, in what was a very unpopular statement at that stage, say that this was using a hammer to crush a peanut.
In this case, I think the provisions are harsh, unreasonable, unfair, and quite out of league and context. This shows up not only in the size of the fines but also by the fact that they will be applied to any activity in the future where the union might in some minor way break the provisions of the collective agreement, not because the union thought that it did, but because it was judged by some judge to have done so.

I wish to pick on one of the comments of the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). It is important that we understand that this legislation would have the effect of imposing minimum fines of $10,000 on union officials. People talk about "union officials" and mean the national president of the union. This means anybody who is a representative of the union which can include a shop steward or someone who is acting in any capacity within the union. It could affect someone during the whole course of the collective agreement that is referred to here, and it could have nothing whatever to do with the Post Office. It could be a national political protest, which we have had from time to time in this country. Political protests which involve work stoppages and national days of protest are political acts and have nothing whatever to do with labour relations in the Post Office. This would expose the individual to a minimum $10,000 fine up to a $50,000 fine.
October 15, 1987

We should not be satisfied with the answer of the Minister of Labour, or the justification that the reason it is a $10,000 fine is tough, it is a minimum fine, but we did it before so we will do it again, and that is the justification.
That is not a very good justification. There is a precedent in dealing with legislation in this country. The reason that we have minimum fines is that when there are no minimum fines sometimes a judge will not give serious consideration to the offence. The legislature will then step in and say, "We have had this crime on the books for many years, the judges will let the people go and they should be treating them more severely,. so we will up the fines".
Would the Minister tell us whether or not there has been any experience where there has been back-to-work legislation, where the judges have been complacent, have not taken the matter seriously, and have not given appropriate fines? Could the Minister tell us whether there have been situations which have shown that without minimum fines of $10,000 the judges do not do their jobs and do not take the matter seriously enough?
We are not talking about maximum fines of $50,000. There may be cases where defiance of legislation of this nature might require a serious fine of $50,000, but we are talking here about a minimum fine of $10,000 with no judicial discretion.
Could the Minister tell us why he has taken that discretion away from the judges? Has there been an experience about which he can tell us where a judge should have given a fine of $10,000 and only gave one of $50, $100, $2,000, or $5,000? Has that been the experience with back-to-work legislation, that judges have not taken it seriously enough and have not treated it properly? If the Minister thinks that that is the case,
I ask him to tell us about those experiences, to tell us what has happened.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the remarks of my colleagues, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston, the Hon. Member for St. John's East, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor, and others. It is becoming obvious that no one in the House has come to the conclusion that the minimum fines are acceptable. They have been found to be too high, too harsh, and unrealistic. They have been called all sorts of names. I do not want to repeat the remarks of my colleagues, but I would like to indicate that I agree with them 100 per cent.
As a practical man, I would like to try to give the Minister an opportunity to correct what I consider to be abusive penalties. As the Hon. Member for St. John's East suggested, the Minister should give to the judge the power that he should have in the first place, that is, to exert his judgment and to decide what a minimum penalty should be. The Minister could do that by removing the minimum penalty and giving the responsibility to the judge, or the Minister could return to the drawing-board and establish new, realistic, minimum fines.
Postal Services Continuation
I would like to move the following amendment which would give the Minister the opening of which he seems to be in need to try to do a better job:
That Bill C-86 be amended in Clause 10 by deleting the words "less than
$10,000 or" from line 8 on page 5 of the Bill, and by deleting the words "less
than $500 or" from line 13 on page 5 of the Bill, and by deleting the words
"less than $20,000 or" from line 20 on page 5 of the Bill.
Either the Minister decides that he wants to leave the discretion entirely with the court or the judge to decide what will be the penalty-there is a maximum, but with this there would be no minimum-or perhaps the Minister, who appears to be ferocious if we look at the amounts in the Bill, wants to set his own more realistic minimum. I will not say more than that. I think I have done my duty by providing the Minister with an opportunity tonight, as we are dealing with the Bill clause by clause, to do a better job.

And if the Minister wants to take this opportunity, we could have a legislation that, while being tough, could at least be more humane, which all our fellow citizens would consider more reasonable, although its goal is to enforce the law.
And I will conclude on these words, waiting for the response of the Minister to see what he wants to do. Will he insist on going too far, with unreasonable penalties, or does he want a realistic legislation that still has teeth without being offensive? That is my question to him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We have the amendment of the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques on the floor. The Chair finds the amendment in order.
Mr. Chairman, we support the amendment of our colleague.
Comrade Keeper.

Mr. Chairman, I note that some of my Liberal colleagues have picked up an idea from a good source, a colleague of mine on the New Democratic Party benches. I do not mean to get under the skins of my colleagues. I enjoy cooperation, and co-operation in a good cause would be to give some flexibility to judges so that fines do not have to be severe where they are not required.
I hope the Minister will be open to this amendment. I do not know whether or not he is or whether he is prepared to give some sort of indication. I do not see any nod of his head or any smile, so I will not expect any openness to the amendment on the part of the Minister. Perhaps we can still hope.
I would like to make a point about these fines for lack of compliance with the legislation. The Minister indicated that the fines were severe, that $10,000 or $100,000 per day were severe fines. I do not dispute that at all; they are severe.
Why has the Government found it necessary to go to such severe legislation? It is simply because it has failed to set the

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
stage for negotiations. It has set in place a policy for the Post Office which was confrontational and made negotiations impossible. Therefore, it must have extreme and severe fines in order to enforce a settlement. That is why the fines are severe.
The amendment of my colleague would be useful. I hope the Minister will listen to some reason and give some flexibility to the courts. I would also point out that while the severe fines are there because the Government has refused to set the stage for negotiations, the Minister has also said, in response to questions from this side of the House, that the fines will apply throughout the life of the collective agreement. It could be that for two years or three years these fines will apply.
Clause 6 indicates that if someone participates in a strike against the employer, he or she would be subject to the enforcement clauses. If, sometime during the life of the agreement arising from this legislation, a worker were to go on a wildcat strike for some reason of a local nature, or some hardship in a particular plant, or for something which ordinary Canadians would understand, he or she would be subject to these enormous fines, these very severe fines.
Surely there is another regime under which such situations could be regulated. Surely these fines are not applied in all cases in which there is a collective agreement and somebody refuses to work and goes on a wildcat strike.
In response to a manager going crazy or something.

Perhaps the manager would have lost his sanity and would have become unreasonable, authoritarian and apply this kind of management style in the local post office. What if you cannot take that kind of harassment from your manager and you walk out and refuse to come to work? You are subject to these kinds of fines. Surely there is another regime under which such a situation could be handled.
I recall reading the book on the Post Office entitled Post Mortem in which there is an account of a manager in the Post Office walked out in order to resolve a local conflict. He managed to get the attention of the political authorities and the situation was resolved. How could anybody who works at the Post Office bring attention to the slightest irritant for which there is no resolution? They would in this case be subject to severe fines. 1 would like the Minister to deal with why he has the severe fines in the legislation, because the Government has not set in place a regime that would lead to a negotiated settlement. Why do these fines have to be in place throughout the whole life of the collective agreement? Surely there could be a limit to how long they are in place. I would like to hear the Minister respond to those two items.

Mr. Chairman, I want to speak briefly on the amendment proposed by my hon. colleague. It is obvious that the clause with which we are dealing now is at the very heart of the Bill proposed by the Minister. He is adamant that there
should be fines of such a size to achieve what he thinks they should achieve. Even though some of us disagree with some of those fines, I suppose that we could live with some aspects of them a little easier if they were amended in a way that would still fulfil the objectives of the Minister while being more reasonable for everyone. Nevertheless I do not like the Bill, but at least it will be more palatable for all individuals concerned. Ideally the maximum fine should be lowered as well.
As a compromise, my distinguished colleague from Saint-Jacques has offered this amendment to us which would still retain the main feature of the Bill, namely, to have the availability of levying large fines while not putting our judges in strait-jackets causing a situation whereby they would have to impose fines which could very well be unreasonable for some offences.
My colleague from Winnipeg has given us examples of an individual wildcat walk-out in a community six months or a year from now which could result in very harsh side effects from a minimum fine which may not be warranted at the time. It is very possible that maximum fines would not be warranted at any time. Nevertheless they would be even less warranted in a year from now in a small community where a local situation has caused some sort of disagreement between management and labour. I think what my colleague has offered is a compromise type of a motion, certainly not making everyone totally happy, but in the good spirit of co-operation, I think that he has proposed something that the Minister, if 1 may suggest, should consider favourably.
I think the Minister himself will recognize that the present Bill as worded now has features, particularly this minimum fine feature, which could be extremely injurious. I said it in my second reading speech and I will repeat it again tonight that extreme law is extreme injury. It is not justice but the denial of it. That is a very old axiom, as the Minister who is a lawyer will well know, but it is very definitely apropos in this kind of a Bill. The Minister being the Minister of Labour not the Minister of management will want to have legislation which could still be as strict as required in his view, but not having that strait-jacket effect or that extreme injury potential effect that I have just described.
I want to support the amendment offered by my colleague and I invite the Minister to give it very serious consideration. In my view it will not substantially damage the fundamental characteristics of his Bill but it will make the legislation somewhat fairer than it is at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak in support of the amendment. It is a very reasonable one. In times like these, the Government ought to be prepared to listen to reason when there is so much emotionalism about an issue and, to be fair, coming from all quarters. We have in this case a very reasonable proposal put by the Hon. Member from Saint-Jacques. When dealing with offences, the courts and judges are very experienced in how to determine what kind of punishment to give.
October 15, 1987

Two factors are taken into consideration. This is part of the law of the country, as the Minister will know. In determining the fine or punishment one of the factors is the severity of the offence as determined by the maximum punishment provided for in the legislation. Note, it is maximum punishment. Minimum punishment is not even looked at to determine the severity. It is the maximum punishment as determined by the legislation. A crime with a maximum punishment of 14 years in jail is considered more serious than a crime with a maximum punishment of two years. Maximum is what is used to determine how seriously the Parliament of Canada wants to view an offence. This amendment has left the maximums there. The judge has a very clear idea from Parliament how seriously the offence is to be regarded and will govern himself accordingly.
As the Member from Burin-St. George's knows, judges in Newfoundland in dealing with offences by offshore fishing captains, Spanish and Portuguese sea captains who break the fishing laws and other federal statutes have no hesitation in imposing fines of $25,000, $30,000 or more based on the seriousness of the offence and based on the maximum punishment provided by the law.
The other principle which judges will consider is one which I am sure the Minister considers important because of this legislation, namely, deterrence. One or the other objective of sentencing is deterrence. If deterrence is needed in a particular offence, then the punishment is harsher. This is a very reasonable amendment and proposal. Two messages are being sent to the judges. One, Parliament considers the breaking of the law very serious because of the maximum fine. Two, if deterrence is important in a particular case, then the punishment can suit the crime if the crime is serious enough to warrant a heavy punishment. These two factors will guide a judge in dealing with any offence under this Bill, but will also provide, by taking out these absolutely outrageous minimums, for discretion for a technical breach for a violation having nothing to do whatever with the purpose of this legislation. The purpose is to stop the current dispute and attempt to resolve the current outstanding differences between the Post Office Corporation and its employees.
Let us have the enforcement provisions deal with the problem, not deal with something else and not set traps and minefields for workers down the road because some manager steps out of line. If a manager steps out of line by doing something wrong and the employee says, "Well, we have to put up with this. We have to tolerate this abuse", the shop steward will be levied a fine of $10,000 minimum if he tells an employee that he doesn't have to put up with such abusive action on the part of the employer. It might have nothing whatsoever to do with the current dispute but might have to do with something else entirely.
Unless this amendment is accepted, we will still have this very severe, arbitrary, automatic and essentially unfair and
Postal Services Continuation
unjust provision which does not allow for no discretion on the part of the court. If this amendment is accepted, the court will be able to respond appropriately to the cases that come before it. I would urge the Minister to accept this amendment as it sufficiently provides for his objectives without tying the hands of a judge who deals with real cases and real facts.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take any more time but I would like to indicate that all sides of the House seem to accept this amendment. I want to ask the Minister whether he will take this opportunity to revise the penalties provided for in the bill; as a matter of fact, he has the choice either to revise them himself or to leave to a judge's discretion the enforcement of the law and the setting of discretionary fines before a court. Could the Minister tell us whether he intends to take this opportunity that is given to him?

Mr. Chairman, I want first of all to thank my hon. colleagues for their very sincere representations and say that I appreciate their concerns; they are similar of course to the points that have been made during consideration of Bill C-85 and Bill C-24, so that-

I have had the occasion to discuss amendments on previous occasions. When we discussed Bills C-84 and C-24 we considered the severity, and they are severe, of these particular clauses and we considered the proposed amendments which were not accepted at that time. The amendments proposed this evening to this particular clause will not be accepted either.
Amendment (Mr. Guilbault (Saint-Jacques)) negatived on division.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall Clause 10 carry?

On division.
Clause 10 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall Clause 11 carry?
On Clause 11-Additional punishment-union

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as if we did not have enough to say on the preceding clause with regard to the harshness of penalties, I must rise again to say that this five-year off-the-job penalty goes way beyond Clause 10 in its harshness and Clause 10 is harsh enough. This penalty comes on top of the penalties that are already provided for in Clause 10, penalties which we have already described as being too heavy.
We are certainly entering a new era of severity, of unusual and inhumane penalties. I do not think that I as a Member of this House can accept that. In some countries of the world they still cut off the hand of someone who has been caught stealing. Because they are still doing that in some countries does not

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
mean that we have to revert back to the Dark Ages in this country.
I do not know how to describe a five-year off-the-job penalty. Some have called it a sledge-hammer. Some have called it a whip with seven strands. Others have called it a shotgun. I think I will call it vengeance with passion.
I do not know what the union leadership or the officers of Canada Post have done to the Minister to make him react in such a vengeful way. I take it as my duty to move an amendment to this clause. I move:
That Bill C-86 be amended in Clause 11 by striking out the words "five
years" from line 28 on page 5 of the Bill and substituting therefor the words
"three days" and by striking out the words "five years" from line 36 on page 5
and substituting therefor the words "three days".
This amendment is symbolic. In fact, my purpose is to move an amendment to strike out entirely Clause 11. Our rules do not provide for that, our rules say that if I do not like a certain clause, I simply vote against it. I wanted to move an amendment that would allow my colleagues and I to say what we think of this measure.

What is the purpose of this additional punishment? To enforce compliance? Obviously, that cannot be the case, since under Clause 10, an individual acting in the capacity of an officer of the Canada Post Corporation or the union who contravenes the Act is already liable to a fine of not less than $10,000 or more than $50,000 per day. It is clear that providing for an additional punishment of five years is not meant as a way to enforce compliance. There must be some other reason, but I can't find it, since the preceding clause is already so extreme.
So what is the point? As I see it, the fines alone are more than sufficient and even too severe. Is this supposed to hit the unions hard or intimidate Canada Post officials? Is it because, as I said previously in the House, the Government, desperate to improve its image, seems to think that a good way to do that is to act tough with postal employees? Maybe the Government thinks it would help improve public opinion polls. I don't know.
I just don't understand. I would ask the Minister to answer the following question: What is the additional advantage? I ask this question because I cannot think of any other possibility.
A reasonable suspension period. Suspensions are included in certain kinds of legislation at the provincial, federal and municipal level in Canada. Policemen have been suspended for fifteen days or even a month. That is a fact. But suspending someone for a period of five years simply boggles the mind, since, as I said before, the purpose is not to enforce compliance, because that has already been amply taken care of by the preceding clause.
Do we want to put a person in a position where he might lose his home because for five years he would not be able to pay his mortgage? Do we want him to lose his car and have trouble
feeding his family? I hardly think that is what the Government has in mind.
Mr. Speaker, even a person convicted of a criminal offense under the Criminal Code is pardoned if he files an application after two years. In other words, anyone who is convicted of assault or damaging somebody else's property can come after two years and apply for a pardon to the Office of the Solicitor General of Canada, and if his behaviour has been good, he will be granted a pardon every time.
According to our laws a person convicted of a criminal offence can be pardoned after two years. Yet, a person who has already paid a $10,000 fine would be suspended from doing his job as an officer of the union or of Canada Post for a period of five years. That is beyond me.
1 have looked at the Charter of Rights and found at least three points in the Charter which this measure may violate.

I may remind Hon. Members that the Charter provides Canadians with legal guarantees. One of these guarantees is set forth in Section 12 of the Charter, which says that everyone has the right not to be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
Of course, it is debatable whether a five-year suspension is cruel or unusual, but no one can convince me it is normal, common or customary.
I would be concerned that people who are affected or threatened by Clause 11 might go before the courts to ask for a ruling on whether this particular clause contravenes the Charter of Rights and the legal guarantees I just read to you. I would not be surprised if those people won their case.
There is more. The Charter of Rights provides Canadian citizens with other guarantees as well. If I could find the other sections-here they are. Under fundamental freedoms, every one has the following fundamental freedoms: freedom of conscience and religion etc., and finally, the one I am interested in here, 2(d)-freedom of association. Sure, just because certain officers of the Union are suspended for a five-year period does not prevent union members from continuing to be part of an association. Of course that can go on. However, I maintain that an association whose officers have been suspended for a period of five years will be hard pressed to administer itself and to have a sense of direction. It merely opens the door to other union Members who would be only too happy to replace the former officers who were suspended and to take advantage of this opportunity to do so. This could lead to anarchy within a union, and I wonder whether that is the purpose of this clause. Because, as I said before, I do not see why the fines provided in the preceding clause should not be more than adequate.
October 15, 1987

There are other freedoms that are also guaranteed by the Charter. Under mobility and residence rights: Every citizen of Canada has the right to enter, remain and leave Canada, and so forth, and finally Article 6(b); every citizen has the right to pursue the gaining of a livelihood in any province.
Anyone whose right to pursue the gaining of a livelihood is guaranteed by the Charter and who is prohibited from working in his particular field, either as an officer or representative of the Canada Post Corporation or as an officer or representative of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, that person is definitely deprived of a freedom and a right guaranteed under the Charter, namely, to pursue the gaining of livelihood. I agree, that person can work somewhere else, but as far as I know, the Canada Post Corporation is a monopoly.

There are not three, four, or five Canada Post organizations in the country, there is only one. If one is prevented from acting as an officer of Canada Post, as he used to, for a period of five years, where will he seek employment in his specialty? This is in violation of Section 6(b) of the Charter of Rights. The same thing applies to an officer of the union. There are not three or four CUPW organizations in Canada, there is only one.
The purpose of this amendment is to point out that this heavy-handed five-year off-the-job penalty is absolutely unacceptable. I do not know how the Minister will react to this amendment. He did not react very favourably to my amendment to Clause 10.
He is not being reasonable.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I do not foresee my Party voting for legislation which contains such horrendous penalties as those contained in this Bill. I do not want to be associated with this legislation. 1 do not want to carry the blame if someone loses his house because the mortgagor forecloses. I want to be able to say for the rest of my life that I opposed such measures as this. I do not oppose it only because it is contained in back-to-work legislation. I would oppose it in any piece of legislation. What is unreasonable in this Bill would be unreasonable in any other Bill. That which goes beyond reason goes beyond my support.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Member for Saint-Jacques has moved the following amendment:
That Bill C-86 be amended in Clause 11 by striking out the words "five
years" from line 28 on page 5 of the Bill and substituting therefor the words
"three days" and by striking out the words "five years" from line 36 on page 5
and substituting therefor the words "three days".
The Chair finds the amendment to be in order.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take a few minutes to make quite clear how we feel about this clause. This clause says that if workers do not comply with the law they will lose their position with the union or with the Post Office. These are very severe enforcement provisions.
Postal Services Continuation
Having introduced enforcement provisions of this nature one would think that the Government had done everything possible on the face of the earth to come to a negotiated settlement. It is clear that the Government has done just the opposite. It has followed a policy of confrontation. It developed its plan for the Post Office behind closed doors. It failed to involve the public or the union in the development of its plans for the Post Office. It kicked the union representatives off the board of the Post Office.
The Government's policy has made a negotiated settlement virtually impossible. In order to justify the penalties in this legislation the Government should have gone in the opposite direction. If it had done everything possible to arrive at a negotiated settlement it may have a case for such severe enforcement provisions.
If workers do not do as they are told they will lose their positions with the union and their jobs at the Post Office. This reminds me of the solidarity union experience in Poland, and the case of Louis Riel in Canada.
In Poland, people were living under a totalitarian regime that did not allow its people to have a voice in the quality of their life. They organized and developed a union to give them strength. Of course, they were crushed because the government of that country did not believe in hearing from the people and did not believe in the fundamental freedoms that lead to representation in a democratic society.
This legislation echoes that because it is telling ordinary workers, people who work at the Post Office, that they do not have the right to choose their own leadership. That is a very important aspect of democracy.
Do not break the law!

An Hon. Member says, break the law. One of the fundamental aspects of law is the concept of natural justice. Also laws in society are based on the concept of democracy. The removal of the right of people to choose representation removes one of the pillars that supports a democratic society. This legislation echoes the situation in Poland and brings to mind the struggle of the solidarity union.
It also reminds me of the case of Louis Riel in Canada. He was not allowed to sit in this Chamber because the government of the day did not want him here. He was elected by his people to serve them and give voice to their grievances. The government said no. Not only did it choose to see that he was hung, it did not allow him to claim his seat in the House.
This legislation reminds me of that situation because the Government is telling people that they do not have the right to choose their own representatives. That is anti-democratic and fundamentally wrong. The Government may want its legislation to be effective and obeyed, but it ought to have a good reason to justify this provision that will not allow someone to represent others if they do not do what the Government wants.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
In fact, the Government has chosen confrontation every step of the way. It did not use the option of a mediator so that it could use this back-to-work legislation.
This provision is unacceptable. Before implementing this provision the Government should prove that it has gone as far as it can to seek an agreement. Instead, it has promoted confrontation and made it impossible to come to a negotiated settlement.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is obvious to everyone concerned that Clause 11 is, in effect, the Jean-Claude Parrot clause of this legislation. I could not help but think as I read Clause 11 that when the Minister was drafting this legislation he had one person in mind, Jean-Claude Parrot.
The Government wants to crush Jean-Claude Parrot and CUPW. It ought to admit its hidden agenda.
The purpose of the legislation is to get the mail moving again. Traditionally, Canadians have been fair and equitable. They have been understanding when it comes to legislation and punishment.
A minister of the Government of Canada could be convicted of corruption, could be convicted of conflict of interest, could be convicted of fraud, could be convicted of every offence in the Criminal Code of Canada and the very next day have the right to again run for public office. The Minister knows that. Why is that the case? If any Hon. Member of this House is convicted of corruption, some Canadians would ask why that person should be allowed to again run for public office. Not long ago there was a case in Nova Scotia where an individual was convicted of an offence and subsequently had the opportunity to run again. It was left up to the people, through a democratic process, to determine whether or not that person should sit again as an elected representative. That was a very basic and fundamental principle of natural justice of democracy.
If there is one law for politicians, one law for Ministers of the Crown, why should there be another law for union leaders? What is the hidden agenda of the Government?
If the purpose of this legislation is to get the 23,000 postal workers back to work, and the Minister, who purports to be a reasonable man, says that he wants a negotiated settlement because everyone believes that is the best possible solution, why is he provoking the union? Why is he provoking Jean-Claude Parrot to defy this legislation?
Not only has he decided in Clause 10 to provide for a minimum penalty of $10,000 a day, with no discretion whatsoever in the court, Jean-Claude Parrot will not be able to be a union representative for five years.
I want the Minister to stand up and deny that that is who he had in mind when he drafted this Draconian, cruel clause, Clause 11. Why does he not admit that it is the hidden agenda of the Conservative Government to crush CUPW.
It seems to me that the Prime Minister wants to be another Ronald Reagan. Just as Ronald Reagan did with the air traffic controllers, the Prime Minister of Canada wants to provoke the postal workers into a situation where 23,000 Canadians defy this law and are fined these excessive fines so that he can then fire them all.
Why does the Minister not admit to the hidden agenda of the Conservative Government? Why else would he have this clause in the legislation?
I challenge the Minister to show us one precedent that is similar to this law. I challenge him to show us some legislation in the Criminal Code of Canada dealing with politicians. He knows that politicians of his own Party stand charged with criminal offences. I would like him to stand up and tell us whether he believes the Criminal Code of Canada should be amended to provide that any politician convicted of a criminal offence should not be able to stand for public office for five years. That is absolutely undemocratic. It is unjust, unfair and inequitable.
If the Minister is honest and sincere in what he is saying in regard to trying to get the two parties back to together again, I would hope he would withdraw Clause 11. He knows we cannot move an amendment to strike Clause 11. We must simply vote against it or move other amendments that would serve to reduce the period of automatic prohibition for a person convicted under this Act to act as a union officer. Why does he not do the reasonable thing and completely withdraw Clause 11? In that way he will be in a better position to say to the union and to management that he wants a settlement? If he allows Clause 11 to stand, it is an open challenge to Jean-Claude Parrot and to CUPW to defy this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I am very disturbed about Clause 11. What it proves is that if one wants to have good labour legislation one does not expect it to come from a Conservative Government. What you get from a Conservative Government is bad labour legislation and this is a good example of that. Clause 11 is completely unnecessary. It is vindictive. It has no place in labour legislation which is passed by the Parliament of Canada. It sets a terrible example for labour legislation in other jurisdictions. I sincerely hope that the Minister will in fact reconsider the inclusion of this clause in the Bill and will in fact withdraw it.
The reason one gets bad labour legislation from Conservatives is precisely because there is always a strong element within a Conservative caucus, and within the Progressive Conservative Party, that wants to bash unions, that wants to kick workers around because they think it is okay. The union is trying to have the opportunity to bargain collectively, to speak up for their rights and to exercise some dignity in the workplace. Here we have an example of the Government going even further and withdrawing rights which ought to pertain to any person, that is the reasonable right to be considered on a
October 15, 1987

Postal Services Continuation
reasonable basis and not to lose one's livelihood because of some set of circumstances which are laid out in Clause 11.
I would like to talk about the specifics of the clause. What it says is that if any worker is convicted of doing certain acts that are outlawed by the Bill he can be prevented from being an officer or a representative of the union for five years thereafter, and he can also be prevented from working for Canada Post for the next five years. A five-year loss of one's work is a penalty which in dollar terms is $150,000 or $125,000 in lost income, depending on the individual's wage rate. Of course, it works out to be far more than that because it may force the individual to move. He may not have other opportunities. It is, as other speakers have said, a Draconian penalty.
One has to ask what are the circumstances under which this might actually arise? I was thinking, for example, of what happens in a situation in Winnipeg, or in the Alta Vista terminal in Ottawa when an individual postal worker, who is a shop steward or an officer of the local CUPW executive, and who works in a situation which has been heating up because of unreasonable actions taken by a supervisor who has been harassing employees and giving orders that are unreasonable, or in other ways creating difficult situations, and the situation explodes and a bunch of workers walk off the job in a wildcat strike? The individual who was an officer of the local had no part in that but he is then in the situation that if he goes to the outside of the plant, even for five minutes, in order to persuade the workers that perhaps they had better come back in and cool off, he can be guilty of participating in the strike and convicted for that act of trying to maintain labour harmony in his particular workplace. He can not only be denied from working with the union for five years but can also lose his job for a minimum of five years. Of course, he will never get it back because he will be simply written off after that by Canada Post.
What kind of need is there for this? There are fines already in the Bill for violations of the Act. They have been used before in back-to-work legislation. They are objectionable but, nonetheless, at least there is an established precedent for them.
We are talking not of a matter of applying this to a short period of time when there might be some high tempers. In fact, the Government has already agreed to delay the back-to-work features so that there is a certain period of time, although not long, for people to get back to work rather than being forced back to work the minute the Bill is proclaimed tomorrow, or whenever that may happen to occur. Therefore, why add this clause? Why go with this needless provocation? Is it really because the Government wants to set RCMP undercover agents to work in postal terminals to harass the leaders of the postal workers union in different places, provoking them into calling a strike or taking some other action and then forcing them out of their job? Is that what the Government has in mind? We have seen this used in the Province of Quebec.

We have just seen in the Province of Quebec how the Government has used agents provocateurs who worked for a union and actually recommended or directed activities which proved to be illegal. Does the Government intend to recruit such agents who will work as agents provocateurs and find ways to oust from his position Mr. Jean-Claude Parrot and have him found guilty under the legislation for having violated the legislation.

Is that what the Government has in mind? I do not know. I cannot justify this particular part of the legislation being in force at all. The representative of the Liberal Party suggested we should take the five-year provision and cut it down to three days. If someone was convicted, they should be denied the opportunity to work for Canada Post for three days. There are provisions in the collective bargaining agreement for grievances, for suspension, for acts of discipline, to be exercised by Canada Post. There is a whole structure under which those disciplinary acts can in fact be grieved if the employee finds them to be unreasonable. Those disciplinary acts can include suspensions for certain periods of time. There is an established manner of procedure.
I do not mind that being in the practice of labour-management relations, but whether it is five years or three days, I do mind, and my Party objects as well to the idea that we enshrine this principle in the law through passing Clause 11. That is why, with regret, I say to the representatives of the Liberal Party that we cannot support that particular amendment. It is not a good amendment because it is not a good clause. It is not a good part of the Bill and it should be taken away completely.
I wonder what has led the Government to this desire to try and bash the postal workers by every device possible? We now know that even a free trade agreement cannot bring the Conservatives up in the polls. They are now trying to bash postal workers because they are old whipping boys for the Liberals and now for the Conservatives and perhaps that is what they will use in order to try to bring themselves up in the polls. But it is just not going to wash.
I know from the calls I am receiving that there are people who are concerned about postal services. That is a very natural concern. They are asking themselves what are the options? Why is it that Canada Post is so intent on eliminating 4,200 jobs over the course of the next few years? Why is it that Canada Post is trying to turn these jobs into jobs that pay only $4 or $5 an hour? Why has Canada Post refused to look at ways in which it can broaden and expand its services rather than limiting them?
Someone called me the other day and asked me what ideas I had in mind. I said, for example, that I would like to be able to go down to my neighbourhood post office or to the central post office in Ottawa and use a facsimile machine to send material to another post office anywhere in the country. I could phone

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
someone in an office there and say, "Look. I am sending you the material you want by facsimile. It will be there in 10 minutes. Go and get it". Within a half an hour I could take something from my desk and have it on the desk of someone with whom I am doing business anywhere in the country. That is a very valuable service. It does not now exist, but it could be offered through every main Canada Post terminal. But the Government says, "Let's close those terminals. We will put those services into neighborhood stores and close those terminals".
Over the course of the last century and a half we have had the postal service as one of the elements that has linked this country together.
The Government is now saying, "We want to run trucks, carry mail bags on airplanes, but we do not want to have Canada Post personnel actually relating to the customers and giving them service. That is something the Government should avoid. We are going to make this into an invisible service where people go to a supermailbox to get their mail, where they put there mail into a box, where the service is all carried out by machines or else by people who are franchisees or acting as agents for Canada Post".
I looked at the document about the commitment to all Canadians which was issued by Canada Post in the last few weeks as it was preparing for this confrontation with the postal unions. It is interesting that there is only one reference to employees. There is nothing in this document at all which is directed, as it should have been, to building up a sense of pride and commitment on the part of those Canada Post employees. They have had that sense of pride and commitment for a long time, but it is undermined when labour legislation such as this is brought in.
It states here that we have established a rigid delivery standard to which every employee is working. It says that we have new and tighter management controls. It says that Canada Post is going to continue to run the Post Office like it was the army rather than like a modern corporation here in the late 1980s.
We are on Clause 11.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton says that we are on Clause 11. That is the Hon. Member who has the Alta Vista terminal in his riding.
You are wrong again.

He clearly supports offensive labour legislation, as do all of his colleagues. If the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton wants to stand up with the postal workers, why was he not there on the picket lines the other day when I was there supporting the postal workers?
Hear, hear!
Why does the Hon. Member not participate in the debate?

One Member of the Hon. Member's Party was there with the postal workers, the Hon. Member for Plamon-don. He had no problems being there. Why was this Member of Parliament not there supporting the rights of workers to be protected against offensive labour legislation? It is the duty of any Member of Parliament to stand up and speak out against legislation that contravenes the Charter of Rights. Why does the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton not do that? Maybe that Hon. Member could get up on debate and say why he supports offensive labour legislation like this.
Because my constituents have said, "Get them back to work".

Under any conditions? The Hon. Member says, "To hell with the Charter of Rights. To hell with labour-management relations. To hell with the labour law. Let us throw that all out the window." That is what the Hon. Member is saying. That is the kind of approach that I find offensive. It is the kind of approach that my Party finds offensive.
The Minister of management should have been acting as the Minister of Labour when he got up the other day. Instead, he stood up as the apologist for Canada Post, defending the fact that Canada Post had failed to bargain in good faith on the question of franchising. Day after day, week after week, month after month, Canada Post refused to talk about that particular issue with its employees who have said, "Let's talk about it. Let's look at it. Let's look at a number of different alternatives". The employees have indicated that they were prepared to look at that and now for their pains the union leaders in that particular case are threatened with being deprived of their jobs for five years under Clause 11, which is the clause we happen to be considering.
The Hon. Member for Gatineau also supports offensive labour legislation, unless she is able to get up right now and say that she wishes to stand aside from this particular thing and ask her Minister to withdraw that particular clause.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I support the unemployed who deserve to get their cheques. I support them in their wish to get their cards. That is what I support.

Does that mean the Hon. Member supports workers serving as strike-breakers? Is that what the Hon. Member is saying? I cannot support that, and a lot of Canadians cannot support that. I am opposed to Clause 11. I want to say to those workers who are watching, who are not directly involved and who may be saying, "Well, we would like to see the mails back", of course, we would like to see them back. But remember that we are talking about the principles of labour legislation that apply to every working man and woman across Canada right now. If it is okay for the Government to use this Clause 11, which would allow somebody to be driven out of his
October 15, 1987

or her job for five years because of an offence that could in fact be trivial, if it is okay for it to use that against postal workers, then it is okay for it to use it, as it did, against longshoremen, against workers in the communications area, and against railroad workers.
It is okay to have a precedent which can be used in provincial areas of jurisdiction. But, what diminishes one worker's rights diminishes the rights of all workers. What diminishes the rights of any worker diminishes the rights of any Canadian. When offensive legislation such as this is put into force, the rights of every worker and every man and woman in Canada. are diminished. That is why this clause should be refused.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with considerable attention to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre. He said in his closing remarks that he opposes Clause 11 of the Bill. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques, has proposed an amendment which would effectively delete Clause 11. Yet he said he was against that amendment. I have some difficulty in understanding the position of the New Democratic Party as it pertains to our amendment to Clause 11.
I will explain to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre how it works. You see, Mr. Chairman, you cannot move to delete Clause 11 because it is against the rules of this House. So what we do is move an amendment which effectively removes the power from the clause, which is what my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques, did. I hope that the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre has understood the purpose of the Liberal amendment, which is to effectively delete Clause 11 under the rules permitted by the House. How can one be against an amendment which negates Clause 11 and be against Clause 11 simultaneously? 1 am waiting for some further explanation in that regard.
If we can get back to the substantive issue here, in Clause 11 what we have in fact is a very harsh clause. The Hon. Member for Gatineau will have plenty of opportunity to speak later, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I am supporting you, Don.

We will certainly be here for sometime to come yet, and with the Hon. Member's assistance possibly even longer.
