What I want to bring to the attention of the Committee of the Whole House is that my colleague from York South- Weston has pointed out quite well that what we effectively have of course is a clause which, if left unamended, would have serious consequences. What happens, I ask the Minister, if there was a technical breach of the collective agreement? Would that clause still apply?
If the Minister is to tell us that it does not apply, then I ask him which clause of the Bill permits a judge or anyone else from not applying that part of the Bill? I see no discretionary authority any where in the Bill which would allow us to remove that clause if it is not applicable. Again, I ask the
Postal Services Continuation
Minister, would it not have been more fair and more reasonable to have left that to the discretion of a judge, even accepting, albeit reluctantly on my part, that the Minister would have said for a time of up to five years? At least let the judge do the job of judging.
I have some difficulty at any time that this House places us in the position where in fact we are imposing a minimum sentence. I recognize that it has been done before. There are certain cases in which perhaps it is warranted. But, in fact, when there is a minimum sentence and a maximum sentence which is the same number, and that is effectively what Clause 11 provides- the five-year feature being a minimum and a maximum of five years-then we are leaving no discretion at all to the judges. At least Clause 10, however repugnant it was, left some discretion for the judge, the difference between $10,000 and $50,000. That is still too high in any respect but, nevertheless, there is some discretion. In Clause 11 there seems to be no discretion at all. The minimum sentence and the maximum sentence is stipulated in the clause.
The Minister may say it is all right because the same type of punishment is put on the employer. My distinguished colleague for York South-Weston very eloquently pointed out earlier tonight that to expect that one would place that same type of fine on the management of Canada Post is somewhat of a remote possibility, to put it at best. We all know it will never happen. Instead, what will likely happen is that some day, six months or a year down the road, there will be a technical breach somewhere in the country and someone will be convicted of this offence. They will be punished in a manner which is most unreasonable, and it will not at all achieve what the Minister is attempting to achieve, that is to get the workers back to work.
There is a compromise available. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques has demonstrated such a compromise-just remove the clause altogether. We will still have the main provisions of the Bill. Alternatively, the Minister could change the Bill to state, no less than six months and no more than five years, and leave some discretion to the judge. It still would not be a perfect Bill, but it would be better, or should I say not as bad as it is in its present state. I invite the Minister to address that section. Perhaps at the same time we could get some clarification from the folks to my left as to which side they are on in relation to Clause 11.

I would like to express my absolute astonishment and concern over the situation expressed by my colleagues. We have to go back a number of years to when the Liberals were in power and remember their spirited defence of the postal workers union and its leader. It is amazing how those hypocrites can be converted on the road to Damascus. It was in fact the legislation of the Liberal Party that put Jean-Claude Parrot in jail. That was done by the Liberals when they were the Government.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
The next thing to remember is that it was Liberal legislation that shut down the postal workers before the full extent of the collective bargaining process could work in 1978. The Liberals put them away before they managed to get out on strike, and before the full nature of the collective bargaining process had taken place. It is absolutely astounding that the Liberal caucus today can stand up in such a hypocritical manner and attempt to suggest that they are the salvation of labour rights in Canada. That is absolute nonsense. The President of CUPW was jailed by that Party, and in 1978 the rights of postal workers were trampled in the House by labour legislation that was as unjust and as repugnant as the legislation that we see before us today.
It is ironic that my colleague made reference to the Metis situation with Louis Riel. It is ironic that Sir John A. Macdonald and the group who hanged Louis Riel happened to be called the Liberal Conservative Party in former times. That was the name of that Party. We see in essence the same today with the false debate between the Conservatives and the Liberals on labour relations, with the Liberals on their feet in sanctimonious protestation protecting workers rights. They were the ones who actually wound up putting the leader of that union in jail, passing legislation in the House that was totally disgusting.
The problem before the House is that there is a clause in this legislation that is absolutely unacceptable. It breaks the principle of democratic trade unionism. It also breaks a principle of fair play in this country. When an individual has broken the law, the common practice is that a penalty upon conviction is served. Once the penalty established by law is served then the person is free to accept his place in society and continue on as a citizen. Once the debt is paid it is paid. A further penalty is not imposed that goes against basic principles of fairness, and the principle of democratic trade unionism.
Out of this misguided clause, a situation is created from which further conflict and dissension will evolve. If the Government attempts to pass this provision that bars an individual the workers feel represents their interests effectively and competently with management, who is involved vigorously in the collective bargaining process in attempting to extract benefits for workers, there is no doubt that they will elect that individual no matter what it states in the legislation. The basic unfairness of that particular clause will make workers re-elect those individuals.
The next thing that will happen is that the Government is forced to respond to that issue, not the nature of labour relations within the Post Office but to that single issue. What will it do? It will simply put up a trustee, or attempt to put a the union into trusteeship. What other option is there? The union is then put under trusteeship. In the final analysis, this particular clause is one of the stones on the road to breaking this union. That is what has to be read here.
This is another mistake made by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell when he stands up and criticizes the NDP for being unable to support any further imposition of penalty where a democratically elected individual cannot represent the group that he or she has been elected to represent. Three minutes, three days, five years, what is the difference? The thing is that it violates the principle and operation of a democratic trade union. Once the penalty has been paid, the offence is finished, and the individual should be prepared to make his way as a citizen. The Conservative Government is sowing the seeds of further conflict within the union.
It is our hope that the Liberals will fight with us to have the Conservatives withdraw this repugnant provision in this legislation. It is not needed. This legislation has the force of a hammer, far too large already. It is not needed, unless the wish is to break the union and bring more conflict within the postal union and management. If some day the Government wishes to place that union under trusteeship and break it altogether, then the correct thing is being done. Then the Government is totally exposing itself and violating the basic principles of democratic trade unionism in Canada. This is absolutely repugnant. It would be our hope that the Liberals would not attempt to mitigate it, and may perhaps even put an arrow in a future quiver for themselves. They have shown such negative approaches to the postal union before when they were in government. I am not talking about my colleagues who are new to the House. It is the Liberal Party that we all know and hold in such total contempt that I am referring to.
The basic issue is that this clause is absolutely unacceptable and it must be removed. The seed of future dissension is in that clause. The possibility of creating enormous conflict where people will go to jail to defend their democratic rights is sown by that clause. What we see here is the present Government's wish to break that union. In good faith, that clause ought to be removed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already spoken on that clause and I did not intend to speak again, but I do not think that I can let the Hon. Member for Comox- Powell River get away that easy.
He based some of his accusations about my Party on facts that were wrong. Perhaps it is nice for him to attack the Liberal Party and to blame it for the fact that Jean-Claude Parrot was jailed a few years ago because of Liberal legislation. Bring it over. If it is different from mine, I would be glad to look at it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will be glad to tell him what is in it. I have done my homework. He will not find a jail sentence in that piece of legislation. If he

goes back in history, he may be able to find that the union leader in question was jailed because he refused to pay a fine. That is standard in Canada. If a person does not pay his fine, he winds up behind bars. The Hon. Member may want to make sure that he pays his traffic tickets. Perhaps he should get his facts right.
Since the Hon. Member seems to want to shoot arrows, I am going to ask him questions. I have been present in the House of Commons throughout this debate. speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
If the Hon. Member has seen me on television, he has seen me moving amendments in an attempt to make this piece of legislation reasonable. I was unable to achieve that. If he sticks with me, he will see me vote against it because I think it is an unpalatable piece of legislation. However, I cannot take that trash from an Hon. Member who does not have the nerve nor the courage nor the competence to write his own amendments, to come to the House of Commons, to try to fight for them, and to convince his fellow Members to accept them.
There is another reason I am on my feet. While the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River attacked us and I rebutted his points, I saw Tory Members laughing on the other side. I saw a grin on their faces. Frankly, I cannot stand seeing the Minister and other Tory Members rejoicing at the same time as they are forcing such a piece of trash through the House of Commons.
I say to NDP Members-and we have been working together on this to try to agree on amendments; we even got the Minister to agree on amendments-that now is not the time for war among ourselves. Now is the time to fight against an unacceptable piece of legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to join with my colleagues on this side of the House and to say that I am particularly appalled by Clause 11. I am appalled by this Bill which is so punitive and unfair that it imposes heavy penalties, particularly on the postal union. In particular, Clause 11 imposes a heavy penalty on top of the heavy fines about which we heard when we were dealing with previous clauses. It deprives either a union leader or a manager of Canada Post of his or her livelihood for five years.
I cannot help but recall the legislation which we were studying and opposing about 10 months ago when the same Minister was imposing back-to-work legislation on longshoremen. At that time the legislation contained a similar clause, except that it was more punitive toward union leaders if I am
Postal Services Continuation
not mistaken. I cannot say that the Minister is being more fair by saying that the same penalty will be imposed on management and on union leaders. That is not being more fair; it is only being doubly punitive. It is deplorable.
The Minister has brought in back-to-work legislation three times or so, if I recall correctly, in the period of his jurisdiction. Each time it gets tougher, tougher, and tougher.
It is not that this is a token plan. This measure takes away a person's livelihood for up to five years. It ruins careers, and one can see what that would do to families. It also takes away the right of unions to choose their own officials. We must not forget about that.
I should like to return to a point which was made in French a little earlier by the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques. I think it was the point which Mr. Borovoy had also made, that the legislation is contrary to our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I would like the Minister to comment on it and to explain it to us.
If my notes are correct, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques also said that Article 12 of the Charter provided legal guarantees that everyone has the right not to be treated to any cruel or unusual punishment, which this is. People have the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association, which this certainly undermines. They have the right to pursue a livelihood in any province.
I would like the Minister to explain how he can bring in legislation with a clause such as this one which certainly appears to be contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If the piece of legislation passes, I certainly hope that it will be challenged in the courts.
I would also like to say to my friends in the Liberal Party that we had prepared an amendment which I understand is out of order. It would do away with this clause altogether. We think that Clause 11 should be removed by striking out lines 22 to 37. We do not agree that there should be such a punitive clause in the Bill.
I urge the Minister to reconsider and to explain how he can bring it in when it contravenes the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to add my own comments on Clause 11 which truly shows this Conservative Government's provocative spirit. They started with the hiring of strike breakers. All along, they refused to appoint a mediator in order to force the introduction of this shotgun bill that goes so far as denying an individual his democratic rights to be elected to a union or office job.

I would like to read into the record a quotation from page 3 of the conciliator's report of 1985. It reads: "If you believe in the collective bargaining system as I do, periods of economic retrenchment are not an occasion for management to beat

Postal Services Continuation
labour up but rather a time which requires the setting of realistic goals".
The conciliator at that time was the Deputy Minister of Finance. It was not a union member or union leader who said that; it was the Deputy Minister of Finance who was speaking about realistic goals.
Definitely the Conservative Government is not talking about realistic goals. It proposed in 1986 a business plan which the workers who are on strike are against because they are losing their jobs. Canadians in general are against it. Rural Canadians are against it because they are losing their post offices. Urban Canadians are against it because their mail is not being delivered to their doors. Many people are contesting it because periodicals and magazines will not be delivered to their homes at the same postal rate.
Canadians are against the new postal system which the Government of Canada wants. Clause 11 proves that the Government wants to break the union so that it can dismantle and privatize Canada Post.
The Government is bragging about Canada Post, saying that it has improved services. However, there are many places to which people must go to receive registered mail or parcels. One week it is one address, and the next week it is another. If they say that they are improving service by adding more outlets, why should they then reduce services at the Post Office? The intention is very clear. The Government wants to destroy the postal system the way we know it now. In order to accomplish that the Government has to destroy the union and Clause 11 does exactly that with a five year penalty.
Mir. de Jong: Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to make a few remarks in the debate. It seems that one of my colleagues wanted to speak on this amendment at the same time.
Oh, oh!

It has become quite obvious to most Canadians what the Government's agenda is. What we are dealing with in the postal dispute is more politics than wisdom. It is a not a real desire to settle genuine disputes and genuine concerns. There are concerns of the working people throughout Canada not just in the Post Office but in many industries as well, concerns about job security. People see their jobs going down the drain, causing them to have lower and increasingly lower standards of living. Statistics point this out. You can see that actual wages have declined in terms of the cost of living over the last number of years. You can begin to understand the concern and desperation of working people.
What is the Government's solution to this dispute? If it were really up to some of the Hon. Members across the way, I am sure they would prefer to call out the army. They see in this dispute an opportunity to win electoral support, at least they hope, by forcing confrontation. I learned early in politics that
the Conservatives, the forces of the right, are not only concerned about who their friends are but who they can succeed in making their enemies. They feel that if they can get working people, particularly organized people and unions, to be their enemies, that will help their electoral causes. I have seen this type of thing in Saskatchewan where the Conservative Party very often goes out of its way to kick out at native people and the poor people on welfare in order to provoke them.
I remember working in a youth agency in Vancouver in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The mayor at that time was Tom Campbell. Tom Campbell as mayor used to provoke a riot around election time because he felt that that would create concern in the local citizenry and help him get re-elected. It is the politics whereby hate can provoke people considered unpopular, then you can help yourself politically. It is a disgusting type of politics. It is the politics of the right that we have seen Maggie Thatcher practice in Great Britain, that we see Ronnie Reagan practice in the United States and now we see the Conservative Government attempting to do the same thing. I suggest that it is not going to work. Canadians have seen though this Government. They have seen through its insincerity, its double dealing, lying and cheating and it is not going to work, Mr. Chairman.
Clause 11 is an attempt to provoke the labour movement and those who are involved in the trade unions even further. It is so obvious what the Government is attempting to do. Fair-minded Canadians will reject this Government, its policies and its legislation. It is phony and divisive and against the nature of the country. Surely the nature of the country is one of conciliation, co-operation and of working through, not the confrontation being practised by this Government. It is not a country where people condone the type of provocation practised by this Government. That is why we will see this Government in power for only a short period of time. It was elected with a very large majority. People wanted an honest change. But what they got was even worse than what they had before. This Government is a passing phenomenon. The Conservatives will be here today and gone tomorrow. This legislation with Clause 11 is another nail in the coffin of the Government.
The Tories are through for this generation, perhaps even for several more generations to come. I urge them as they approach the end of their mandate to begin to realize that the politics of Ronnie Reagan and Maggie Thatcher is not going to work in this country. I hope the Conservatives begin to realize that there are some real problems people face concerning job security. I hope that they come up with some genuine and honest solutions that are needed as we move into the 21st century instead of the type of legislation that we see here which is short-sighted and mean. It will just not work.

When the Minister has an opportunity to rise, and I am sure he will have that opportunity in the very near future, I would like him to tell us whether or not he sought the advice of the Justice Department with regard to Clause 11, and if so, tell us if he is prepared to table in the House the opinion of the Justice Department on whether or not Clause 11 is in compliance with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in particular whether or not Clause 11 is in breach of Section 2(d), Section 6(b), and Section 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
As the Minister knows, Section 12 of the Charter provides that everyone has the right not to be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Cruel is defined in The Canadian Law Dictionary-

That is what Clause 11 is all about. I know that many Members of the Conservative caucus do not support the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Notwithstanding, it is the law of Canada.
Section 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides that everyone has the right not to be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. I submit that to automatically suspend a union officer for five years after being convicted of an offence under this clause and after having been forced to pay a minimum fine of $10,000 per day is cruel and unusual.
Did the Minister ask the Justice Department for an opinion on whether or not Clause 11 of this legislation breaches in any way or offends in any fashion Section 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms? Did he ask for an opinion on whether or not it offends Section 6(b) which provides that every citizen of Canada has the right to enter, remain and leave Canada to pursue the gaining of a livelihood in any province? Clause 11 which would prohibit someone from working for a union seems to me to breach Section 6(1 )(b) of the Charter which gives Canadians the right to pursue the gaining of a livelihood in any province.
Not only does Clause 11 prohibit an individual from being employed by a union, it also prohibits someone from working for a union without being paid. If a union decided to appoint an individual who had been convicted of an offence under this legislation to represent the union in any fashion whatsoever, it would not be able to do so. Let us assume for a moment that a

lawyer or another individual who has expertise in labour law is asked by a union to represent it in some fashion but that person has been convicted of an offence under this legislation. He or she would not be able to represent that union for five years.
Surely the Minister has considered the hardship that that will cause for the individual and his family. It will be a real hardship for a person not to work for a union for five years if in his entire life he has known no other occupation.
Finally, has the Minister asked the Department of Justice to render an opinion on whether or not Clause 11 is in breach of Section 2 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in particular Section 2(d) which provides that everyone has certain fundamental freedoms including freedom of association?
In my respectful submission, Clause 11 which automatically prohibits an individual from associating with the union would be in direct contravention of Section 2(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms as well as breaching other Sections of the Charter.
If the Minister did not seek the opinion of the Department of Justice, can he explain to the House why? If he did, will he table the opinion in the House of Commons?

Mr. Chairman, we find Clause 11 to be the most offensive part of this very offensive Bill. We seem to forget at times that we are talking about a fundamental right of Canadian men and women to work for their wages and to fight for working conditions and against a punitive plan that will be imposed upon them by Canada Post, a plan which will see people who have spent long years working the night shift relegated to working the night shift again after they had established enough seniority to be able to have a day-shift job at a wicket.
The Government has established a plan that it hopes will eliminate the deficit. It will not do that, but it will destroy the Post Office by destroying the working conditions of the men and women who work for the Post Office. That is why we are opposed to this Bill and that is why we are basically opposed to Clause 11 which is absolutely punitive.
Clause 11 states that any union officer who is convicted under this Act will not be eligible to hold office in his or her union for a period of five years. This is a clear attack on the rights of working men and women to direct the affairs of their own unions and it is an attack upon rights of working men and women to bargain collectively. It attacks the basic freedom of Canadians as guaranteed by our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the freedom of association.
This Bill is right in line with what many Tories think about unions. I recall that when the Hon. Minister of State for Science and Technology was a back-bencher, year after year he introduced a private Member's Bill calling for right-to-work legislation that would destroy unions. It goes back to the kind of attitude we saw under the leadership of R.B. Bennett. After Canadians had experienced the kind of Government that R.B. Bennett offered, the Conservatives were out for a good many
years. That will happen again when the next election comes around.
R.B. Bennett, speaking 55 years ago in November of 1932, called for the iron heel of ruthlessness against any people who were speaking up for progressive social change in Canada. That was "Iron-Heel Bennett" and we have the same thing from this Government except some people might suggest that it is a different kind of heel, a "Gucci-shoe heel".
Clause 11 has no place in legislation dealing with labour. I am surprised that a Minister of Labour would bring in legislation which contains such a clause. It is repressive and provocative and will not lead to better relationships between the union and the Post Office. If the Government has any desire for better relations it will withdraw this clause immediately. I urge it to do so in the interests of the welfare of the men and women who work for Canada Post.

Mr. Chairman, I take this debate far more seriously than I think many Members of the House do. When I first saw Clause 11 I, like many Canadians, thought for a brief moment that perhaps the Government was just looking for some headlines by seeking to impose $10,000 to $50,000 fines and threatening workers with the loss of their positions for five years.
However, when we take the mask off this issue and look inside to see what the Conservative Government's agenda has been on the Post Office, we realize that something quite different is in fact going on here. The Government is attempting to paint CUPW and its leadership as the creators and perpetrators of all the problems in the Post Office. That is hardly the case. The Minister responsible for Canada Post privatized many of the potentially money-making and more financially secure operations of Canada Post.
This is a self-fulfilling prophecy. The Government wants to look tough on these issues. It wants to give voters the impression that it is tough and is in control. Anyone who mucks around will get a fine of $10,000 per day and union leaders will be stripped of their right to represent working people. I do not think there are many trade unionists in this country who bought this. Fair-minded Canadians who have any dealings with a CUPW member, whether it be a neighbour, friend, daughter, sister or mother, know what the workers are like.
When one takes a close look at Clause 11 one sees other things trickling out. It just happens that the agreement which will be substantiated by this legislation will run out in the latest month in which there can possibly be a federal election. The Government has carefully calculated so that there is no opportunity for a strike or other such activity in the time leading up to the next election.
Clause 12 deems the entire union to be a person. I have seen this in legislation before, usually in far-right legislation. I think the Minister would like to withdraw this. I hope he does withdraw Clause 11. Situations will arise in the next couple of years in which the management will do things which are unacceptable and cannot be fed back into the mediation process properly. The problem will go to the officers of the union who will have to'decide what to do.

Mr. Borovoy, a well known and nationally respected legal mind on the matter of civil liberties has pointed out in very clear terms that this is contrary to the Charter. It is unconstitutional. Many Members of this House were here five years ago when the Constitution Act of 1982 was enacted. The words included in that Act are there to protect collective rights, to protect the rights of trade unionists and their leadership. If such legislation were introduced in Chile or some other such place, the Minister of Labour would probably be the first to say that it was Draconian, that it was uncivilized to bring forward such concoctions.
When you strip away the mask you have some understanding of the strategy with which the Government has come forward. It has cut back on funds, refused to allow a real collective bargaining process to proceed, demanded franchising out, and gradually withdrawn services. In my own constituency we have seen the effects of reducing the numbers of workers. The lines of people coming in to pick up parcels have been lengthened. People are told that they have to buy their stamps and money orders elsewhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Don't exaggerate. That's nonsense.

Government Members are obviously out of touch with the postal service in their own constituencies. I know what has happened in my constituency.
The Government is trying to convince the public that an unruly union is the problem with postal service in Canada, that it is all the fault of CUPW and J. C. Parrot. In fact the incompetence lies on that side of the House and an awful lot of Canadians know that that is the case and will not lay the fault at the door of trade unionists or CUPW members.
The Minister of Labour must know the meaning of Clause 11. It is a call to arms to a union like CUPW. If they are going to take an action it will have to be a collective action which will really shut the operation down. They know that the moment they do something their leadership will be gone so any action would have to be much more vigorous, protracted, and prolonged than would otherwise be the case. The Government is setting up all kinds of straw situations. I would describe this as a gasoline clause. It is meant to incite ill feelings by the public toward CUPW workers and create situations in which very dramatic action will be required.
While listening to other speakers, I was troubled by the lack of serious thought which many Members of this House have given to the seriousness of what is being done in the House tonight. The Government may well want to consider why it would bring forward such an unworkable plan. It has put forward a firing squad situation for collective bargaining. CUPW had no possible opportunity to deal in a realistic manner with the proposals which Canada Post was putting forward.
The Government is still tonight attempting to blame its incompetence in providing proper postal service on CUPW which, of course, is preposterous. Through Clause 11 the Minister responsible for Canada Post is trying to isolate Jean Claude Parrot and the other leaders of CUPW and make it almost impossible for them to stand up for their collective and
Postal Services Continuation
democratic rights. Clause 11 can be described as nothing other than dog vomit and it should be removed from the floor of the House of Commons.

Mr. Chairman, there have been some very strong opinions on this clause expressed here on the floor of the House of Commons in Committee of the Whole. Members used their time to speak as well on issues which had been discussed on other clauses. I would like to address two points with respect to Clause 11.
First, the same clause was in Bill C-24 that was adopted here in November, 1986. To my knowledge, Mr. Parrot was not a member of that particular union at the time so that the argument of the Hon. Member for York-South Weston that this clause was designed for Mr. Parrot is quite inaccurate.
With respect to the fact that this clause was used before, it is a favourite clause because 1 am using it again. I remind Hon. Members that there was an inaccuracy in Bill C-24 because, as first drafted, it dealt only with the union officers.
You refused to change it.

After debate in the House, it was amended to include the equivalent clause with respect to the employers. The exact clause is here. As a matter of fact, the Member for Skeena said that it would at least be a saw-off at the time to have the equivalent penalty for the employer. That is exactly what is here and he agreed with that amendment at that time.
I do not intend to either accept the amendment or to withdraw the clause. It will stay in this legislation.
I want to correct something that was stated by the Member for Ottawa Centre. I believe the Hon. Member for Winnipeg would agree with me that the clause in question does not prevent a union person from working for the corporation. It prevents the union representative or officer from acting in that capacity but not from working for the corporation since subparagraph 2 applies to the employer representatives or officers. I wanted to correct that. I believe Hon. Members will agree with it.

No, you have.

It is a shameful admission by the Government that its favourite clause is the most heinous clause in the Bill. Even temporary workers?

People do not defy legislation en masse unles it is so terrible that it cannot be obeyed. I am not talking about this particular legislation but about general principles.
The Member for Burin-St. George's, who is from Newfoundland, knows that recently in Newfoundland the members of a union defied legislation because that legislation was considered by the vast majority of people to be unjust and wrong.
Without any suggestion of a massive violation of legislation and before there was even a full scale strike, the Government is imposing back-to-work legislation which itself provoked a strike. But the legislation contains in it a terrible-

speechtext: It does not say that here.
I know it does not say that here. That legislation was decried from one end of the country to the other.
Speak to the Bill.

It is the same kind of legislation. We are talking about principles but they do not want to talk about principles. They want to talk about ordering postal workers back to work and trying to resolve a crisis that they created.
The Minister of Labour is very proud that it is the second time the Government has included his favourite clause. Perhaps the Government will now introduce amendments to the Canada Labour Code suggesting that members of a union who do anything contrary to the Canada Labour Code will be banned from being officers or representatives.
Now the Government has proposed an equality clause which prevents the employers from violating the legislation. It reminds me of a quote, by Anatole France who said the law in its majestic equality forbids both the rich and the poor from sleeping under bridges on rainy nights, from begging in the streets, and from stealing bread. That is the kind of equality we see in this legislation.
The rich do not need to steal bread. This legislation is designed to support the managers of Canada Post. Why will they violate the legislation when it is their legislation? The Government is simply introducing that provision to show how fair-minded it is. It is rank hypocrisy.
The Government is putting down the workers and saying that being an officer of a union is an illegitimate activity in this country. Unions were built by people who were trying to improve their lot. They were built to protect workers from employers like the people at Canada Post. Unions exist to fight against management that is inept and arbitrary and does not give them a say. The management says it will not let the
workers negotiate important matters that concern their working conditions.
Matters of collective bargaining and contracting out are negotiated in hundreds of collective agreements throughout the country. Yet the Government says that Canada Post does not have to negotiate this because it will order them back to work. Not only will it order them back to work, it will use its favourite clause by which it will ban people from being members of unions if they do not obey the legislation.
The Government says it will ban people from being members of the union if they do not obey this legislation in every dot and tittle automatically. There will be no discretion or question. It will be totally arbitrary, following the dictates of the people who run Canada Post. That is what we have from this Government. That is what this clause represents. I said earlier that I was not sure what the worst clause in this legislation was. I am convinced now that this clause is absolutely the worst clause. It is the most horrendous clause because it takes away the rights of freedom of association and freedom of assembly. It takes away those rights from workers across this country. It sets a terrible precedent. We have the Government condoning, first of all, strike-breakers in a Crown corporation. That will set an example for private employers. We will follow Peter Pocklington who set the example for this Government. He did not make it as Leader of the Conservative Party but he is its ideological leader. He sets the example and the Government follows with this legislation. We have Peter Pocklington calling the tune and this Government following.
We have a very good example of the kind of attitude this Government wants to promote in the Crown corporation called Devco. The Cape Breton Development Corporation had a manager who recently resigned under pressure not only from this House but from the Nova Scotia Government, the New Democratic Party in Nova Scotia and the workers in Cape Breton. He is the man who is said to have said to the workers who complained about going to work underground under the conditions that existed in the coal mines: "You fellows should consider yourselves lucky. In South Africa we send-''and I think he used the word "niggers"- "those guys below ground in bare feet". That is the kind of Crown corporation attitude this Government has allowed to exist. Now we have the Government condoning the use of strike-breakers in the Post Office. We are passing legislation very much equivalent to the South African legislation which is imposed on journalists they do not like. A journalist is not allowed to work in South Africa if he says things the government does not like. We now have our Government saying: "If you break this law, we will not allow you to be a member of the executive of the union or a representative of the union or work for the union in any capacity. You cannot even sweep floors for the union". That is the legislation we have before us. That is the example this Government is setting as to how it thinks labour legislation should operate.
It is totally unnecessary. If this Government had any sense it would take this clause out of the legislation altogether. I am
October 15, 1987

afraid the Government does not have any sense. I am afraid the only response, unfortunately for the Government, the people of Canada will be able to make is to vote the Conservatives out of office. That is the only response the workers of Canada can have.
1 plead with the Conservatives for their own sake, if not for the sake of the workers of Canada, to take this measure out because it is very bad legislation. It is a very bad measure. It ought not to be any part of a civilized country's legislation in the face of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, freedom of association, freedom of assembly and freedom to elect the leaders of your choice.
This Government as a matter of course, says: "We used it once before. We will use it again and we will use it in every piece of legislation we have". It is the favourite clause of the Minister.
If that is his favourite clause, I would suggest to him that perhaps he ought not to be Minister of Labour. He ought to learn something about human rights and something about justice. He should not condone this kind of nonsense in his legislation, if he wants to have harmony in the Post Office, if that is one of his aims. Perhaps he does not want to have harmony in the Post Office, but let us assume he does. If he is a proper Minister of Labour and doing his job, what he will want is what all the people of Canada want and everyone in Canada wants to have a decent postal service, harmony in the Post Office and a postal service that is efficient and operates properly. If that is what the Minister wants, then he ought to pass legislation that is going to lead to that and not pass this sort of legislation which provokes workers and right-thinking people into believing this Government does not want to have harmony in the Post Office.
Many Canadians believe there is trouble in the Post Office and a lot of them do not know why. This is an opportunity for the people of Canada to understand why there is not harmony in the Post Office. We have two examples. First, we have rotating strikes and normal collective bargaining being carried on. The only major irritant up to then was the Government condoning the use of strike-breakers and scabs in the Post Office. Postal service was operating more or less as it had been before.
According to the managers.

Yes, according to the managers. The next escalation of this strike was not caused by CUPW. Who caused the escalation? The Minister of Labour caused the escalation by introducing this legislation. Now we have a full strike. Now we have the Government saying that because of this full strike we must pass this legislation. That is the kind of information the people of Canada need to know and understand. It is this Government and the management of the Post Office-which the Government has told what to do-who have caused the disruption of the Post Office.
It is they who do not want to have harmony in the Post Office because if they did, they would not have this clause in the Bill. They would not have the Bill at all. They would have a different Bill that would provide for proper negotiations and

mediation, as we have suggested, and they would insist that the Post Office management discuss and negotiate on the major issue in the dispute, and that is the issue of franchising.

Mr. Chairman, just briefly, the Minister of Labour was speaking a moment ago and I assume he did not want to leave the impression on the record that I had either voted for or supported the clause in the last go-round of the legislation because I voted both against the clause and against the legislation, against his favourite clause.
During debate I do recall pointing out the unfairness of the clause, but it only applied to the longshoremen. It did not apply to anyone else. I said there was an obvious unfairness in the legislation. 1 do not think that the Minister would want to leave the impression that I either supported or voted for it.
Even though he tried.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose that answer would demonstrate what has happened, but my recollection, and I stand to be corrected, of course, is that the Hon. Member supported the amendment that I proposed to make it applicable to the employer as well as to the union. I would doubt very much that the Hon. Member voted against that amendment. However, I stand to be corrected once we check the record.
Because Hon. Members are repeating arguments they had put before the House earlier this evening, that does not necessarily make the arguments more convincing. They become repetitious. We have heard them before and perhaps they will induce someone like myself to use one of their suggestions. For instance, using the words "favourite clause", I was repeating something that was said on the other side. If it is not a favourite clause, it is certainly a clause that has been used before. Unfortuntely, it would not be a clause that would have to be used if the parties came to a settled agreement, which are the best agreements, and which they should have achieved after 15 months of negotiations in this case.

Mr. Chairman, if the Minister of Labour is not convinced of the rightness of the cause, then perhaps he will consider that this particular clause, Clause 11, can also be applied in cases which have nothing to do with this dispute. We could have some event down the road a year or two from now in a small postal station or a small postal plant where one of the managers of the Post Office gets out of whack-and I am sure there are thousands and thousands of people in middle management in the Post Office, I do not know what they are doing and they probably do not know what they are doing themselves-but someone runs amok-

So we have all sorts of people who could run amok in the Post Office and there is a response, and a reasonable response, by the members of the union to refuse to work, to refuse to obey orders, to refuse to do things that are unreasonably requested of them, or to be provoked into doing something that has nothing whatsoever to do with this strike.

We do not want to give the managers of the Post Office a licence to run roughshod over the workers for the life of this agreement under pain of their being exposed to this type of clause and this type of legislation.
Clause 11 provides that a shop steward, or an official or representative of the union, in that situation does not even have to do anything at all. All he has to be found to have done by a court is not take what the court considers to be reasonable steps to prevent people from walking off the job. We have a brand new code here now for the behaviour of shop stewards who have to take reasonable steps to prevent people from going on a wildcat strike. A judge has to determine that after the fact. If the judge determines that, no, there were reasonable things that one could have done that one did not do, then that person is banned from holding office in the union for a period of five years and cannot work for the union for five years. All of those measures are brought in by this legislation.
If what the Minister wants to do is to get workers back to work, he should have legislation that is aimed at that, not legislation that sets a terrible precedent for labour legislation all across the country. If he has done it before, then shame on him for having done it before. He should realize his mistake and should not do it again. The fact that this clause or something similar to it was contained in a previous Bill is no excuse for continuing it on. I would ask him to do the proper thing and remove the clause.

cogent argument, an argument which has been well put, an argument which clearly carries a great deal of weight. I ask the Minister to tell us why it is that he is not prepared to make those sorts of changes.

With respect to the arguments that were put forward by the Hon. Member for St. John's East, I agree with the Hon. There were two other points that I raised that I would like to hear from the Minister on before we move to a vote on this crucial clause. I ask the Minister if he will respond to the question which a great many people have asked in this country, and certainly a great many members of CUPW have asked me on picket lines, why was the Minister not prepared to appoint a mediator at least to explore the possibility of avoiding this Draconian piece of legislation?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I wish to say that there is a problem with Clause 13. If one looks at the Bill, one will find in Clause 4 that both union officers and management have obligations. If Clause 13 is left as is, those obligations would have to be carried in a very short period of time. Clause 13 has to do with the coming into force of this Act, and it states:
Postal Services Continuation
This Act shall come into force on the twelfth hour after the time at which it
is assented to.
If one returns to Clause 4, it states:
4. (1) The union and each officer and representative of the union
(a) shall, forthwith on the coming into force of this Act, give notice to the employees that, by reason of the coming into force of this Act, postal operations are forthwith to be continued or resumed-
When one reads Clause 4, one realizes that each and every member of the union, and each and every worker has to be notified by the union leadership and informed of the passage of this Bill. They have to be told that postal operations are to resume, and told to return to work. The Minister has agreed to this, and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Churchill has devised an amendment to correct this. He has also agreed that the 12 hour period is certainly too short for the mammoth task of reaching 23,000 card-carrying members across the country to give them the message. They are scattered all over the place, and the problem is all the greater since it seems that the coming into force of this legislation will happen over the weekend. We have negotiated with the Minister and the three Parties to find a solution and make this more reasonable.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Churchill, has done a lot of work on this. I think that he would be happy to claim paternity of the amendment. I am willing to let him have paternity if he agrees to let me have maternity, because I had something to do with the gestation of this baby. I do not know if my friend has a copy of the amendment with him, or if he wants to read it into the record. I think that I have given the rationale for the amendment, and I will leave the floor to my colleague who represents the riding of Churchill.

I thank the Hon. Member for that gracious introduction. I will move the motion:
That Bill C-86 be amended in Clause 13 by striking out lines 41 to 43 at
page 5 and substituting the following therefor:
"13. This Act shall come into force on the day immediately after the day on which this Act is assented to, but not before the twelfth hour after the time at which it is assented to.

Mr. Chairman it is not my intent to speak long on the amendment. It is obviously an amendment on which the two opposition Parties have come to agreement with the Government. It is one of the amendments which will allow the legislation to pass through the House of Commons today. We still do not believe that the legislation is good legislation. We made very evident tonight that we oppose it. There are many errors in the legislation and there is still a fundamental imbalance in it. In an attempt to get some amendments through the House to improve the legislation which the Government was willing to accept from the opposition Parties, I join my colleague in the Liberal Party in moving this amendment and in the other amendment we moved last night.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation
It is not my intention to speak on third reading. I will ask one of my other colleagues to do that. I would like to point out, however, that this House by passing legislation of this sort will leave a fundamental sense of unfairness not only among the people who work in our post offices but among a number of other people in society.
If people have heard some of the comments-I do not know whether they have been transferred by our electronic Hansard and through the media-by back-benchers who have never spoken in this House there will be a sense that this House does not treat all citizens equally. There is a basic contempt for some of our citizens by Members of this House of Commons.
I do not mean to lecture the House but I do believe that, when we are passing legislation about which so many Canadians feel strongly and which many Canadians believe offends and hurts them, this House and its Members should show more concern about how Canadians feel. I am not speaking about any individual clause in the Bill. We have done that as we went through it. I believe that the comments made by some Members of this House do offend the sensitivities of many Canadians and I do believe that was unnecessary and it will only create a further sense of unfairness.

Mr. Chairman, if I understood correctly, what is involved is the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) concerning the coming into reflect of the legislation. We had discussions on the matter, Mr. Speaker, and of course we feel it is a worthwhile amendment, so much so that it uses the terms that appeared in Bill C-85-we in agree on that amendment. I would take this opportunity, despite our differences-

Notwithstanding the differences of opinion that we may have had through this debate, in the Committee of the Whole in particular, Mr. Chairman, I still want to thank my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques, and the Hon. Member for Churchill. We had some discussions which perhaps did not please everybody involved but we had some serious discussions on the possible amendments. I thank them for their co-operation and I support this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of clarification for the Minister of Labour. I have obtained Hansard for November 17 and 18, 1986, regarding the point the Minister made earlier. When the Minister moved the amendment to Clause 13, it carried on division. There was not a recorded vote on that.
However, the remarks to which the Minister might have been referring appear on page 1265 of Hansard for November 18. They were in lock-out of the longshoremen. Referring to Bill C-24, this is what I had to say about that particular clause:
Let me deal with Clause 13, particularly Clause 13(2). The Minister moved quickly on the suggestion made in the speech by my friend, the Hon. Member
for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). He agreed in principle that what is being applied to union officers must be applied to corporate officers as well. 1 am sure that everyone involved would have preferred that Clause 13(2) simply be deleted. I find no comparable precedent in the last decade of legislation before the House that was solely directed against a union. That is why the criticism directed against Bill C-24 as it now stands is correct. It is clearly anti-union.
I refer the Minister as well to the Votes and Proceedings for November 17, 1986 at page 198. The Minister is recorded as being in favour of it and I am recorded as being against it.

-I think the Minister has agreed in principle that, although he will not take the clause out as it applies to unions, he is prepared to apply it evenly to corporations as well as the union. It is a saw-off. I would prefer to see Clause 13(2) dropped.

speakeroldname: The Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Labour) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-86, an Act to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services, be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, since last week we have been hearing many comments on the labour dispute and the legislation now before us. It is important in my view, at this stage, Mr. Speaker that we review the circumstances under which we introduced the Bill and that we put them into context.
October 15, 1987



We have been told that the Government acted prematurely, that we disrupted negotiations between the parties.
Let us review the record for a moment. The parties spent some four months in direct bargaining before notifying me of their dispute. I appointed a conciliation officer and the parties spent a further three months negotiating under his auspices. Because the dispute still remained unresolved I appointed a conciliation commissioner and the parties had another five months of third party assistance. When Commissioner Foisy's report and recommendations were released to them, both parties made encouraging noises that the stage was now set for meaningful negotiations. Their actions, however, did not demonstrate their intention to conduct such meaningful negotiations.
The assessment conducted by my Associate Deputy Minister informed me that the dispute could not be resolved through the collective bargaining process short of a lengthy test of economic strength. The Government was not prepared to sit by and watch the inevitable deterioration of the Canadian postal system while the parties engaged in their private battles. There were no negotiations going on and no prospect of such negotiations when the Government introduced this legislation. We had no intention of allowing a national emergency to develop while the parties implemented their respective strategic plans heedless of the effect on our postal system.
We have been accused of causing the escalation of an otherwise peaceful dispute. Every Member of this House is aware of the record of negotiations between these parties. The escalation of the dispute was inevitable as each side sought to enforce its will upon the other. It was precisely this escalation of violence that this legislation sought to avoid.

After reviewing the circumstances that obliged us to table this Bill, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the substance of the Bill. The concept of mediation-arbitration has provoked a lot of criticism, especially from those who do not fully understand the process. Mediation-arbitration combines the best elements of mediation and arbitration. When the process is used properly, we do not have a weaker form of arbitration but a fortified or stronger type of mediation.
Mr. Speaker, our Government maintains its belief that the best settlement is a negotiated settlement. Including a mediation-arbitration process in this legislation as a mechanism for resolving the conflict makes it possible for negotiations to continue. Mr. Speaker, although we cannot guarantee the parties will settle all their differences through negotiation, we do not want to deprive them of that opportunity. For the parties, mediation-arbitration maybe the only chance they will have to establish a new basis for constructive labour relations, and I urge them to take advantage of all the benefits they will be able to derive from this process.
Postal Services Continuation
We have been criticized for the penalty clauses provided in this Bill. I can only respond with surprise to this criticism because in November of last year, the Opposition passed these very same provisions with alacrity in the case of the West Coast longshore industry.
The record of the parties to this dispute is well known. While we expect that persons who hold responsible positions will act responsibly, we wish to give a very strong signal to anyone contemplating the fines in this case that they do so at their own risk. Personally, I hope that this penalty will never be used. Nevertheless, it is there if it is necessary.
I must repeat that it is never a pleasant task for a Minister of Labour to have to introduce back-to-work legislation. It is an admission that the collective bargaining system has failed. In the case of Canada Post and CUPW, the Government had no alternative but to move to this option of last resort if there is to be any hope of a future for our national postal system.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words to summarize the position we have held throughout this debate on Bill C-86. We have said from the moment this Bill was tabled that there was no national emergency warranting the use of such harsh legislation.
At the time the Bill was tabled and in the days preceding its tabling, there was little violence on the picket lines. The mail was moving and the mail is still moving, as a matter of fact. That is what the Government has claimed throughout this period.
We said that mediation would have been the right approach for the Government to have taken. We called for it, the workers called for it, but the Government refused. It chose to use a tougher approach.
The Minister has just repeated that at the time the legislation was tabled, there was no more negotiation between the parties, but the Minister fails to recognize that even before the legislation was tabled, 75 per cent of the clauses in the collective agreement had been agreed to by the parties. One cannot say that the bargaining process was not working.

I think it is clear and should be clear to everyone that the score of the strike expanded as soon as Bill C-86 was tabled. What had previously been a series of rotating strikes, never on the same day and never in the same location, moving across the country, has now become a national strike. Violence has started to surface, and there is more and more of it. I think we will have to realize that the Government is at least partly responsible for events that have occurred since the Bill was tabled. We have discussed the use of strike breakers several times since the beginning of the dispute.

October 15, 1987
Postal Services Continuation

The use of scabs had the expected results. When the unemployed are pitted against regular workers who are trying to protect their livelihoods, their daily bread, their regular jobs, it is very hard to expect that violence will not take place.
Now that the Government has acquired experience and practice in using scabs, replacement workers, on two occasions, may I suggest that the Government put this experience into practice by appointing replacement Tory Members of Parliament to replace those Members who were speechless during the entire debate. I make one exception. I must give the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) credit for rising in the House and at least reading a press release into the record. The rest of them were all watching, nodding and approving of the harsh, unusual penalties. Maybe what this country needs from now on is a herd of scab Tory MPs to represent the people of more than 200 ridings in Canada.
The Government has stuck to the hard line. Throughout this debate, the Minister has refused to amend Clause 10 which contains unusually harsh penalties and very heavy fines. He has refused to move on the five-year off-the-job penalty contained in the horrendous Clause 11. We think this is wrong. We think that this alone would be cause for us to vote against the legislation.

However, I must give the Minister credit for accepting two amendments from the Opposition, one to amend Clause 7 that will give the mediator-arbitrator a free hand and let him make his own decisions without considering the report by the conciliation-commissioner Foisy, which we think was not a fair report, and the Minister also deserves credit for accepting an amendment to Clause 13, which of course concerns the effective date of the Bill and will simplify the Union's task of reaching its 23,000 members. However, we still feel it is not enough, and I am sorry to say our Party will have to vote against the last stage of this Bill. My only hope is that when subsequent legislation is introduced in this House, the Government will have an opportunity to reflect on the inflexibility of the Bill before the House today, and 1 hope today's experience will not be repeated.

Mr. Speaker, before I address the legislation, I wish to say a few words of thanks on behalf, I am sure, of all Hon. Members, to those who help us do our jobs, the staff of the House of Commons, for aiding us this evening. I wish to thank the security staff, the Hansard reporters, all of the pages, the Clerks, the officers of the House, the console operators, the bus drivers and the television operators. On behalf of all Hon. Members, I would like to thank them for their efforts to make this session possible.
Hear, hear!

I will come directly to the legislation because I do not want to speak too long. There are, however, a few key points which must be made. The Government has presented the notion that if only the parties to the dispute had negotiated in a reasonable fashion and come to an agreement it would not have had to act, that it would have sat back and allowed the natural collective bargaining process to take place. Is it accurate to say that the Government has been at arm's length from these negotiations, that it has not been at the table? Let us examine in brief what has happened in these negotiations to see whether that stands up to any objective test of reality.
When the Government introduced the legislation which we are presently debating the result was to turn a series of rotating strikes, during which the mail was being delivered, into a national strike. By introducing its back-to-work legislation the Government provoked a national strike. How can it claim to be at arm's length when the introduction of this legislation provoked the national strike and, having driven the working people to the wall, provoked the violence which we have seen on television during the last few days, violence for which the Government has sought to blame the Opposition?
Before the Government brought in this legislation it threatened, day after day, to introduce back-to-work legislation. The impact of that was to remove the incentive of the management of the Post Office to negotiate. It told management to sit quietly on its duff and do nothing, that it would bring in legislation to impose an agreement that management wants because management is trying to impose the Government's plan. How can the Government say that it is at arm's length from the negotiations when its constant threats of back-to-work legislation prevented negotiations?
There is more, Mr. Speaker. Did the Government use all of the options at its disposal in order to keep the mails moving until a negotiated settlement was arrived at in order to have good labour relations at the Post Office? Not at all. One of the Government's crucial failures in this situation was a failure to use a mediator. It failed to have an objective third party sit at the table to facilitate communications and attempt to solve the problems in order to arrive at a negotiated settlement. The Government threw that option aside and in its place put a new two-headed monster called a mediator-arbitrator, a concept which was originally introduced by the Liberal Party when it was in Government. That concept destroyed the notion of mediation.
An oxymoron.

With regard to one of the key issues, the public policy with regard to franchising, the Government refused to be flexible. We are against the policy of franchising, not only because it threatens job security but because it also threatens service to the public. If the Government wanted to be pigheaded and continue with the policy, it did not need to be rigid. It
October 15, 1987

could have been flexible in order to arrive at a negotiated settlement.
During the negotiations the negotiator said categorically that he would not compromise on franchising. Taking that position on the cue of the Government he made a negotiated settlement impossible. How can the Government claim it was at arm's length from these negotiations?
Rather than being at arm's length it was the pupeteer pulling the strings on both sides of the table. It was ensuring that management was rigid and would not negotiate at the same time as provoking a national strike and promoting the violence which appeared on television. Rather than being at arm's length from the negotiation the Government was manipulating the situation. It was the pupeteer who led to this dispute.
The Government did that in order to impose its plan for the Post Office. Is that plan worth it? Its plan waters down the delivery dates of mail so that it will still take eight days to get mail across town. The Government's plan attacks rural service and the wages of women. It undermines the concept of bilingual service through the franchising out of postal service. It treats suburban residents in an arbitrary fashion by giving service to one street while a neighbouring street does not get home mail delivery.
The Government's claim that it was at arm's length and only intervened because the parties could not come to an agreement is hollow. We have made that case and it is evident to every Canadian who has been observing the negotiations that the Government was the pupeteer manipulating the situation. The Government created the false crisis in order to justify this legislation.
This legislation is unjustifiable. The Government should have been been preparing the climate for negotiations rather than seeking confrontation in order to justify bringing in back-to-work legislation.
Hear, hear!
